author: kauanpolydoro
body: Moves untrusted release payloads into a dedicated Actions-disabled inbox repository. The trusted publisher reads payloads by immutable SHA, retains cryptographic validation, and becomes idempotent if source cleanup is delayed. This removes every source-controlled write credential from the official Releases repository.\n\nValidation: 3 workflow contract tests; Ruff; actionlint; git diff --check.

author: doutorferr0
body:
Fecha a **#64** — o item 1 da #61, que a #61 separou de propósito porque a zona é outra (`problema.ts`).

> **A #63 MERGEOU** (`154c684`) e esta branch foi rebasada na `main` — agora ela tem dois commits: o `3e7aa93` desta issue e um `648f059` de sync, explicado abaixo. A #61 já foi fechada na mão.
>
> ~~**PR EMPILHADA na #63.** Ela traz a tabela de títulos para dentro deste repositório; sem a #63, este código não tem contra o que se medir. Os dois primeiros commits desta branch (`9819ad4`, `112f689`) são os da #63 e somem quando ela mergear — **mergear a #63 primeiro, depois rebasar esta na `main`.** O commit desta PR é o `5ea8a9f`.~~

## O commit a mais: `chore(contrato)` — o contrato andou de novo

Enquanto esta PR esperava, a **`cabinet-erp-web#271`** (`696c427`) mergeou e publicou o bloco 3 da aba `Principal` do cliente: `personType`, `identityDocument`, `identityIssuer`, `identityIssuerState`, `gender`, `birthDate`. O `check:contract` mede contra a `main` do front, então **esta PR ficaria vermelha por uma mudança que não é dela** — e a próxima também.

Só cópia e codegen (`38138f3270e2`). **Nenhum caminho novo e nenhum campo obrigatório**, medido antes de commitar: zero entradas e zero saídas na lista de paths, `required` intocado, os seis anuláveis em `PartnerDto` e `PartnerWriteRequest`. As três guardas seguem verdes sem código novo.

**Servir os campos é a `api#59`, que tem dono e implementação pronta** (`feat/parceiro-bloco3`, `efd0ef9`, ainda sem push). Está avisado na issue para NÃO rodar o sync lá: dois commits acrescentando as mesmas linhas é conflito à toa. Ela rebasa na `main` depois desta.

## O defeito

O contrato dá **um título canônico por `type`** (RFC 9457 §3.1.2, tabela do `ProblemType`), em PT-BR, porque a tela imprime o `title` como veio. O servidor mandava a frase do STATUS, em inglês, escolhida à mão no construtor de cada helper: `'Unauthorized'`, `'Forbidden'`, `'Bad Request'`, `'Not Found'`, `'Conflict'`, `'Not Implemented'` — mais um `'Error'` em `servidor.ts` para 4xx que não fosse 400, que não é frase de nada.

**`Conflict` em cima de sete conflitos** com saídas diferentes na tela devolve a informação que o status já deu: documento repetido oferece vincular, pedido já convertido oferece abrir o pedido, sem empresa ativa pede escolher empresa, e o operador lê o mesmo cabeçalho nos três.

## O conserto

**`ErroHttp` deixa de RECEBER o título e passa a derivá-lo do tipo.** Quem escolhe o tipo já disse tudo o que havia para escolher — passar os dois deixaria a mesma URN sair com dois cabeçalhos em dois caminhos, sem nada reprovando. `about:blank` cai na frase do status, que a mesma tabela escreve (`Requisição inválida` · `Não autenticado` · `Sem permissão` · `Não encontrado` · `Conflito` · `Erro interno`).

O construtor perdeu um parâmetro, então **o compilador achou os nove pontos**: seis helpers em `problema.ts` e três em `servidor.ts` (404 fora do contrato, 400 de validação do Fastify, 500).

**O balde, e ele foi medido, não suposto:** `415` é alcançável — `content-type: application/xml` numa rota do contrato (`text/plain` **não** serve para medir: Fastify tem parser para ele, e o pedido chega ao handler). O status não está na tabela, e agora sai `Requisição inválida` em vez de `'Error'`. Caso em `tests/http.test.ts`.

## A guarda é o ponto da PR

`TITULO_POR_TIPO` é uma **segunda cópia da tabela do contrato**, e cópia envelhece calada — é o defeito que a **#58** documentou no `CLAUDE.md` (o piso da prova negativa sobreviveu a cinco migrações valendo outro número). Então `tests/titulos-do-contrato.test.ts` **descobre a tabela no `contracts/openapi-v1.json`** e cobra cada linha achada, o mesmo padrão da `papeis.test.ts` e da `cobertura-do-contrato.test.ts`.

Duas camadas, e elas pegam coisas diferentes:

1. **`tsc`** — `Record<Exclude<TipoDeProblema, 'about:blank'>, string>` é exaustivo: URN nova em `TIPO` sem título **não compila**. Falsificado à mão: apagada a linha de `senha-fraca` → `TS2741: Property 'urn:cabinet:erro:senha-fraca' is missing`.
2. **A guarda** — o `tsc` não sabe qual é o TEXTO. Ela confere texto a texto contra o contrato, mais a linha do `about:blank` (as seis frases de status), mais `enum` sem linha na tabela.

A regra é função sobre dados, e os **três modos de reprovar são exercidos com tabelas de mentira**: título trocado → `pedido-ja-convertido: o servidor manda "Conflito", o contrato escreve "Pedido já gerado"`; URN inventada → `não tem linha na tabela do contrato`; linha apagada do contrato → nomeia a URN órfã. Piso de leitura (≥20 linhas) para a guarda não percorrer lista vazia se a expressão parar de casar — o defeito que a `procedencia.test.ts` documenta.

**`urn:cabinet:erro:resposta-nao-json` não é emitido por este servidor de propósito** (quem o sintetiza é o cliente, e o contrato diz isso). Agora é caso de teste: a diferença entre o `enum` e o que o servidor manda tem de ser **exatamente** essa URN — ausência declarada, não buraco.

## O tamanho real, medido antes

**Um** teste da bateria asseria título em inglês (`tests/http.test.ts:72`). O medo de "arrasta a bateria inteira", escrito na #61 e na #63, **não se confirmou** — está corrigido aqui e na issue #64.

## Para o hub

**O `detail` do Fastify continua em inglês** e não entrou nesta PR: `"Unsupported Media Type"` no 415, `"body must have required property 'email'"` no 400 de schema. É decisão ANTIGA e escrita em `servidor.ts` ("a mensagem dele é útil e não expõe nada"), tomada quando o `title` também era inglês — agora a resposta sai com cabeçalho em PT-BR e frase em inglês, o que é uma inconsistência nova. Traduzir mensagem de validação do Fastify é trabalho próprio (e talvez decisão de contrato: `fields[]` existe justamente para o erro por campo). **Não mexi porque `detail` é frase, não discriminador, e a issue era sobre o `title`.**

## Verde

`biome ci src tests scripts` (`.` reprova por `biome.json` de worktree alheia — ver #63) · `tsc --noEmit` · **555 testes, 29 arquivos** (544 + 10 da guarda + o 415).

author: chethanuk
body:
## Description

`ocr` treats every byte it reads as UTF-8. A GBK, GB18030, Big5, Shift-JIS, EUC-JP or EUC-KR source file is not, so `json.Marshal` of the prompt replaces each undecodable byte with U+FFFD and the model reviews replacement characters. Line resolution fails on top of that: `existing_code` matched against mojibake never finds the line the comment is about. Measured on a four-file fixture repo (ASCII, GBK, Big5, Shift-JIS), the marshalled review payload carried 60 U+FFFD before this change and 0 after.

`internal/textenc` detects a file's charset once and decodes it in memory. Nothing is written back, so `ocr` stays a read-only reviewer. Detection sits behind a `utf8.Valid` fast path, so a UTF-8 repo never reaches the detector at all and this cannot regress the encoding that already works; `TestDecodeUTF8RepoNeverDetects` asserts the call count is zero. The confidence gate is 90, measured rather than picked: across the fixture set every correct top-1 answer scored 100 and the highest wrong answer scored 68.

The charset-to-decoder mapping is a literal map, deny by default, rather than an `ianaindex` lookup. `ianaindex.IANA.Encoding("GB-18030")` returns `invalid encoding name`, and `GB-18030` is the exact label `chardet` emits for Simplified Chinese, so a name lookup resolves Big5, Shift_JIS, EUC-JP and EUC-KR fine and breaks on the one charset this issue is mostly about. There is a test row per label that fails if anyone swaps the map out later.

### Both sides of the diff

A diff carries two encodings whenever the commit changes one, which @bailu-ZZ raised on the issue. `-` lines are old bytes, `+` and context lines are new, and no single charset serves both. The decode is therefore decided per line, from the line's side: the frame already records each payload line's `+`/`-`/space prefix — a fact about the diff format rather than a guess about its bytes. New-side lines are decoded with the file's charset. Deleted lines are decoded only when they are not already valid UTF-8, since with no base ref their own bytes are the only evidence there is. Nothing here needs the base ref, which matters because the parser only ever has HEAD.

The file stays the detection evidence wherever it carries a signal. git runs with `-U3`, so a hunk with one short CJK comment scores below the gate while the whole file scores 100. Only when the new file is valid UTF-8, and therefore says nothing about the old side, do the non-UTF-8 deleted lines become the evidence.

Decoding a unified diff cannot be a `strings` pass over the whole text: `--- a/x` is a frame line outside a hunk and content inside one, and a `.sql` file's `-- 中文注释` is payload, not a header. `internal/diff/decode.go` splits each section using the same `inHunk` state the parser already tracks, decodes the payload, and rebuilds. If the decode moved the line count the section stays raw — a diff whose line count moved no longer describes the file. Conversion is all or nothing: one line that fails to convert marks the file and leaves both streams raw, so the model can never see one line decoded beside a raw neighbour.

### Detection has to be deterministic

`chardet.DetectBest` is not. `DetectAll` fans its recognizers across goroutines and finishes with `sort.Sort`, which is not stable, so results tied on confidence come back in completion order. Measured on 800 bytes where Shift_JIS, GB-18030 and Big5 all score 10: 200 calls in one process returned Shift_JIS 179 times, GB-18030 15 and Big5 6. The visible effect was `ocr scan --preview` reporting a different `detected_charset` for the same file between runs. This ships a `deterministicBest` that breaks ties on charset name.

### Files that cannot be decoded

A file whose bytes are past reviewing as text is excluded with `undecodable_encoding` and named on stdout with its detected charset. A file that is marked but still reviewed gets a warning on stderr instead. Marking and excluding are kept separate, because collapsing them regresses ordinary files — a UTF-8 Go file with one stray `0x92` detects as windows-1252 at confidence 57, and a 242-byte Latin-1 French file as ISO-8859-1 at 52. Both would be dropped from review entirely over a handful of bytes. Such a file is marked and still reviewed. Two things make it `Unreviewable`: a replacement-character density above 20%, or a NUL byte, which is what separates a legacy text file from a binary one. Measured across the fixture set, legitimate files land between 0.57% and 11.04% and genuine garbage between 37.41% and 100%, with nothing in between.

This is the one place behaviour changes for a file that is reviewed today: a file that is pure garbage now drops out of review instead of being reviewed as mojibake, and `undecodable_encoding` is a new value in the exclusion reasons that consumers of the JSON output can see. It is documented alongside the other reasons in `pages/src/content/docs/{en,ja,ru,zh}/{architecture,faq}.md`.

### Limitations

- A commit that converts between two legacy charsets, say Big5 to GB-18030, decodes the deleted lines with the new side's charset. These charsets accept each other's bytes and produce plausible CJK with no U+FFFD, so the guard in `Convert` cannot see it. Detecting the deleted lines separately does not rescue it either: under `-U3` they rarely carry enough evidence to clear the gate.
- A deleted line whose legacy bytes happen to be valid UTF-8 is carried through raw — for GB-18030 that needs every character to be lead `0xC2`-`0xDF` with trail `0x80`-`0xBF`. New-side lines are not exposed to this, because they are decoded from their side rather than their bytes.
- When only one or two short deleted lines are legacy, their union can score below the gate, and the file is then marked rather than decoded.
- `file_read` decodes files up to 2 MiB and streams anything larger with its bytes raw, unchanged from today. Detection needs whole-file evidence, and a head window is actively harmful: a file whose first non-ASCII line sits past the window collapses from confidence 100 to 55 and turns into a false skip.
- UTF-16 is detected by its BOM and decoded as a whole file, but not at the diff seam. git calls UTF-16 files binary, so they normally never reach the decoder; a repo that forces a text diff for them gets hunk lines split mid-code-unit by git, which cannot be decoded per line, and the file is excluded rather than guessed at.
- Single-byte charsets (ISO-8859-1, windows-1252) are not decoded. Their mojibake is mild, `chardet`'s single-byte scores are weak, and those files are marked and still reviewed, which is today's behaviour.

Two direct dependencies: `github.com/saintfish/chardet` (pure Go, no transitive deps) and `golang.org/x/text`, already in the module graph as indirect.

## Type of Change

- [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change that fixes an issue)

## How Has This Been Tested?

- [x] `make test` passes locally
- [x] Manual testing (describe below)

`make check`, `make test` (2042 tests, `-race`) and `make coverage` pass. Coverage is 91.4% against the 90% gate.

Tests are table-driven and grouped by the failure each pins: the charset map row by row, including the `GB-18030` row that fails if it becomes an `ianaindex` lookup; the detector asserted at zero calls for valid UTF-8; diff headers, prefixes and line counts byte-identical after decode, with `TestDecodePayloadLinesThatLookLikeHeaders` covering the `-- 中文注释` case; comments resolving to the correct line through decoded Chinese; the mark-versus-exclude boundary; review and scan agreeing on the same file byte for byte; `file_read` and `code_search` returning the same UTF-8 as the review path; and `TestParseDiffTextNeverWritesToTheWorkingTree` for the read-only guarantee. Each encoding-change direction has its own row, and `TestDecodeSameEncodingBothSidesUnchanged` compares GBK output byte-for-byte against the same repo committed in UTF-8.

I ran mutation testing over every line this PR adds to non-test source: 73

author: babs
body:
Adds `crane` (google/go-containerregistry) to `ghcr.io/babs/kaniko-w-ecr-repo-creator`.

## Why

The GitLab CI component's branch-build reuse feature needs crane to read and rewrite image config blobs. Without it, the feature silently degrades to a full rebuild — no error, no warning, just a log line indistinguishable from a legitimate cache miss.

## Source

Copied from `ghcr.io/babs/oci-toolbox:1` rather than upstream go-containerregistry. Deliberate choice to reuse the in-house toolbox, with the trade-off accepted: it couples this image to oci-toolbox (which is itself built with this image) and follows a floating `:1` tag, so the crane version can drift between rebuilds.

## Verified locally

Image builds; crane resolves and runs, and the pre-existing tooling is unaffected:

| Tool | Result |
|---|---|
| `crane version` | `v0.20.7-0.20251028202801-aab7c77e9d78` |
| `jq --version` | `jq-1.8.2` |
| `envsubst` | substitution confirmed (not a passthrough) |
| `ecr-repo-creator --help` | `v1.6.0` + usage |
| `/kaniko/executor version` | `v1.27.5` |
| `docker-credential-ecr-login` | present, resolves |

Note: `oci-toolbox:1` resolved from the local Docker cache during this build, so a remote-side change to that floating tag would not have been picked up — inherent to the `:1` choice above.

## After merge

1. Cut a new semver tag — `release.yml` only publishes on semver tags, so merging alone ships nothing.
2. Bump the consuming component's `kaniko_version` input default to that tag. Until then, consumers still pull the crane-less `1.6.0`.

body:
## Tóm tắt

Thiết kế lại trang đăng nhập cho chuyên nghiệp hơn, theo tinh thần thương hiệu **HCRC Workspace** (đã được duyệt trước qua demo 2 phương án — chọn Phương án A).

- Chia đôi màn hình: bên trái là panel thương hiệu (nền navy, logo H, slogan, 4 module nổi bật — Văn bản & Hợp đồng / Quy trình phê duyệt / Lịch họp & Công việc / Báo cáo định kỳ), bên phải là form đăng nhập trên nền trắng.
- Trên màn hình nhỏ (< 880px), 2 panel xếp chồng dọc thay vì chia cột.
- Dùng lại đúng bảng màu/logo đã có sẵn ở sidebar (SVG chữ "H", xanh navy/blue) và font "Be Vietnam Pro" toàn app — không thêm yếu tố thương hiệu mới.
- Thêm submit bằng phím Enter (trước đây form không có `<form>` bao ngoài nên chỉ bấm nút mới đăng nhập được).

## Chi tiết kỹ thuật

- Toàn bộ `id`/hàm JS gốc (`#loginSection`, `#txtUser`, `#txtPass`, `#btnLogin`, `login()`, `finishLogin()`, `logout()`) **giữ nguyên** — chỉ thay khung HTML/CSS bên trong `#loginSection`, không đổi logic đăng nhập.
- Thêm khối CSS mới, tiền tố `loginpage-` để không đụng class nào khác trong file.
- Thêm `#loginSection.hidden { display: none !important; }`: trang hiện tại phụ thuộc Tailwind CDN (Play CDN) tự gắn `!important` cho `.hidden` để thắng `display:grid` của `#loginSection` — thêm rule riêng để việc ẩn form sau khi đăng nhập không phụ thuộc vào hành vi ngầm định của CDN bên thứ ba (phát hiện được khi verify bằng một bản dựng Tailwind khác, xem phần Kiểm tra bên dưới).

## Kiểm tra

- `node --check` tương đương cho toàn bộ script inline trong `index.html`: OK.
- Quét trùng `id`: không phát sinh trùng `id` mới (1 cặp trùng `systemUsersDatalist` đã tồn tại từ trước, không liên quan thay đổi này).
- Cân bằng thẻ `<div>`: 1195 mở / 1195 đóng — khớp.
- Playwright demo trên bản build thật của `index.html` (mock `/api/auth/login`, `/api/data`, `/api/auth/me`, dùng engine Tailwind thật để bản chụp phản ánh đúng CSS thật):
  - Trang đăng nhập hiển thị đúng thiết kế chia đôi màn hình, cả desktop và mobile.
  - Đăng nhập qua nút bấm **và** qua phím Enter đều chuyển màn hình đúng (`#loginSection` ẩn, `#userHeader` hiện, tên người dùng hiển thị đúng).
  - Sau khi thêm `#loginSection.hidden { display: none !important }`: xác nhận form đăng nhập ẩn hoàn toàn sau khi đăng nhập, không còn phụ thuộc `!important` ngầm định từ Tailwind CDN.

## Ảnh chụp demo

Đã gửi ảnh chụp desktop/mobile (trước đăng nhập) và sau đăng nhập cho người dùng xác nhận trước khi tạo PR.

author: georgeflerovsky
body:
Five commits off `main`, eighteen files. Everything a node needs to survive a long run under load:
two defects that kill it, defaults that decide how long it takes to come back, and the format that
decides how large it gets. Kept as one PR because three of the five are config changes and there is
no sense running CI four times for them; the commits stay separate so any one can be reverted alone.

| | commit | changes behaviour? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `fix(codecs)` — never encode through scalus's thread-unsafe hex cache | fixes a crash |
| 2 | `fix(remote-l2)` — give a Restore room for a rebuild that grows with uptime | fixes a failure to start |
| 3 | `config(rocksdb)` — bound store open time, with real defaults | **yes** |
| 4 | `config(consensus)` — batch, soft-block and hard-stack defaults | **yes** |
| 5 | `perf(persistence)` — Request journal as a canonical protobuf record | **yes — needs fresh stores** |

---

## 1. Encoding a `ByteString` races on scalus's hex cache

`ByteString.toHex` is a `@threadUnsafe lazy val` (scalus 1.0.0, `ByteString.scala:45`): an
unsynchronised, non-volatile cache. That annotation is scalus saying there is no publication
guarantee — a thread reading the field while another writes it can observe `null`.

We do exactly that. One `UserRequestWithId` is fanned out to the peer liaisons and the coil relay at
once, so several actors encode the same `ByteString` on different threads of a work-stealing pool.
The loser reads `null`, `Json.fromString` throws, the encoding actor dies, and consensus goes with
it: block production stops while admission stays up and sheds everything arriving. Roughly one
saturated run in five.

The fix computes hex through scodec's `ByteVector`, which is thread-local, at one allocation per
encode — the pattern the encoders in this file that were already correct follow. **Five sites, not
one**: whether a fan-out can reach a given one *today* is not the criterion, since the annotation
makes them all unsafe and the fix is the same shape and cost at each.

## 2. `restoreTimeout` was about two minutes from expiring in production

A remote ledger answers a `Restore` by replaying its **whole** event log — there is no snapshot — so
the bound has to exceed a full rebuild, and a rebuild grows linearly with uptime. Measured on the
production box: **~8 minutes over ~42M events, growing 2–3 minutes per day**. The default was 10.

An expiry is terminal, not slow: `restoreTo` is deliberately not retried (a retry restarts the
rebuild) and every boot calls it, so the node does not recover late — it fails to start, and stays
failed, with the margin shrinking daily. Raised to 60 minutes as a stopgap; the real fix is a ledger
snapshot, which makes the rebuild bounded instead of linear.

## 3. ★ Store open time — now with defaults that do something

A node on the box took **18 minutes** to open its store, and the RocksDB `LOG` dates every phase:

| | |
|---|---|
| manifest read | 12:33:21.699 |
| first `Recovering log #286` | 12:33:21.710 — **+11 ms** |
| last `Recovering log #1224` | 12:51:35.767 |
| `DB pointer` returned | 12:51:39.108 |

Table-handler preload — the one open cost that grows with the store — was those **11 ms**.
Essentially all 1,097 s was **WAL replay**: 470 files, ~30 GB, at an effective 27 MB/s on a volume
that does 137.

So `maxTotalWalSize` is the setting that matters, and `0` is a bad default because it does not mean
"unbounded" — it means *derived*, as `Σ_CF(writeBufferSize × maxWriteBufferNumber) × 4`. The measured
store had 31 column families at the stock 64 MiB × 2, deriving a ceiling near 16 GB. Nothing in a
slow start names a setting as its cause.

| variable | was | **now** |
|---|---|---|
| `HYDROZOA_ROCKSDB_MAX_TOTAL_WAL_BYTES` | `0` (derived, ~16 GB) | **2 GiB** |
| `HYDROZOA_ROCKSDB_SKIP_STATS_UPDATE_ON_OPEN` | `false` | **`true`** |
| `HYDROZOA_ROCKSDB_AVOID_BLOCKING_IO` | `false` | **`true`** |
| `HYDROZOA_ROCKSDB_SKIP_SST_SIZE_CHECK_ON_OPEN` | `false` | `false` — deliberately |

**Why 2 GiB.** It is roughly **one full write buffer per column family** (31 × 64 MiB ≈ 1.94 GiB).
Below that the cap starts forcing partially-full memtables out on families being written normally,
trading replay time for write amplification. At or above it, the cap only bites the pathology it is
meant to catch: a rarely-written family pinning every WAL segment it has a write in — which is every
segment. At the replay rate above, that is a **~80-second ceiling on WAL recovery** where there was
an 18-minute floor.

It bounds **future** growth only. A WAL already on disk is still replayed once, so this shrinks the
*next* open, not the one that adopts it.

**Why one is deliberately left off.** `skipCheckingSstFileSizesOnDbOpen` is not like the other two.
They skip bookkeeping — table properties that reseed as compaction runs, and obsolete-file deletion
that moves to a background job. This one skips *verifying that each SST is the size the manifest
claims*, which is how a truncated file is caught at open instead of at the read that needs it. Its
saving is a `stat` per file, against a WAL replay that dominates the open by orders of magnitude.
There is nothing to buy with it.

## 4. Consensus defaults

Changed in **both** places that carry them — the scaffold template a new deployment writes into its
private config, and the Scala fallback used when a field is absent. Them disagreeing later is the
failure mode worth avoiding. None of the values is new; all three are what the load-test runs have
used while the deployed head ran stock.

**`peerLiaisonMaxRequestsPerBatch` 42 → 500.** The mesh-consensus batch size, governing admission
headroom: the head sheds via backpressure while nothing is saturated — CPU, disk and memory all idle
at the point it starts refusing — so where it sheds is set by config, not hardware. Straight about
the evidence: **which of the four headroom knobs dominates was never bisected**, so this is the prime
suspect, not a measured winner. 42 was a joke, not a measurement.

**`softBlockMinPeriod` 250 ms → 100 ms — not for throughput.** It was measured *not* to be the
limiter, twice: a block's lead time is N serial WS round-trips to the L2 ledger, so cadence does not
move the ceiling, and a sweep that lowered this on the box did not raise it. It is changed for
**latency** — the floor is a minimum gap between soft-confirmation forwards, so below saturation it
is straightforwardly how long a user waits to see their request confirmed, and a public run spends
most of its time below saturation.

**`hardStackMinPeriod` 3 minutes → 30 seconds.** Hard confirmation for a stack is held until its
`creationEndTime` plus this period, so it is the floor on how often the head closes a stack — the
dominant term in how long a user waits for hard confirmation. Three minutes was a sensible rate
limit for a head nobody was waiting on.

**It does not multiply settlement transactions or their fees.** Stacks are partitioned head-based
and a settlement belongs to a `Major` partition, so settlements track **major blocks** — driven by
L1 work, deposits and withdrawals — not by how often a stack closes. Closing stacks more often
spreads the same majors across more stacks.

What it does multiply is **SECs**. A minor-containing partition emits exactly one standalone
evacuation commitment, for its *latest* minor; the earlier minors in that run are superseded by it.
Shorter stacks mean shorter minor runs, so fewer minors are folded under each commitment and more
commitments are produced. A SEC is **not an L1 transaction** — it commits a block header and takes a
synthetic `l1TxId` — so the cost is per-peer header signatures, their aggregation and the storage,
not L1 fees. More stacks also means proportionally more slow-consensus rounds.

Also: the `RateLimits` scaladoc claimed the defaults were zero and these lanes go unlimited unless
configured. They were 250 ms and 3 minutes; the doc predates them.

author: stephane-segning
body:
## Summary

`adr/0004-avif-measurement.md` is cited by three comments in `src/services/image/handler.rs` (lines 59, 65, 827) and **has never existed** — confirmed with `git log --all --diff-filter=A -- 'adr/0004*'` (empty). An agent claimed to have written it during wave-2 development; it was never committed, so the AVIF figures those comments rest on had no recorded method.

Source of truth: #49 (AVIF), `adr/0003-webp-measurement.md` (method).

This writes the ADR by taking the measurement properly.

## Intent

The figures were being quoted as fact — in PR #74's description and in issue comments — with no reproducible provenance. That matters more here than it normally would, because this project has already retracted **two** format-size claims that turned out to be measurement artefacts:

- `adr/0001` claimed AVIF at 0.42–0.79× (unreliable method)
- an early WebP measurement claimed 0.96×, i.e. no benefit at all — wrong, caused by a synthetic random-noise fixture and unmatched quality scales. The correct answer, 14–16% smaller, is in `adr/0003`.

An unverified third number in the same family should not stand.

## Verification

Two independent measurements were taken, by separate agents, and this branch carries both commits so the lineage is visible:

- `a4788e4` re-ran a scratch harness left behind by the wave-2 session, after reading it line by line and confirming the 24 Kodak PNGs were genuine.
- `ed9abbc` **discarded that lineage entirely** — fresh Kodak download, newly authored harness depending on `emgr` as a path dependency so it calls this crate's own `ImageService::encode_webp` and the same `JpegEncoder::new_with_quality` / `AvifEncoder::new_with_speed_quality` calls `handler.rs` uses.

They agree within run-to-run noise (0.7241 vs 0.7347 avif/jpeg; 0.8753 vs 0.8733 avif/webp), which is the strongest evidence available that neither is an artefact.

Method follows `adr/0003` exactly: DSSIM-matched quality on the real Kodak True Color corpus, not equal nominal quality and not synthetic fixtures.

| Claim | Measured (n=24) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| AVIF/JPEG 0.73× | median **0.7241**, mean 0.7091 | **Confirmed** — within 0.01 |
| AVIF/WebP 0.87× | median **0.8753**, mean 0.8589 | **Confirmed** — within 0.005 |
| AVIF encode ~335 ms | median **367.8 ms**, mean **457.5 ms**, range **261–986 ms** | **Partially confirmed** |

**The size claims hold. The encode-time claim does not, in a way that matters operationally.** The median is close, but the mean runs 36% above the cited figure and per-image cost varies nearly 4× with content — `kodim14` takes 986 ms. A single "~335 ms" understates the worst case by almost 3×, which is the number that matters when sizing the CPU concurrency bound (#30) and single-flight coalescing (#37).

It also reproduces the trap for parallelism with `adr/0003`: naive q75-vs-q75 gives 0.52×, a far larger apparent win, because AVIF at nominal q75 scores **1.81× worse DSSIM** than JPEG at q75. It is not smaller at equal quality — it is smaller at worse quality. That is the same mechanism behind both prior retractions, now documented for a third format.

`bench-imgproxy/fixtures/generate.py` was checked and rejected as a corpus: despite filenames like `photo_4k.jpg`, it builds them from the same synthetic `gradient_noise_rgb` generator `adr/0003` already showed gives wrong answers.

## Risk Assessment

- Documentation only. No source file touched; `cargo check`/`cargo test --features local_fs` run as a precaution and clean.
- The three code comments were left unchanged — they reference the ADR generically without embedding numeric claims, so nothing in them is contradicted.
- **Caveat recorded rather than hidden:** the harness's WebP reference uses `webp::Encoder::from_rgb` while production's `encode_webp` uses `from_rgba` (needed for grayscale). That discrepancy is inherited from `adr/0003`, not introduced here, and should not move the ratio for opaque photos — but it is now written down instead of being an unexamined difference between measurement and shipped code.
- AVIF decode was needed only to score DSSIM against the source; it required `image`'s `avif-native` (dav1d) feature **in the throwaway harness only**, never proposed for `emgr`.

## Reviewer Focus

1. The encode-time spread (261–986 ms) and whether `.auto` negotiation staying per-URL opt-in is a strong enough guard given a ~1 s worst case.
2. Whether recording both measurement commits, rather than squashing to the final one, is the right call — it documents that the first reused inherited work and the second did not.

## AI Usage Declaration

AI (Claude Opus 5 orchestrating Sonnet sub-agents) took both measurements and drafted the ADR. The orchestrator independently confirmed the file's absence from all of git history before commissioning the work, and confirmed the committed artefact exists afterward. The duplicate measurement was accidental — a stalled agent was relaunched and both completed — but the agreement between two independent runs is reported as evidence rather than discarded.

- [x] A human is accountable for this change.
- [x] Numbers come from runs whose method and corpus are documented and reproducible.
- [x] The one claim that did **not** fully hold is stated as such rather than rounded to agreement.

They download a hardcoded allowlist into a temp bundle, then run `scripts/install-superliora.mjs`. `source.mjs` statically imports `checkout-health.mjs`, and that file exists on main, but both allowlists omitted it. No package.json / latest / latest.json bump. No TUI changes. ## Checklist - [x] I have reviewed the repository contribution notes. - [x] I have linked a related issue, or explained the problem above. - [x] I have added tests that prove my feature works. - [x] Ran `gen-changesets` skill, or this PR needs no changeset. - [x] Ran `gen-docs` skill, or this PR needs no doc update. Previously the allowlists omitted it while `source.mjs` imported it, causing ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND after the Node 24.15.0 download. - Adds `checkout-health.mjs` to `install.ps1` `$InstallModules` and the `install.sh` bootstrap loop. - Adds a test that parses both allowlists and walks static imports from `scripts/install-superliora.mjs` and `scripts/install/source.mjs` to ensure all `scripts/install/*.mjs` dependencies are fetched; updates assertions to avoid mutating sort for `oxlint` and fixes regex capture group typing for TypeScript; extends the existing test to assert the new module is included. - No changeset or package bumps; no TUI changes. author: justinlooney
body:
Closes #87. Refs #86 — the second of the award track.

87 MB of assets and not one second of audio, while the writing kept promising otherwise. Amara sends you to the chapel bells at dusk **twice**. MATH 201 §1.1 teaches functions with *"the chapel bell rings once per hour struck: the number of chimes is a function of the hour"* — a worked example about a sound the campus could not make.

## One deliberate departure from the issue

#87 budgets **1.5 MB of Opus, streamed**. This ships **zero bytes**. Every note is synthesised: a struck bell is inharmonic partials with per-partial decay, and wind, insects, footsteps and falling water are all shaped noise, so the whole soundtrack is arithmetic.

That serves the budget's *actual* intent — don't undo #73 — better than any file could, needs no licence and no `CREDITS.md` entry, and suits a repo with no build step. Flagging it because it's a substitution, not a shortcut.

## The bell

Not a note. Six partials, each decaying at its own rate, the high ones first — the hum an octave under the strike, the strike, the minor third that gives a bell its ache, the fifth, and the clang that's gone almost at once.

Rendered through an `OfflineAudioContext` and measured rather than admired:

```
rms       0.420 attack  →  0.045 at 1s  →  0.0000 at 4.5s
bright    310 zero-crossings/s early  →  193 late
```

That darkening is what makes it read as metal rather than a sine with a sad face.

`bell(hour)` strikes `((h % 12) || 12)` times — **13 rings once, midnight rings twelve** — so §1.1's example is now true of the campus it's taught on. It rings on the turn of the hour and never on arrival, because a bell that greets you is a doorbell.

## Footsteps know what they're standing on

From the geometry, not a guess. Every walkway already published its polyline and width to `window.__walks` as an audit hook, so this is a point-to-segment test against the real paths — all 21 of them. Paving is a brighter, shorter burst than turf.

It stays true when a path moves, which is exactly the failure the comment above `walkway()` describes being re-derived by hand every time somebody breaks it. The hook was built for tests and turned out to be the right runtime answer too.

## The rest

- **The fountain is positioned** — a `PannerNode` at campus (474, 474), listener travelling with the walker, so it's *somewhere* rather than everywhere.
- **Day and night are different rooms** — the bed opens out by day, closes down after dark and the insects come up, driven off the `setVisualBinary` switch that already existed.
- **Nothing is built before a gesture.** A context created earlier is born suspended and stays that way. The choice persists; a remembered *yes* still waits to be asked again next visit. Autoplay policy, and manners.

## Not done, named rather than quietly counted

**Birdsong.** #87 asks for it in the day bed. Procedural chirps sound like a bad ringtone, so there are none — the day bed is wind and air. That's a real gap against the issue.

## The ninth job

`tools/check-sound.mjs`, 10 checks. Nothing in it listens, because a runner has no speakers: it renders the bell offline and measures the samples, and asks the live page what its graph is doing. Against `main` it fails with *"the campus is up but exposes no sound module"* — a different sentence from *"the campus did not ignite"* on purpose.

The two checks that matter most aren't about sound at all: nothing is built before a gesture, and a remembered yes still waits to be asked again.

**One note on testing user activation.** The probe clicks with `force: true`. Hovering the button starts a 300 ms transform transition, and on a software rasterizer at 1–3 fps Playwright's stability check sees a different bounding box every time it looks. `force` skips the actionability **wait**, not the input — it's still a trusted click, and a trusted click is the only kind that counts as user activation, which is the entire subject of two of these checks. A scripted `el.click()` would have passed the click and failed the point.

## Verification

Local: `worker` ✅ · `css` ✅ · `sound` ✅ 10 checks · `cache-version` guard ✅, with `opening`, `owner`, `ledger`, `a11y` and the full smoke drive running.

## What's left in #86

**#89** (commit to a visual identity) and **#90** (motion design). #89 is the 40%-weighted one and the root of the epic's first finding — *"art direction is a genre, not a voice."*

body:
## Summary

Integrates 45 commits from `gitlab/master` (upstream Veloren) into `development`, per the `gitlab-master-merger` skill. Human review required before merging.

## Conflict resolution — the one real cluster

Nearly everything auto-merged cleanly (turn-rate/energy-threshold fixes, a clippy-lint-driven style pass, two new unrelated features — `battlemode_change` areas and a `particle_chance` graphics setting — and routine i18n/content housekeeping). One real, coherent cluster needed manual resolution:

**`CharacterItem.location` generalized from `Option<String>` to `Option<Location>`**, migrating the character-select screen's location display onto the localized `Content` type. Spans `common/src/character.rs`, `server/src/persistence/{character/mod.rs,mod.rs,character_loader.rs}`, `server/src/lib.rs` (`parse_locations` → `get_location_names`), `common/net/src/msg/server.rs`, `client/src/lib.rs`, `voxygen/src/menu/char_selection/ui.rs`, `voxygen/src/hud/diary.rs`. None of it touches anything we designed on purpose — it's a legitimate upstream i18n improvement landing adjacent to our own additions (pact/class list-view defaults, a spell-book-skip comment, our own `resolve_waypoint_site_name` helper). Resolved by taking upstream's refactor and re-threading our own additions around it; kept `resolve_waypoint_site_name` (restoring its `persistence::parse_waypoint` dependency under the new conversion function) since a caller reading persistence for a disconnected player still needs it.

Also fixed for consistency, not a conflict: our own new `GroundAoe` particle effect (added independently of this sync) now goes through the new `particles_chance` throttle every other particle spawn in that file uses.

Also updated the `gitlab-master-merger` skill itself (2 commits, already reviewed/merged separately as PR #207 and folded in here): added a missing step to re-run `tools/xindeler-rename.sh` post-merge, and dropped a stale `asset_tweak` feature reference from its documented clippy command.

Also fetched and re-hosted the one new LFS binary this sync brings (`assets/world/structure/natural/troll_cave.vox`, 174 KB) from gitlab.com's LFS store to our own VPS.

## Xindeler customizations: preserved ✅

Confirmed zero diff (this sync didn't touch them) on `common/src/comp/attunement.rs`, `server/src/sys/attunement.rs`, `common/src/combat.rs`, `common/src/comp/ability.rs`. `common/src/comp/inventory/mod.rs` picked up one small, unrelated cosmetic clippy-driven refactor (a match-guard → if/else conversion), evaluated and confirmed safe.

author: tavakohr
body:
## The defect class

The leaf grammar finds a condition inside an operand, then asks one question
about whatever text is left over: **does it state a condition of its own?** If
not, the leftover was prose and was discarded.

That is the wrong question on its own. Text can decide what a condition
**means** without stating one, and two kinds do.

**A negating word inverts it.**

```
ADSL.USUBJID with no ADCM record where ADCM.CMATC3CD in ('D07AA','D07AB','D11AH')
  read as ->  CMATC3CD IN ('D07AA','D07AB','D11AH')
```

A row labelled *"Did not receive any TCS or TCI"* selected exactly the subjects
who did. Worse than computing nothing: it computes something, and it looks
right.

**A qualified reference in front of the condition scopes it.**

```
ADSL.USUBJID with an ADCM record where A AND with an ADCM record where B
  read as ->  AND(A, B)          -- row-wise, one record satisfying both
```

The authored question is per-subject over two records; the read one asks for a
single record satisfying both. Different sets of subjects — and it is the exact
counterexample `.where_restriction_plan()` is built around (`T1` in
`test-where_restriction_plan.R`).

## Why now

These misreadings exist on `main` today but are not executed: a compound
cannot be carried into a row `DataSubset`, so the row reserves *for an
unrelated reason*. The next PR removes that accidental barrier. This one must
land first, or the carrier starts executing wrong filters.

## The invariant

An operand is accepted only when the text around the recognised leaf leaves
its meaning intact. Negation anywhere, or a qualified reference scoping it
from the front, means the operand was not fully read — and an operand that was
not fully read reserves.

**Position decides**, which is what keeps the rule narrow. The forms this
grammar has always read go on reading:

| form | still reads |
|---|---|
| `HEAD; <filter>` — a semicolon ends the head | yes |
| `A='Y'; label DS.VAR` — a note after a complete condition | yes |
| `A GT 0 (per protocol)` — a descriptive suffix | yes |
| `A='NOT REPORTED'` — literals are masked first | yes |
| `A='ADZZ.ZZFL'` — a value that spells a reference | yes |

## Accepted false positive

`count of ADEFF.USUBJID with ADEFF.ANL01FL='Y'` states a *statistic* in front
of a genuine filter, and now reserves. Distinguishing it from the existential
form needs a positive grammar for head directives, not an exception carved out
of this guard — narrowing here would reopen the hole. One row waits for that
grammar; two demonstrably wrong filters stop shipping.

## Evidence

**Tests** — `test-residue_meaning.R`, two invented vocabularies, no fixture
identifiers: negation-only cases (isolated so the prefix rule cannot be what
catches them), the authored shape, the two-existential trap, a scoping prefix
on a single condition, all five still-accepted forms, values containing
negating words and reference-shaped text, plus a scope assertion so a grammar
change turns the accepted-form section red rather than vacuously green.

**Suite** — 9425 pass / 0 fail / 0 error / 4 skip. **Goldens** — 24/24, all
three unchanged.

**Mutations** — via the new `tools/mutation_harness.R`:

| mutation | verdict | caught by |
|---|---|---|
| drop the negation rule | detected, 12 failures / 0 errors | `A1`, `A2` |
| drop the scoping-prefix rule | detected, 4 / 0 | `B1`, `B2` |
| drop the semicolon boundary | detected, 4 / 0 | `C1`, `D`, and the pre-existing `a genuine row filter is still a row filter` |

**Real study (APX-DRM-301)** — analysis IDs, output membership, ordering,
layout kinds, method IDs and variable roles are all **identical to `main`**
by diff. 128 analyses both sides. The only differences are three
`flat -> reserved` transitions, each one a filter `main` was computing
incorrectly:

- `AN_T_14_1_4_006` *"Did not receive any TCS or TCI"* — was selecting the complement
- `AN_T_14_2_1_008` *"Difference in response rate"* — was scoping a between-arm difference to one arm
- `AN_T_14_2_1_003` *"Number evaluable, N'"* — the accepted false positive above

CDSC-ALZ-201 is unchanged through both readers.

## The harness

`tools/mutation_harness.R` exists because a mutation run went wrong here: an
inline mutation table lost its escaping, every anchor silently missed, every
mutant ran an **unmutated** source, and the run reported `0 failures` for all
of them — which reads as *"the tests do not catch this"*, the direction that
costs you a real gap. The harness now refuses verdicts it cannot stand behind:
a mutation that does not alter the file is **unapplied**, not undetected; only
assertion failures count as detection (an errored mutant is unresolved,
because something blew up before a claim could be compared); and every restore
is proven byte-for-byte in `finally`.

author: jallum
body:
## Why

The Foreman's reconciliation rule (`do_reconcile_workers`) answered a membership question on the workers' behalf: on every layout push it decided which hosted workers to retire. FDB has **no** component that decides another process's retirement — every role self-detects displacement and throws `worker_removed` on itself: TLogs compute `isDisplaced` against ServerDBInfo (`rejoinClusterController`, TLogServer.actor.cpp), storage servers validate their rejoin against a commit proxy's txnStateStore (absence = `worker_removed`). The hosting process only observes the exit and deletes files.

Course item B, first half (bedrock-q67.38, settled 2026-08-20 after FDB source check). Depends on #178 (the seed had to stop carrying `transaction_services` first).

## What

- **Foreman**: keeps its push-relay role (one per node — the natural distribution point from the cluster push to the workers it hosts) and gains a janitor cast: `worker_retired` disposes the directory, registration, and entry of a worker that decided its own retirement (`:transient` restart keeps a deliberate shutdown down). `do_reconcile_workers` / `workers_to_retire` are **deleted** — the Foreman never answers a membership question again.
- **Shale (log worker)**: log topology is epoch-constant, so the pushed log set IS the membership authority. On each relayed push: displaced iff the layout's epoch progressed past ours AND its log set omits us. The epoch guard keeps absence during an in-flight recovery from being a death sentence; a never-locked cold-boot resurrection is judged by any completed layout.
- **Olivine (materializer)**: membership lives in the committed keyspace (`materializers/<tag>`), not the wiring push — so rejoin validation is one tag-keyed ask to a pushed commit proxy: new `CommitProxy.resolve_materializer/3`, answered from `RoutingData` (the serverList analogue) under the same cadence rule as `fetch_routing`. Absence or another worker's id is an authoritative verdict; `:locked`/`:unavailable`/`:timeout` are not — the next push revalidates.

## How

- `Foreman.Impl.do_relay_tsl/2` sends `{:tsl_updated, tsl}` to every running hosted worker; `do_worker_retired/2` reuses the existing removal path (terminate-if-alive → deregister → rm -rf).
- `RoutingData.resolve_materializer/2` is a tag lookup in the same routing view that serves clients — one authority, two readers.
- Worker verdicts are handler-level and unit-tested as such: `shale/displacement_test.exs` (epoch-progression guard matrix) and `olivine/displacement_test.exs` (verdict vs non-verdict matrix, stub proxy).

Deferred to q67.21 (recorded on the ticket): in-band privatized-mutation delivery for mid-epoch removals — do not build the private-mutation path before removals exist. `services` leaving the TSL is the second half of q67.38, next PR in the stack.

Full suite (2582 tests), credo --strict, dialyzer green.

body:
Three fields the game's own item defs carry that this library was dropping. All three are plain reads off the def - no enrichment, no new tables.

**`Classes`** — the classes allowed to equip an item, or null for the ones that stay class-neutral by leaving the key out. Several items name more than one, and `fury` names four whose main stats disagree, so this is a list rather than a single class.

**`Explanation`** — the line the game writes under an item's name ("Rains fire upon the enemy"). 241 of the 529 items carry one. It is the game's prose about the item: nothing parses it, and an effect it describes is implemented elsewhere or not at all. The doc comment says so, so nobody reads figures out of it.

**`Ability`** — the named effect an item grants while worn (`burn`, `freeze`, `secondchance`, `restore_mp`). Thirty items carry one.

The ability doc comment is deliberately about the mechanism rather than the effects. Equipping files the item's own `attr0`/`attr1` under that name on the player (`node/server.js:1230`), summed across every worn piece naming it, and each ability's rule is then implemented separately wherever combat reads it by name — burn rolls `attr0` as a percentage per hit, scaled by the map's burn multiplier (`node/server.js:3062`). So the field names an effect and the two attributes are the only figures the item contributes to it; describing what each of the sixteen abilities does would be inventing rules this data does not carry.

`GItemTests` covers all three, including the nulls an item that names none of them takes.

author: leaf-agent
body:
The original `z` race exposed several independent answers to whether a browser event was sent, accepted, read, projected, and safe to undo. This change replaces them with one ordered, idempotent client outbox and one server-side execution record per attempt. Ambiguous responses retry the same attempt; acceptance advances delivery order; replay and undo stay gated until a complete authoritative projection accounts for that attempt.

Recorded state now has one semantic model. Registry declarations name coordinates as `(owner widget, unit, facet)`; one projector combines the authored baseline, surviving action/report winners, and unresolved recorded outbox actions. Whole-widget reconstruction preserves ordered siblings and nested ownership, terminal refusals remain tombstoned until their correction commits, recordless actions paint only after acceptance, and a failed state render rolls global history back to the last complete read.

The server authenticates before reading event bodies, validates mutable history and appends under one log lock, coordinates concurrent copies of an attempt, returns accepted state in the POST response, and expresses deterministic refusals in the outbox protocol. The browser rejects an attempt reused for two active gestures before it can account the wrong payload.

Coverage includes lost and delayed responses, concurrent retries and undos, definitive refusals, poll-proven acceptance, send serialization, stale and malformed state, authoritative replay and undo, semantic facet precedence, nested/thread widgets, sibling position composition, live-gesture deferral, and refusal recovery. The exact integrated local suite reports 997 passed and 1 skipped; all pre-commit hooks pass.

## Summary

- Define Spark spend verification work as the maximum of used linking tags, coin-group IDs, and serialized cover-set block references.
- Add an activation-gated 25-work-unit limit to block and transaction validation, and apply the same accounting in priority, package, and add-to-block miner paths.
- Move proof-cache lookup ahead of cover-set reconstruction while keeping cache reuse chain-context safe: cache only exactly resolved cutoffs, separate historical and single-input verifier modes, never let cached failures decide block consensus, and clear the cache on disconnect/reset.
- Avoid materializing full cover-set vectors when proof verification is already being deferred to the batch verifier.
- Add regression coverage for activation boundaries, excess serialized references, mempool/block enforcement, miner templates, negative-cache isolation, unresolved cutoffs, and reset invalidation.

## Security rationale

Spark verification cost scales with both proofs and referenced cover sets. Existing block-size and transparent-value limits do not directly bound that work, allowing a valid cache-cold block to amplify cover-set reconstruction and proof verification. The new accounting gives consensus and miners the same deterministic upper bound; the cache changes remove avoidable reconstruction for previously verified transactions without making chain-dependent or policy-only cache results consensus-authoritative.

## Draft / activation blocker

**This is not yet an active public-network mitigation.** Mainnet, testnet, and devnet intentionally set `nSparkSpendLimitStartBlock = INT_MAX`. Regtest activates the rule at its Spark single-input height.

Before this can merge as a production consensus fix:

1. Benchmark maximum-shaped spends against current/worst-case cover sets on representative hardware.
2. Confirm or revise the provisional 25-unit limit.
3. Select fixed future activation heights through a coordinated node/miner upgrade; do not reuse a past height.
4. Exercise devnet/testnet before activating mainnet.

## Validation

Passed locally:

- `git diff --check`
- C++20 syntax compilation of `src/miner.cpp`, `src/spark/state.cpp`, `src/chainparams.cpp`, and `src/test/spark_tests.cpp`

Not run locally:

- the linked Boost unit-test binary; the repository's configured `depends` artifacts were unavailable in this workspace

CI in the supported dependency environment should run the Spark unit tests and benchmark the provisional limit before this leaves draft.

author: brfrn169
body:
## Description

Running ScalarDB on Aurora means that a writer failover stalls writes while the client waits for DNS to propagate. Measured against real Aurora clusters, that stall was about 26 seconds.

The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper avoids the wait by discovering the cluster topology and reconnecting to the new writer directly, but ScalarDB could not use it: `RdbEngineFactory` dispatches on the JDBC URL prefix and did not recognize `jdbc:aws-wrapper:`, so startup failed outright.

The interesting part turned out not to be the URL handling. ScalarDB already reports failover outcomes correctly, but for two different reasons on two different code paths, and neither was covered by a test. Most of this PR is about making those reasons explicit and keeping them from being broken.

## Related issues and/or PRs

N/A

## Changes made

**Accept the wrapper's URLs**

- `RdbEngineFactory` recognizes `jdbc:aws-wrapper:` and picks the engine from the URL underneath the prefix. Only Aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL are accepted; the wrapper also supports MariaDB, but allowing an untested combination would let it fail in subtler ways than an unsupported-engine error at startup.
- `JdbcUtils` hands the connection pool the wrapper's driver. Each engine's `getDriverClassName()` is left untouched.
- The URL given to HikariCP keeps the `jdbc:aws-wrapper:` prefix. Stripping it is only how the RDB dialect is identified; the prefix is what routes the connection through the wrapper at all. The unsupported-engine error also reports the URL the user configured rather than the stripped one.
- MySQL gets `wrapperTargetDriverDialect=mariadb-connector-j-3` added automatically. ScalarDB reaches MySQL through MariaDB Connector/J and does not bundle MySQL Connector/J, but the wrapper defaults to the MySQL Connector/J dialect for a `jdbc:mysql://` URL. A dialect the user set explicitly is left alone.

**Bundle the wrapper**

- Added to `core` as an `implementation` dependency, following how the AlloyDB connector is handled. All of the wrapper's declared dependencies are optional, so nothing is pulled in transitively — in particular, MySQL Connector/J is not among them and no MySQL code ships.

**Pin the failover exception handling**

No new classification code was needed, but the existing behavior was undocumented and untested:

- `JdbcTransaction#commit()` infers "outcome unknown" from the rollback failing. That only works because HikariCP evicts a connection whose SQLState starts with `08`. Setting HikariCP's `exceptionOverrideClassName`, which AWS recommends, would keep the connection alive, let the rollback succeed as a no-op, and report an unknown outcome as a `CommitException` — whose contract tells the caller it is safe to retry.
- `JdbcDatabase` relies on `isConflict` not matching failover SQLStates. Eviction is irrelevant there; adding `08*` to `isConflict` would turn an unknown outcome into a `RetriableExecutionException`.

Added a driver that simulates the failover exceptions so both paths can be exercised against a real HikariCP pool without a database or AWS credentials, plus a test that pins the wrapper's own exception contract so a version bump cannot silently change it.

**Refuse to start when HikariCP has an exception override configured**

The inference above only holds while HikariCP actually discards the connection. `HikariConfig`'s constructor reads `hikaricp.configurationFile`, so `exceptionOverrideClassName` can arrive without ScalarDB configuration being touched — and AWS documentation recommends setting it. Startup now fails instead, because the alternative is invisible: it surfaces only during a failover, looks like an ordinary retry, and gets found by noticing duplicated data.

**Classify what a scanner throws**

A scanner reports a read failure as an `ExecutionException` wrapping the `SQLException`, so iterating one was the only CRUD path that could not recognize a conflict. It now unwraps and classifies like a single operation.

**Stop discarding the commit failure**

When the follow-up rollback failed, the thrown `UnknownTransactionStatusException` described only the failed rollback, so a caller hitting a failover saw "Rolling back the transaction failed" with no trace of the SQLState that made the outcome unknown. The original failure is now kept as a suppressed exception.

## Checklist

- [x] I have commented my code, particularly in hard-to-understand areas.
- [x] I have updated the documentation to reflect the changes.
- [x] I have considered whether similar issues could occur in other products, components, or modules if this PR is for bug fixes.
- [x] Any remaining open issues linked to this PR are documented and up-to-date (Jira, GitHub, etc.).
- [x] Tests (unit, integration, etc.) have been added for the changes.
- [x] My changes generate no new warnings.
- [x] Any dependent changes in other PRs have been merged and published.

## Additional notes

**One change reaches beyond Aurora.** Refusing to start when `exceptionOverrideClassName` is set applies to every JDBC deployment, not only wrapper users, because the inference it protects is not Aurora-specific either — a plain connection drop mid-commit reports the same SQLState class on any backend. An existing deployment that sets the override will now fail to start. That is intended: such a deployment is already exposed. Worth a look during review.

An earlier revision of this PR also reported a CRUD-phase connection failure as a conflict. That has been dropped after review: SQLState class 08 describes the cause rather than whether a retry helps, and it covers both a writer failover and a database that has gone away for good. `CrudException` already tells callers they may retry, so nothing changes for applications, and Consensus Commit reports the same event the same way.

**Verified against real Aurora clusters** (PostgreSQL 17.10 and MySQL 8.0.44, two instances each, since a managed failover promotes a reader). The clusters were deleted afterwards.

| | Write failures / attempts | Error window |
|---|---|---|
| With the wrapper | 1 / 560 | ~0 ms |
| Without | 90 / 617 | 26,159 ms |

Also confirmed there: Aurora MySQL connects through the existing MariaDB Connector/J, it is not mistaken for TiDB, and every failover exception carries its `08` SQLState on the exception itself rather than on a cause — which matters because HikariCP walks `getNextException()` but never `getCause()`.

**A note on `08S02`.** AWS documents it as "failover succeeded outside of a transaction", but that does not hold for how ScalarDB drives transactions. The wrapper decides between `08S02` and `08007` using `pluginService.isInTransaction()`, which tracks transaction state by parsing SQL text (`BEGIN` / `COMMIT`). ScalarDB uses the JDBC API instead, so the wrapper does not see a transaction in progress, and a commit that failed with uncommitted changes still reports `08S02`. Observed on a real cluster. It is handled correctly either way — both states start with `08`, so HikariCP evicts and the outcome is reported as unknown — but it is the reason no failover SQLState is treated as "nothing was applied".

**User-facing documentation is not in this repo.** A hand-off covering the configuration reference, the exception semantics, and why `exceptionOverrideClassName` must not be set has been prepared separately for the docs repository.

**Aurora is not needed to test this.** The wrapper works against any MySQL or PostgreSQL, so pointing the existing Docker-based integration tests at a `jdbc:aws-wrapper:` URL would put this on CI without AWS credentials. Worth a follow-up issue.

## Release notes

Added support for the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper, which enables fast Aurora failover for Aurora PostgreSQL and Aurora MySQL. Configuring HikariCP with an exception override is now rejected at startup, since it would cause a transaction with an unknown outcome to be reported as a definite failure.

body: Draft of Linear [42-17](https://linear.app/42-golems/issue/42-17/openapi-contract-in-pkgapi-with-codegen-for-go-stubs-and-ts-client). Human-owned (`CODEOWNERS` on `pkg/api/`). This is a proposed contract for review, not a locked product shape. ## What landed - `pkg/api/openapi.yaml` covers the listed stage-1 surface: runs (list/create/get, event WebSocket, steer, background), plans (get, approve, request-changes, branch), agents (list/get/PATCH), approvals, memory (entries + proposals accept/reject), audit (list + verify), checkpoints (list + restore), plus existing `/health`. - `task generate` still writes Go stubs (`pkg/api/gen/go`) and the TS client (`pkg/api/gen/ts`). Both are committed. - `task generate:check` regenerates and fails if `pkg/api/gen` is dirty. CI runs that as a required `generate` job. Local `task ci` includes it too. - Path and query binding in the Go stubs needs `github.com/oapi-codegen/runtime` (pinned in `go.mod`). The `/health`-only spec was stdlib-only; a real surface with `{id}` and `last`/`limit`/`cursor` is not. ## View mapping The mockup is not in this repo. The seven views are taken to be the seven resource groups on the listed surface. Details are in `pkg/api/README.md`. If a mockup screen is something else, say so in review rather than stretching an endpoint. ## Gaps left unguessed (please decide) These are the places a mockup control does not map cleanly. They are documented instead of invented: 1. **Apply.** Kernel is draft → cross-exam → approve → apply. The listed surface has no `POST /plans/{id}/apply`. If the plan view has an Apply button, it has no endpoint. 2. **Cross-exam.** No operator endpoint. Status can be displayed; an operator action cannot. 3. **Plan list and plan diffs.** No `GET /plans`. `Plan.body` is text, not hunks/file lists/secret-scan findings. 4. **Stop / cancel / foreground.** Background is listed; those are not. 5. **Create-run form.** Only `agent_id` is required. Tracker issue, workspace, sandbox options are not specified. 6. **Live event taxonomy.** `RunEvent.type` is an open string. The generated TS client emits a GET helper, not a WebSocket client. Reconnect is `last=N` only. 7. **Agent config / policy.** PATCH accepts `name`. Model, tools, autonomy, and leases/grants/scopes are not on this surface. 8. **Approvals inbox cannot decide.** It deep-links to the subject resource. `kind` is an open string. 9. **Checkpoint create and restore semantics.** No `POST /checkpoints`. Restore is listed; whether it mints a new run or rewinds in place is not locked. 10. **Bind port.** Server URL is loopback with no port. ## Tested locally `go test -race ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go build ./...`, staticcheck with `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.0`, and a second `task generate` that produced bit-identical `gen/`. Linear Issue: [42-17](https://linear.app/42-golems/issue/42-17/openapi-contract-in-pkgapi-with-codegen-for-go-stubs-and-ts-client)

body:
## Problema

`budgets` tem unique em `(user_id, category_id, month, year)`, e o `copyFromPreviousMonth` inseria o lote inteiro sem olhar o mês de destino. Bastava **uma** categoria já ter meta ali para o Postgres rejeitar o INSERT todo:

```
duplicate key value violates unique constraint
"budgets_user_id_category_id_month_year_key"
```

Nada era copiado e a tela não mudava. O toast de erro existe, mas some sozinho e mostra a mensagem crua do Postgres — na prática o usuário via a cópia "vir vazia", sem pista do motivo, e concluía que o botão tinha copiado metas zeradas.

Cenário comum para cair nisso: criar uma meta manualmente no mês novo e só depois clicar em "Copiar do Mês Anterior".

## Mudanças

- copia **só as categorias que ainda não têm meta** no destino; as que já existem ficam como estão, que é o esperado de quem já ajustou o mês
- quando não há nada a copiar, mensagem em português explicando isso, em vez do erro de constraint
- o toast passa a informar quantas vieram e quantas foram mantidas

A decisão de o que copiar saiu para `planBudgetCopy`, função pura em `src/lib/budgetsToCopy.ts`. O resto do fluxo é ida e volta ao supabase e não dava para cobrir sem mock.

## Verificação

- **367/367 testes**, sendo 7 novos cobrindo destino vazio, sobreposição parcial, sobreposição total, preservação do valor planejado, metas sem categoria e imutabilidade da entrada
- eslint limpo nos arquivos tocados; `tsc` na baseline de 39 erros pré-existentes; build passando

## Como foi encontrado

Reportado como "copiei as metas do mês anterior e veio sem valor nenhum". As primeiras quatro hipóteses (cópia zerando `planned_amount`, duplicatas, `parent_id` faltando no select, policy AAL2 bloqueando o insert) foram descartadas uma a uma com consultas ao banco; a resposta veio do toast capturado na tela pelo usuário.

body:
This pull request introduces a new, highly configurable system for detection box overlays, allowing users to customize the appearance and placement of badges on detection boxes. It also adds a global HUD text scaling option that affects the top-bar category names, and updates the settings UI to expose these new options. The changes improve both flexibility and accessibility of the overlay and HUD elements.

**Detection Box Overlay Customization**

* Added `BoxOverlayStyle` and `BoxLabelPlacement` types to encapsulate all badge display options, including icon, category, confidence, placement, and scale. (`waste-sort/Core/Detection/BoxOverlayStyle.swift`)
* Refactored `DetectionBoxView` and related views to use `BoxOverlayStyle` instead of individual flags, supporting dynamic badge content, placement, and scaling. (`waste-sort/Core/Detection/DetectionBoxView.swift`, `waste-sort/Features/Live/LiveCameraView.swift`, `waste-sort/Features/Photo/PhotoSortView.swift`) [[1]](diffhunk://#diff-79b5ebfeaf7803dd70bf14bda146eaf01b4057f5b7e6e4ef15743f4949e3fba2L318-R318) [[2]](diffhunk://#diff-79b5ebfeaf7803dd70bf14bda146eaf01b4057f5b7e6e4ef15743f4949e3fba2L329-R329) [[3]](diffhunk://#diff-79b5ebfeaf7803dd70bf14bda146eaf01b4057f5b7e6e4ef15743f4949e3fba2L354-R361) [[4]](diffhunk://#diff-79b5ebfeaf7803dd70bf14bda146eaf01b4057f5b7e6e4ef15743f4949e3fba2L365-R375) [[5]](diffhunk://#diff-79b5ebfeaf7803dd70bf14bda146eaf01b4057f5b7e6e4ef15743f4949e3fba2L379-R418) [[6]](diffhunk://#diff-4eec3b0c41966b831ac9f155c2599831529401d9b7822d538d2fa2409effcd5eL155-R155) [[7]](diffhunk://#diff-5a27ce34debc7f7dde26c2666235d12ceaa9654f425b7f321e2a9aecf684b189L150-R151)

body:
Implements [docs/tickets/redesign-05-downloading-screen.md](docs/tickets/redesign-05-downloading-screen.md).

## Summary

- `DownloadState.DownloadingRemainingChapters` gains a `storyName: String` field, threaded from `initialChapter.storyName` at all four construction sites in `selectChaptersToDownload`.
- Factored a shared private `TaskStateHeader(title: String?, onCancel: () -> Unit)` composable: 64dp row, 48dp close `IconButton` (`Icons.Rounded.Close`) at 4dp start padding, then the title at `titleLarge`/`onSurface` when non-null. Used by both `FetchingFirstChapterView` (`title = null`) and `DownloadingRemainingChapters` (`title = storyName`), both now wired to the real `onCancel` from ticket 04.
- `DownloadingRemainingChapters` now uses the lambda `progress = { ... }` `CircularProgressIndicator` overload (no deprecation warning); `FetchingFirstChapterView` uses the no-`progress` (indeterminate) overload. Both are M3-only now.
- Deleted the `Box` that stacked the progress label inside the ring; the label ("Fetching story" / "N of M chapters") is now a separate stacked element below the ring. `FetchingFirstChapterView`'s ring now renders above its text (previously below).
- Copy updates to sentence case: "Fetching story", "Looking up story", "$currentlyDownloading of $totalToDownloads chapters", "id: ${storyId.id} · chapter: ${chapterId.id}".
- The rate-limit notice now renders inside a `surfaceContainerHighest` 12dp `Card` with 16dp padding and centered text; the notice string itself (`ao3RLNotice`) is untouched.
- Added dark-theme variants of both Downloading previews (`DownloadingRemainingChaptersDarkPreview`, `DownloadingRemainingChaptersNoticeDarkPreview`).

`SelectChaptersToDownloadTest` needed no changes - it drives `selectChaptersToDownload` through its public `setState` callback and only asserts on `.notice`, not on `storyName`.

## Step 5 finding: nav bar bug (not fixed in this PR, see below)

The ticket asked me to verify redesign-01's Scaffold migration didn't leave `DownloadScreen` inside the launcher's Scaffold content slot in a way that shows the nav bar during download. **It does, for one of the two entry points:**

- `DeepLinkActivity` (the primary flow, reached via the browser share sheet) renders `DownloadScreen` directly under `ReSyncTheme { Surface { ... } }` with no `Scaffold` at all - correctly full-screen already.
- `LauncherActivity` → `LauncherScreen` (Search tab) → `SearchStoryScreen`, however, renders `DownloadScreen` conditionally *inside* `SearchStoryScreen`, which itself lives inside `LauncherScreen`'s `Scaffold` `content` slot (`LauncherScreen.kt:39-47`). `Scaffold`'s `topBar` and `bottomBar` render unconditionally regardless of what's in `content`, so when a user manually enters a story/chapter ID via the Search tab and downloads it, the "reSync" `TopAppBar` and the bottom `NavigationBar` stay visible around this full-screen task state - contradicting the design ("no navigation bar on this frame").

I did **not** fix this here: doing so properly means hoisting the download-in-progress state from `SearchStoryScreen` up to `LauncherScreen` (or otherwise having `LauncherScreen` bypass its own `Scaffold` while a download is active), which touches `LauncherScreen.kt` and `SearchStoryScreen.kt` - both outside this ticket's declared area (`DownloadScreen.kt`) and outside a "small clarification." Flagging prominently per the ticket's instruction rather than silently working around it or scope-creeping this PR.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `DownloadState.DownloadingRemainingChapters` has a `storyName: String` field, populated from `initialChapter.storyName` at all four construction sites in `selectChaptersToDownload`.
- [x] `SelectChaptersToDownloadTest` passes (`./gradlew testDebugUnitTest --tests "*.SelectChaptersToDownloadTest"`).
- [x] Both `FetchingFirstChapterView` and `DownloadingRemainingChapters` render a header with a `close` `IconButton` bound to a real `onCancel`.
- [x] The Downloading screen shows the progress ring, then "Fetching story", then "N of M chapters" as three stacked elements. No text is rendered inside the ring, and no `Box` overlays them.
- [x] `CircularProgressIndicator` is called with the lambda `progress = { … }` overload in `DownloadingRemainingChapters`, and with no `progress` argument in `FetchingFirstChapterView`. `./gradlew assembleDebug` produces no deprecation warning for either call.
- [x] The rate-limit notice renders inside a `surfaceContainerHighest` 12dp card.
- [x] Both composables use only `androidx.compose.material3` components.
- [x] `FetchFirstPreview`, `DownloadingRemainingChaptersPreview` and `DownloadingRemainingChaptersNoticePreview` render without error with the new signatures; dark-theme variants of the two Downloading previews added.
- [ ] Nav bar during download from the Search tab: found broken, reported above, not fixed (out of this ticket's declared scope).

## Verification

- `./gradlew testDebugUnitTest --tests "*.SelectChaptersToDownloadTest"` - passes
- `./gradlew assembleDebug` - passes, no deprecation warnings (confirmed with a forced `compileDebugKotlin --rerun-tasks` to bypass Gradle's up-to-date cache)
- `./gradlew test` - passes

## Stacking

This PR is stacked: base branch is `redesign-03-confirm-chapters-screen` (PR #689), which itself stacks on redesign-02 → redesign-01 → redesign-04 → redesign-00 (PR #688 → #687 → #686 → #685). **None of these are merged yet.** Please diff against `redesign-03-confirm-chapters-screen`, not `main`, when reviewing.

author: killerwolf
body:
Closes #8

Reprend le travail de `feature/maj` sur un `main` à jour, et le termine.

## Ce que fait cette PR

**Reprise de `feature/maj`** — la branche remplaçait ESLint + Prettier par Biome, mais épinglait la **1.8.4** alors que Biome est en 2.x, et partait d'un `main` qui a divergé depuis.

**Montée 1.8.4 → 2.5.9** via `biome migrate`, qui adapte le schéma :
- `organizeImports` → `assist.actions.source.organizeImports`
- `files.ignore` → `files.includes` avec patterns négués

**Nettoyage induit** — ESLint, Prettier et leurs 5 plugins disparaissent des devDependencies. Il ne reste que `@biomejs/biome`, `electron`, `electron-builder` et `rimraf`.

## Neutralité

Le diff sur `main.js` et `renderer.js` est intégralement cosmétique :

| Transformation | Équivalence |
|---|---|
| Réordonnancement des imports + protocole `node:` | Aucun effet runtime |
| `event` → `_event` | Renommage d'un paramètre inutilisé |
| `forEach` → `for...of` | Aucun de ces appels n'utilise l'index, de valeur de retour ni de tableau creux |
| `parseInt(v)` → `Number.parseInt(v, 10)` | Les PID sont toujours décimaux, jamais préfixés `0x` |
| Suppression des `// eslint-disable-next-line no-console` | Commentaires devenus sans objet, Biome ne flague pas `console.error` |

## Deux ajouts a11y à risque nul

Biome 2.x remonte des règles que la 1.8.4 ne voyait pas :

- `lang="en"` sur `<html>` — invisible, mais nécessaire aux lecteurs d'écran
- `type="button"` sur `#savePreferences` — le bouton n'est dans aucun `<form>`, le `type` implicite `submit` n'avait donc aucun effet

## Un point volontairement écarté

`useSemanticElements` signale trois `<div role="button" tabindex="0">` dans la sidebar. Les convertir en vrais `<button>` leur ferait hériter du style natif et impacterait le CSS `.sidebar-item` — donc un **changement visible**, hors du périmètre « aucun changement fonctionnel » de ce lot. La règle est désactivée et le sujet part dans un ticket dédié.

## Vérification

`npx biome check .` — totalement vert, 6 fichiers.
Les scripts `npm run lint` et `npm run format:check` utilisés par la CI fonctionnent.

author: tesseractaz
body:
v0.52.0 computed the flag, unit-tested it, and mutation-verified it — then never added it to the attribute literal `_publish()` sends. Home Assistant showed `None`. **Live verification caught it minutes after the deploy**, with a phone demonstrably unreachable.

Same trap as the dead `M` key in the Z-Wave TUI: computing a value and *publishing* it are different things, and a test of the computation proves nothing about the wire. The new test asserts the **published** attribute — present, `True` on a partial sample, `False` (not omitted) on a complete one — and fails if the payload line is removed again.

body:
## Problem / Motivation

When a user forks a session, the new tab loses the parent's active project directory: `slot.project` is never copied, so the fork falls back to the config/workspace default on its first message — resetting the working context (agent resolution, steering files, CWD) the user forked from. Only `folder_id` (the sidebar grouping) was inherited, and a single comment conflated the two unrelated concepts, making it look like `project` was already handled.

## Why it matters

Forking exists to branch your current working context. Losing the project directory silently reroutes the fork's agent resolution and CWD to the wrong tree — the user notices only when a command runs in the wrong checkout.

## What changed (motivation → approach → change)

Symptom: fork loses project → root cause: `chat_fork.py` copies `folder_id` but never `slot.project` → fix: copy `slot.project` onto the forked slot, and split the misleading comment into two (project directory = working context; sidebar folder = UI grouping).

- `src/kiro_crew/dashboard/chat_fork.py` — copy `slot.project`; split the comment.
- `test/test_dashboard_chat.py` — two new tests.

## Tests

- `test_fork_inherits_project` — sets a project on the source slot, forks, asserts the fork carries it.
- `test_fork_inherits_empty_project` — forks a projectless slot, asserts the fork stays projectless (no default fallback).
- Full `TestForkSlot` class: 45 passed (43 pre-existing + 2 new). isort/flake8/mypy clean.
