author: rhc54
body:
### The problem

A peer's connection socket and the socket a handshake is running on are not always the same descriptor, and `prte_oob_tcp_peer_recv_connect_ack` assumed they were.

On the inbound path `recv_handler` hands the function a socket it has just accepted, and only publishes it as `peer->sd` once the handshake has succeeded (`oob_tcp.c:702`). Until then `peer->sd` is whatever else that peer has: nothing at all, an outbound attempt of our own, or a working connection carrying traffic. Every failure arm below the peer lookup called `prte_oob_tcp_peer_close()` on that peer — closing the wrong descriptor and leaking the right one, since `recv_handler`'s cleanup only releases its conn op.

The consequence is worse than a leak. A connection that offers a valid IDENT header naming a daemon of this namespace and then dies mid-payload — a daemon restarting, a simultaneous-connect race, a half-open socket — made us tear down the *established* connection to that daemon, fail every message queued on it back to its originator, and report a lost connection. All on the word of a socket that never finished proving who it was.

### The fix

Close the peer only when the socket really is its own — which is also what rotates it onto the next address in its list — and otherwise let the failure cost nothing but the socket it arrived on.

Ownership is asked of the peer rather than inferred from the direction the handshake came in, because the simultaneous-connect arbitration in `retry()` abandons our socket in favour of the accepted one and carries on with it. That arm now records the adoption instead of leaving the descriptor it just closed in the field, where it invited a second close of a number the kernel has since handed to somebody else.

The nack arm branches on direction up front for the same reason. A nack says "you dialed me while I was dialing you, and I will be the one to finish it" — an answer to a call we placed. Arriving on a socket somebody opened to *us* it says nothing about any connection of ours, so the socket is dropped and the peer left alone.

Two `show_help` messages and one verbose trace were naming `peer->sd` as the socket the handshake failed on; they now name the socket it failed on.

### The FIXME and the todo entry

That nack arm is where the `FIXME: this shouldn't happen. We need to force next address to be tried` sat, and where `docs/todo.rst` pointed. Its remedy is neither needed nor correct there: on the only path that reaches it, the peer has no attempt in flight that this socket has any bearing on.

The entry's stated defect — a peer closed rather than retried at its next address — was already fixed in ee070ee8bd, which made `peer_close` itself the rotation point for a peer that has never reached CONNECTED. The entry was written three days later, from the comment rather than the code. Both it and its row in the "Every marker in the code" table go with the FIXME.

### Verification

- Warning-free build with `--enable-debug` (warnings are errors)
- `make check`: 22/22
- Single-host DVM smoke: `prte --daemonize` → `prun -n 4 hostname` → `pterm`
- Full `contrib/dockerswarm` ten-node suite, rebuilt from this tree: **636 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped** (the skips are the known "no network device in these topologies" cases)

One gap worth stating: none of the repaired arms is reachable from a well-behaved DVM, and this PR adds no test for them. Reaching them needs a client that speaks the OOB handshake wire format well enough to send a valid IDENT header and then misbehave, which would bind a test client to a header layout the project deliberately keeps free to change. The suite above confirms no regression on the paths that are reachable; it does not cover the repaired ones.

author: reviealnow
body:
## What it does

Adds **Fleet** back to the Monitoring nav — the entry P69 (#81) removed — and
gives it the part of a backhaul capture the Overview strip has never had room
for. The strip stays exactly where it is.

### Why reverse P69

P69's reason was stated plainly and was true at the time:

> The dedicated Fleet section duplicated a full nav slot for what is a
> glance-and-switch view.

A card then held a status, a CPU figure and a crash count. What it holds now is
a measurement, and two concrete things were being lost:

1. **Three measured fields had no reader anywhere in the frontend.** The uplink's
   `snr`, `peer_mac` and `radio_band` are parsed from the DUT's own `iwconfig`,
   returned by `/api/fleet/nodes/{id}/rssi` (`fleet_api.py:207`) — and rendered
   nowhere. We pay a synchronous serial RPC for them and then drop them.
2. **Per-child RSSI was joined into one string.** `FleetStrip.tsx` rendered
   `peers.map(...).join(" · ")`, so with three children you get
   `-58 dBm · -81 dBm · -62 dBm` and no way to tell which child is which. That
   number is the answer to "which one is hearing badly", which is the question
   the two-direction capture (#123) exists to answer.

## Shape

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `components/FleetCard.tsx` | **new** — one DUT's card, extracted from the strip, `variant: "strip" \| "grid"` |
| `components/FleetSection.tsx` | **new** — the grid, the per-node detail, `Capture all` |
| `monitoring/useRemoteRssi.ts` | **new** — the last capture, held above both views |
| `components/FleetStrip.tsx` | now just the horizontal layout + its hide rule |
| `shell/navigation.ts` · `pages/AppShell.tsx` · `styles/dashboard.css` | nav entry, route, grid + detail styles |
| `dut-dashboard/README.md` | module map (it still named `FleetSection.tsx` as the strip's old name, from P69) |

No backend change, no new WebSocket, no new dependency.

**One card component, deliberately.** The strip and the section would otherwise
be two accounts of the same DUT, and the next correction would land in one of
them. Same reason the capture moved into `useRemoteRssi`: held inside a card, it
was re-fetched or silently lost every time the other view mounted.

**Nothing captures on entry.** A capture occupies that DUT's serial console, so
the section shows what was last measured and asking for more is a button.
`Capture all` walks the mesh nodes **in turn, children before roots** — a root
cannot name its own backhaul VAP from its own console, so a root captured first
falls back to whatever interface was configured.

## How to test

```bash
DUT_ADMIN_PASSCODE='<choose one>' ./dut-dashboard/scripts/start_lan.sh
```

1. **Fleet** appears under Monitoring, above CPU / Memory, and is visible to a
   guest (viewing is telemetry; capturing is admin).
2. With a mesh node registered and its console open, press **Refresh RSSI** on
   its card. The detail block below the card shows interface, signal, **SNR**,
   **band**, backhaul SSID and **parent BSSID**, and one table row per child.
3. A root's card reads `None — this is the root of the mesh` rather than
   `Not captured`, and says out loud when its downlink interface came from
   configuration rather than detection.
4. **Capture all (N)** — N counts mesh nodes with a console open; it is disabled
   at zero and hidden entirely for an engineer.
5. **Overview is unchanged**: the strip still hides itself below two DUTs, still
   switches DUT on click, and carries no detail block.

## Verification

Driven in the browser, asserted against the DOM.

* **The new fields render the values they were given** — compared field by field
  against the source payload rather than checked for "something appeared":
  interface, signal, SNR, band, SSID and parent BSSID all matched, mismatches
  `[]`.
* **Two children, not one.** A single row proves nothing about whether the
  second survives; both rows matched their BSSID / dBm / quality.
* **The capture order was checked with the fleet list in the *wrong* order.**
  With the root listed *first*, a naive walk of the list and the correct
  behaviour differ — calls came out `['childnode', 'rootnode']`. And immediately
  after the click only one request had been made, which is what separates
  sequential from parallel.
* **The strip did not change**: its card text matches the pre-refactor string
  character for character, class is still `fleet-card--strip`, and it contains
  no `.fleet-detail`.
* **Roles**: guest sees the section and both cards, no `Capture all`; admin sees
  it, correctly reading `Capture all (0)` and disabled when no mesh console is
  open.
* A layout defect found by looking at the rendered page and fixed here: the grid
  stretched every card to the tallest in its row, so a local DUT's short card
  (384px of content in a 933px row) was mostly blank and read as broken.
* Gates: `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build`, `pytest` 657 passed / 252
  subtests, demo verify 10 pages + 55 behaviour.

**Real-DUT acceptance — done (2026-08-21).** An AP6 on a Raspberry Pi
(`nelson@192.168.30.124`, `/dev/ttyUSB0`), registered through the Settings card,
connected from the strip, captured from the section:

```
role     node
uplink   ath15 · -38 dBm · near · SNR 54 dB · 5GHz
         essid "dutBrowser_Backhaul - PD1005VMG3" · peer ce:4f:86:95:ce:e5
downlink ath14 · detected backhaul · no children associated
```

Every field the detail block renders was compared against `/api/duts` for that
DUT, value by value: no mismatches. The three fields this section exists for —
`snr`, `radio_band`, `peer_mac` — are measured values on screen for the first
time. The per-child table was exercised on real hardware only in its empty
state (this node has no children); the two-row case remains checked against an
injected response.

Two things the hardware showed that reading could not:

* The first capture after a connect failed with the endpoint's own
  `Console reported no wireless interfaces; try again in a moment` — the DUT's
  shell had received `????iwconfig` (line noise on the first write after the
  console opens). The card surfaced that message unchanged and a retry
  succeeded. Pre-existing behaviour of the remote console path, not of this
  change, but worth a look separately.
* **A locally-cabled mesh root cannot be captured at all**: `capture_rssi`
  requires a remote SSH configuration, so the AP6_840E on this machine — which
  is the parent this node reports — has no way to show its own backhaul. The
  section reads correctly for it (no mesh rows at all), but the fleet's root is
  invisible whenever it is the one on your desk. Also separate from this PR.

**Deferred by the author:** the demo kit does not have this screen yet, so its
offline pages now under-show the product by one Monitoring section — to be
picked up once the feature itself is settled (`README_demo_kit.md` is explicit
that showing less misrepresents as much as showing more, and only "more" has a
chip).

author: brona90
body:
Phase 3a of the Doom port: the Spacemacs/Doom property that pressing `SPC` pops
a **named menu** rather than requiring memorised chords. Every binding and every
prefix carries a human-readable description; nothing renders as a raw symbol.

Doom is untouched and remains the daily driver.

## What is here

- `lisp/my-bindings.el` (new) owns the whole leader map: 14 named prefixes
  (`+buffer +code +file +git +help +insert +local +notes +open +project
  +quit/session +search +toggle +window`), ~150 named keys, 8 small `my/`
  helpers standing in for Doom commands that do not exist outside Doom, and
  `which-key-add-keymap-based-replacements` for the three borrowed maps
  (`project-prefix-map`, `help-map`, `evil-window-map`) that general never sees
  the individual keys of.
- `which-key` gets its own `use-package` block instead of one
  `(which-key-mode 1)` buried in the `emacs` block. It is **built in** to
  Emacs 30 and deliberately NOT added to `package.nix` -- a MELPA copy would
  land earlier on `load-path` and shadow it.
- Key choices follow Doom's so muscle memory transfers.

Two settings are load-bearing and both were measured, not assumed:

- **`setopt`, not `setq`, for `which-key-dont-use-unicode`.** It carries a
  `:set` function that re-derives `which-key-separator` and
  `which-key-ellipsis`. `setq` flips the flag and silently keeps `" : "` /
  `".."`; `setopt` gives `" → "` / `"…"`.
- **`which-key-allow-imprecise-window-fit nil`.** Its default is
  `(not (display-graphic-p))` *evaluated at load*. This is a daemon: at load
  there is no frame, so the default computes to `t` and stays `t` forever,
  including in GUI frames made later. Measured as `t` before pinning.

## Verification

The leader keymap is **walked**, not checked against a hand-written list --
that is exactly how #15's six broken keys shipped:

```
leader entries reachable: 738
VOID: 0
named: 490   unnamed: 0
```

Real daemon started from the read-only store `configDir` (`emacs --batch` does
not load `init.el` at all, so a batch run reports success while loading
nothing). Gate: alejandra/statix/deadnix by **exit code**, `build-home` OK,
phase-2 smoke still green, nothing written into the store config dir.

## Three more void commands, same shape as #15

- **All 13 forge commands.** `:after magit` defers the `:commands` autoload
  stubs too, so `SPC g '` resolved `forge-dispatch` and failed on press --
  identical to the `org-gcal :after org` bug. `forge.el` opens with
  `(require 'magit)`, so dropping `:after` is safe.
- **`recompile`.** `compile.el` cookies `compile` but not `recompile`, so
  `SPC c c` worked and `SPC c C` did not.
- **`consult-xref`.** Was void, so `consult-customize` discarded the xref
  preview settings on every startup and warned about it. That warning had been
  written off as cosmetic; it was this. `*Messages*` is now clean at startup.

`org` needed `(require 'org-loaddefs)` rather than a long `:commands` list --
most org commands live outside `org.el`, so `(autoload SYM "org")` would fail
at keypress with "failed to define function".

## Known deviations

Listed in full in `GRADUATION.md`. The ones that will be felt: `SPC c e` is
elisp-only (Doom's dispatches by major mode through quickrun); `SPC c d`/`c D`
have no dumb-jump/online fallback behind xref; `SPC c k` is `eldoc-doc-buffer`,
point-local only. `SPC m` is still global rather than mode-local -- the evil
intercept map means a real mode-local localleader needs a dispatcher keymap.

Commit is unsigned: the YubiKey PIN was not live.

author: trrueee
body:
## 问题与根因

R5.2 已将 durable GitHub state 切到 DLC-owned SQLite，但 Core 仍保留静态 FastAPI、ORM、tools/resources/context、桌面 connector/store/dock/artifact renderer 与生成客户端。这使“无包时完全无 GitHub 能力”不成立，也让 GitHub 继续成为 Kernel 的业务域特例。

## 方案

- 删除 Core GitHub 后端域模块、静态路由、ORM 模型和内置 runtime contributions。
- 删除桌面静态 GitHub composition、store、API facade、CSS 与对应旧测试，重新生成 OpenAPI client。
- 将 R5.2 单向导入缩成 `engine.migrations.github_dlc_state` 迁移专用 helper；保留历史表与 revisions，但不提供运行时 CRUD。
- 通过 Alembic `include_object` 排除已退役历史表的 autogenerate 删除建议。
- 增加 Core absence 工程合同与 R5.3 质量证据。

## 范围与非目标

本 PR 只完成 R5.3 Core removal。保留 `dlcs/dbfox.github` 外置包与其 fixture；不实现 R5.4 packaged lifecycle E2E，不改变 Marketplace/OAuth/private repo/write 权限，也不删除受支持升级仍需的历史表。

## 测试证据

Windows x64 本地：

- `python -m pyflakes engine build_sidecar.py conftest.py scripts`：通过。
- `python -m mypy --no-warn-unused-configs --follow-imports=skip engine build_sidecar.py`：299 source files 通过。
- DLC backend public-API Mypy：6 source files 通过。
- Alembic fresh `upgrade head` + `alembic check`：无新操作。
- migration/engineering/registry/backend-host/real-package 聚焦回归：37 passed。
- 扩展后的迁移、engineering、registry、runtime 与 real-package 集：120 passed（修复门禁断言后相关集再次通过）。
- `npm run lint`、`npm run typecheck:test`：通过（仅既有 Fast Refresh warnings）。
- `npm test -- --maxWorkers=1`：95 files / 424 tests 通过。
- `npm run build`：production build、token 检查、bundle budget 通过。
- API client 第二次生成 diff hash 相同：`805acb396bac7e2244cab03f0c0b68c0b80dae9c`。

## 平台覆盖与未验证项

本地仅验证 Windows x64。Linux/macOS、Frozen Sidecar 与其余完整 backend matrix 交由本 PR GitHub Actions；本 WP 不改 Tauri/Rust、sidecar packaging 或 release-contract 路径，因此不单独触发三平台 release workflow。

## 影响

- 安全/架构：无包时 Core 不再暴露 GitHub 静态能力；GitHub 只能经已验证、启用并重启激活的 DLC 进入 typed host seams。
- 兼容：静态 `/projects/{project_id}/github/*` API 被移除，generated client 同步删除。
- 迁移：旧表不删，历史导入仍幂等、fail-closed、可重放。
- 新依赖、双写、fallback、第二 SSOT：无。
- 回滚：squash revert 可恢复静态实现；不会回写或删除 DLC-owned data。

## 技术调研与复用决策

- 调查过的现有方案（项目内 / 标准库 / 框架 / 社区）：现有 ContributionCompiler/Backend+Frontend Host、R5.2 Alembic cutover、Alembic `include_object` 官方扩展点、PyInstaller hooks/hidden-import 官方分析机制、当前 `httpx` 生产调用图。
- 最终采用方案（直接复用 / 官方方案 / 最小适配 / 明确约束自研）：直接复用 public DLC seams；用 Alembic 官方过滤点做最小迁移工具适配；删除静态 import 使 PyInstaller 分析图自然收敛。
- 未采用其他方案的原因：空 facade、兼容 router 或 ORM 镜像会继续制造 Core 业务特判和伪 absence；删除历史表会破坏旧数据库升级。
- 新增依赖或自研实现的主要风险：无新增依赖；迁移 helper 是 R5.2 已验证逻辑的缩减，不承载新业务行为。
- 是否新增兼容层、映射层、迁移债务；删除条件与负责人：不新增兼容层。历史表/helper 是既有升级债务；负责人为 DLC Platform，删除条件是相关 revision 早于未来正式支持的升级地板。
- 后续验证与清理方式：本 PR CI 全绿后 Ready/merge；R5.4 用真实包验证 absent/install-disabled/enable+restart/disable+restart/uninstall retention。
- 调查限制（无网络/无文档/未实测时如实说明）：已核对项目源码及 Alembic/PyInstaller 官方文档；未在本地实测 Linux/macOS frozen artifacts。

## 检查清单

- [x] 已运行与修改范围匹配的质量门禁（见 `docs/quality/engineering-gates.md`）
- [x] 行为、命令、配置或支持范围变化已同步更新当前文档
- [x] 重要技术决策已按“技术调研与复用决策”填写，并落入 PR/当前文档
- [x] 未提交 `.env*`、Token、数据库、日志、安装包、Sidecar 二进制或无关改动
- [x] 未通过降低鉴权、SQL、安全、capability、供应链或发布门禁来让测试通过

Part of #59（仅推进 R5.3；总 issue 在后续阶段完成）

author: jasoncarreira
body:
Lockstep bump to **0.7.2** for all three packages, plus both adapter pins.

## What's in it

One change since 0.7.1 — **#322**, which stages the canonical workflow into the run directory so the driver can read it.

Every package has shipped-file changes, so none of these is a courtesy bump:

| package | shipped changes |
|---|---|
| `feature-factory` | `bin/factory.js` (staging in `init`), `WORKFLOW.md` (the read contract) |
| `opencode-feature-factory` | `skills/feature/SKILL.md`, synced `WORKFLOW.md` |
| `prime-agent-feature-factory` | synced `WORKFLOW.md` |

## The upgrade note

A **contract change**, not a behaviour change for existing callers. The canonical workflow now states where the driver reads it from:

- a host whose agents may read outside the workspace may read the copy beside its skill — Prime does this, unchanged;
- a host that denies `external_directory` must read the copy `factory init` stages into the run directory, **after** `init` rather than before, because admission and the `init` invocation are specified by the host `SKILL.md`.

The bytes are identical either way. The OpenCode adapter uses the staged copy, because 0.7.1 denied `external_directory` for every agent and the canonical workflow ships outside the workspace — so the read the skill mandated was the read the guard refused, intermittently, depending on whether the skill loader inlined the file.

**Why it matters beyond the intermittent failure:** the only other way past that read is `--auto`, which blanket-approves *every* permission ask. That is acceptable under human supervision and not acceptable for an autonomous agent embedded in another product. This is what makes running without `--auto` possible.

## Verification

- Full workspace suite green: 182 + 51 + 7 + 6, exit 0, including `test/pack.test.js`, which enforces one version across the workspace and adapter pins equal to the factory version.
- Diff is minimal: one line in the factory manifest, two in each adapter, plus the changelog and lockfile.

## Release sequence after merge

Per `RELEASING.md`, the factory is tagged first and allowed to publish before either adapter, since both pin it exactly:

```
feature-factory-v0.7.2
opencode-feature-factory-v0.7.2
```

**Co-Pilot custom description block.** Creators can write a free-text block once in Brand Profile that Co-Pilot appends verbatim to every YouTube description it generates (socials, discount codes, sign-off, emojis). Their exact spacing/blank lines are preserved — it goes in as a single untouched string element.

author: ajnunezg
body:
Four test failures inherited through #2362 (which merged red, so main never ran them). They are **not** one bug and they do **not** all get fixed on the same side — three different verdicts below, no assertion relaxed.

## Review map

| Area | Verdict | Side fixed |
|---|---|---|
| Re-embed truncating the corpus at 24 chunks (3 failing tests) | Code regressed — a design landed unwired | Production |
| `MemoryExtractionPromptBuilder` dropping the `[id] role:` header | Code regressed — half a deliberate change | Production |
| Background tick hydrating before "presentation demand" | Test premise deliberately superseded | Test |
| Harvest re-visiting an already-harvested row | Test premise deliberately superseded | Test |

## 1. Re-embed silently stopped at 24 chunks — one bug, three symptoms

`ProjectionPipelineServiceTests.test_reembedJob_paginatesFullCorpus` (24 != 30), `.test_reembedJob_paginatesBeyondNominalPageSize` (24 != 250), and `UsageAggregatorTests.test_projectionWorker_waitsForDeferredReembed_thenWakesAutomatically`.

24 is `ProjectionPipelineRuntimeTuning.reembedSliceSize`. #2307 landed the **entire** paced-continuation design — `ReembedSliceResult.hasMore`, `ProjectionJobProcessingOutcome.deferred(until:)`, `DataStore.deferProjectionJob`, `reembedContinuationDelay`, and `UsageAggregator.scheduleNextProjectionSweepIfNeeded` — but never wired `process`/`runSweep` to it. `process` returned `Void`, so `runSweep` marked every re-embed job `.completed` after its first slice and **the rest of the corpus was never re-embedded**. `ProjectionJobProcessingOutcome` and `deferProjectionJob` had zero call sites; `reembedContinuationDelay` was stored and never read.

`process` now returns the outcome, and `runSweep` parks the same durable row on a future `availableAt` when `hasMore` — which is exactly what the deferral machinery, and `runProjectionSweep`'s own comment about "a delayed re-embed", were built for. `processReembed` also loses `@discardableResult`, so dropping `hasMore` again is a compile error rather than a silent truncation.

The two pagination tests predate the paced design and drove it with a single `runSweep`, which cannot cover 11 slices. They now drain the continuation the way the worker does, on an injected `OpenBurnBarFakeClock` (deterministic, no sleeps). **Their full-coverage assertions are unchanged** — still "all N chunks must have v2 embeddings".

## 2. Prompt builder dropped the citable id

`MemoryExtractionExtractorTests.test_promptBuilder_truncatesSingleOversizedRecentLine`.

#2319 correctly switched the single-oversized-turn path from `prefix` to `suffix` — the newest text is why extraction ran — but took the `[id] role:` header with it. The prompt contract says *"Do not invent ids"* and drops any citation that does not resolve, so a surviving slice with no id in front of it is a slice the model cannot cite. Both invariants were reachable: the header now leads and the tail fills the remaining budget. #2319's intent is preserved.

## 3. Background tick hydration — contract superseded, test not updated

`ReloadUsagesIfChangedTests.test_backgroundTickDoesNotHydrateBeforePresentationDemand`.

#2307's commit body is explicit: *"DataStoreCoordinator returned from the cold-presentation guard without hydrating, leaving the always-on-screen status item icon-only until the user opened the popover — defeating the automatic first number. Hydrates once after the first ingestion; later background ticks still return cheaply."* The `didHydrateForStatusItem` hook and the test asserting the opposite landed in the same squash, and the hook shipped with no coverage of its own.

The test now pins the shipped contract **and the part that was never covered**: hydration happens *exactly once*, and a later tick with an unchanged write marker does not re-run the multi-window aggregate (asserted via `debugRefreshGenerationForTesting`). Renamed to `test_backgroundTickHydratesOnceForTheStatusItemThenStaysCold`. The O(delta) invariant this file exists to protect is still enforced.

## 4. Harvest idempotency — contract superseded, test not updated

`AgentConversationExtractionSourceTests.test_harvest_enqueuesQuietConversationsExactlyOnce`.

The test expected the second sweep to re-visit the row and collapse onto its existing job (`second == 1`). #2319's paged harvest drops content states that already carry a job *before* it enqueues anything, so the second pass costs **zero** enqueues — strictly better than what the test described, and consistent with the return value's name (`enqueued`). Pinned at 0; the job-count assertion stays at 1.

## Also fixed: a fixture that was measuring the wrong thing

The pacing fixture in `UsageAggregatorTests` hashed the **in-memory** `ConversationRecord`. The content hash folds in `startTime`/`endTime`, and `Date()` carries more precision than the column keeps, so gap repair saw phantom drift on every run and slipped an extra reproject-and-embed into the measurement. It now hashes the stored record, which is what makes the test's own "must not be removed by gap repair" assertion meaningful.

## Not reproducible: `test_fxAskJSONParser_buffersMultiLineObject`

Reported alongside the four above, but `FxAskJSONParser` does not exist on `main` — `git log --all -S fxAskJSONParser` puts it on `feat/living-glass-sweep` (#2379) only. Every `CLIBridgeTests` case passes here.

Diagnosed anyway, for #2379: **the fixture is wrong, not the parser.** The first fragment is written `#"{"output":"hello"#` — the raw-string delimiter swallowed the closing quote — so the parser buffers `{"output":"hello` + `\n` + `, "session_id":"sess-1"}`, putting a literal newline *inside* a JSON string literal. JSON forbids that, `JSONSerialization` refuses, and returning no events is correct. Verified with a standalone probe: as-written never parses, `#"{"output":"hello""#` yields `output=hello`/`session_id=sess-1`, and a genuinely pretty-printed multi-line object parses too. The newline-joined buffering is right — a line reader can only split where a real newline was, and valid JSON never puts one inside a string.

## Validation

Full `OpenBurnBarTests` target, macOS Debug, Xcode 27.0 (27A5194q): **6041 tests, 72 failures — none in any touched area.** `ProjectionPipelineServiceTests`, `UsageAggregatorTests`, `ReloadUsagesIfChangedTests`, `MemoryExtractionExtractorTests` and `AgentConversationExtractionSourceTests` are all green. The remaining failures are pre-existing #2362 fallout with no overlap with this diff: UI snapshot references, the grok/kimi backend and deck-identity gaps, the new `fleet` control deck, and file-plane quarantine.

Re-verified after rebasing onto green main (7781db4866): **278 tests, 0 failures** across `ProjectionPipelineServiceTests`, `ProjectionPipelineServiceMattersTests`, `UsageAggregatorTests`, `ReloadUsagesIfChangedTests`, `RefreshTickPerfTests`, `MemoryExtractionExtractorTests`, `AgentConversationExtractionSourceTests`, `OpenBurnBarMigrationTests`, `OpenBurnBarSearchIntegrationHarnessTests`, `LocalSearchSchemaStoreTests`, `CLIBridgeTests`.

```
xcodebuild test-without-building -project OpenBurnBar.xcodeproj -scheme OpenBurnBar \
  -configuration Debug -destination 'platform=macOS,arch=arm64' \
  -derivedDataPath .derived-data/livinglayout -clonedSourcePackagesDirPath .spm-cache-new \
  CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO -only-testing:OpenBurnBarTests/<Class>
```

`swiftlint` clean on every touched file.

## Invariants preserved

- Re-embed still performs at most one embedding batch per lease — launch and idle CPU stay bounded, which is the whole point of the paced design. Deferral does not bump `attempts`, so a long corpus cannot exhaust `maxAttempts`.
- A deferred job leaves projection health `.healthy` (only failed/canceled degrade it), so a paced re-embed shows up as queue depth, not as failure.
- `ProjectionSweepReport` is unchanged — no new `Codable` key that would break decoding of persisted health JSON.

## Known risks

- **

author: tkgally
body:
This is a knowledge-base run. It changes no dictionary entries and no website files — only the project's internal notes, backlogs, and metrics history. Nothing here affects the live site.

Two jobs: clear the backlog of notes that polishing runs have been leaving behind, and refresh the quality-metrics page now that enough runs have accumulated.

## What the harvest found

Eighteen notes were waiting, from five runs over the past week. As usual, each proposal was measured against the whole dictionary before being written down, and five did not survive that check.

**The one genuinely new result** concerns a backlog item called P50 — entries that the polishing lane has already passed but that still contain no internal word links (the small clickable links inside example sentences that let a reader jump to another entry). It has been measured three times:

| Measured | Polishing position | Unlinked entries behind it |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-09 | 06845 | 55 |
| 2026-08-15 | 06947 | 54 |
| **today** | **06985** | **57** |

The lane moved forward 38 entries and the backlog **grew by three** — the first increase since the item was opened. All three new members sit inside the stretch the lane just crossed.

That matters because of what it implies. The polishing cursor stands at 06985, so the lane has by definition already walked past every one of these 57 entries. They are not entries waiting their turn; they are entries the lane opened and left without links. Five of them still carry a "last modified" date from January, meaning the visit changed nothing at all. Two spot-checks confirm they are perfectly ordinary entries whose examples are full of linkable words. So the diagnosis changes from "the lane skipped a batch" to "the lane is quietly dropping one checklist item, on whole runs of consecutive entries" — and the useful next step is finding out why, rather than scheduling a catch-up pass.

**A related process finding.** Two separate polishing runs this week proposed building a detector for unlinked entries — the sixth and seventh time that idea has been proposed, and the project settled it long ago (the unfiltered count is 23,460 entries, which simply reflects how far polishing has got, not a defect). This run checked why the answer keeps not sticking and found it immediately: neither the polishing prompt nor the relevant skill file mentions the ruling at all. The knowledge is in the wiki; the sessions that need it never see it. Filed as a recommendation for a short "already settled — don't re-file this" section in the polishing prompt.

**Refuted by measurement, so not filed:** a suspected class of verbs with an over-broad "business" label (4 entries dictionary-wide, and 3 of them are legitimately business-related); a suspected blind spot in one of the checkers (it does scan the field in question, and the three examples cited had already been fixed by the run that reported them); a proposed candidate-vetting rule for technical medical terms (1 of 163 queued words matches); and a documentation complaint that turned out to be half right.

**Filed:** five tooling recommendations, one new cleanup item, two entry follow-ups, and — for an item that has been open since January without one — its first scope estimate (46 entries, far smaller than earlier reports implied).

## Quality metrics, refresh 38

Covers the last 15 automated runs.

- **The "tags" reviewer looks unreliable and isn't.** Its headline accuracy jumped from 17% to 42%, which on its own means nothing, because the number mixes real findings with five well-known families of nuisance suggestions. Stripping those out gives **80%**, against **78%** last time. Two windows, different parts of the dictionary, the same answer — the first time this can be called stable rather than merely repeatable.
- **The furigana checker produced a second consecutive window of exactly zero useful findings** — 0 corrections out of 140 flags across the two windows combined. Both nuisance families are now identified as faults in how the model *reports* readings, not errors in the dictionary, and an unrelated run reached the same conclusion independently and verified five cases by hand. The recommendation is now stated without hedging: stop running this pass over already-polished ranges.
- **The review queue grew again, and this refresh names the cause.** The 15 runs wrote 482 entries, and 256 of those — 53% — came from just two bulk-fix runs. Since the queue tracks "changed since last reviewed", a productive bulk-fix run is structurally the biggest thing that grows it. Not an argument against those runs, but a reason the queue number can't be read as a quality signal.
- **A stale table was quietly leading the page to a wrong conclusion.** The all-time summary hadn't been recomputed in several refreshes and understated every total by three or four times. Recomputed, it reverses a standing claim: the broad dictionary-wide review, not the per-run self-check, is the highest-accuracy source overall. The old claim was true when written and decayed afterwards.
- **A caveat on everything above:** 11 of the 15 runs happened within 30 hours, then nothing ran for **74 hours**, then 4 more. This window covers six days where the last covered a day and a half, so any per-window rate isn't comparable and one of them was skipped rather than reported.

## Two things need Tom

1. **A spelling ruling.** Internal links pointing at the entry for ください are written two ways — 1,323 in kana, 237 in kanji. Both work and nothing is broken; it is purely a consistency choice. Recommendation is the kana form: it is already 85% of usage, so cleanup is 237 instances instead of 1,323, and the polite-request ください is conventionally written in kana. The ruling needs to go into the inline-links skill file, which these sessions don't edit — otherwise the split regrows as fast as it's cleaned.

2. **New evidence for a decision already waiting.** The approved list of meaning-category tags still has no word for "place/location". A ruling on this has been pending since 2026-08-13. This week added a witness from the opposite direction: 場所 ("place") uses the generic fallback tag *correctly*, and still can't be tagged properly, because there is nothing better to use. No new decision needed — just another reason to make the one already queued.

Both are written out in full in `reviews/needs_curator.txt`.

## Verification

No entry files changed (`git status` over `entries/` is empty), so the usual independent-model re-check of changed entries doesn't apply and no external review budget was spent. No site rebuild, since wiki edits don't touch the published files.

Session log: `polishing/sessions/routine_2026-08-21_001.md`

author: calvin-archastro
body:
[Review on ArchCode](https://archdev.ai/ArchAstro/intern-mcp/pull/12)

## Problem and author intent

Intern's coding agent writes and commits one browser bundle, but local previews previously had no host runtime for SDK-backed capabilities. The same committed `new Client().me` code must run locally and under the production host without source changes. Sites also need to use the current public SDK instead of inheriting a stale dependency.

This PR keeps runtime selection outside the checkout: MCP wraps the temporary preview snapshot, injects the reviewed Intern SDK host resolver, and supplies a per-preview in-memory `me` implementation. Every `intern_prepare_site` now resolves public `@archastro/intern-sdk@latest` and pins the exact resolved version into the site manifest and lockfile.

## What changed

- Added a loopback preview host that proxies the unchanged site runtime and injects `/.intern/runtime.js` before application modules.
- Added reserved local ME endpoints backed by the SDK's `MemoryMeImplementation`.
- Seeded the sandbox from the authenticated Intern session and reset it whenever a preview is replaced.
- Passed the authenticated session into preview construction without writing runtime state into the checkout.
- Taught the MCP instructions to generate only default-imported `Client` / `new Client()` application code and never commit adapters or `globalThis.intern` assignments.
- Made site preparation query the public npm registry with `--prefer-online`, resolve `@archastro/intern-sdk@latest`, save the exact version as a development dependency, and update only package metadata.
- Isolated npm in a temporary same-basename sandbox, rejected symlinked package metadata, disabled lifecycle scripts, and atomically copied back verified regular `package.json` and `package-lock.json` files.
- Replaced the MCP's Git-SHA SDK dependency with exact public package version `0.1.0`; npm now installs it as a normal dependency instead of embedding it in the MCP tarball.
- Added a Vite + Chrome compatibility gate to the default check path.

## Scope

Local Intern MCP preparation, preview runtime, and packaging. Production gateway injection remains outside this repository.

## Risk assessment

Medium. This adds a public npm request during prepare, an HTTP proxy, and mutable per-preview state. Prepare fails loudly if the SDK cannot be resolved. Npm scripts are disabled; checkout package metadata is guarded against symlink writes; the proxy is loopback-only; absolute targets and oversized requests are rejected; and shutdown forcibly terminates stalled connections before snapshot cleanup.

## User impact

Models can commit normal site code such as:

```ts
import Client from "@archastro/intern-sdk";

const client = new Client();
const current = await client.me.get();
```

`intern_prepare_site` refreshes and exactly pins the SDK. `intern_test_site` supplies the local implementation without changing committed application source or build bytes.

## Testing

- `npm run check` passes formatting, lint, build, 47 tests, clean-package installation, and the SDK browser compatibility proof.
- Canonical MCP lifecycle proof: [`src/server.test.ts`](https://github.com/ArchAstro/intern-mcp/blob/agent/add-intern-mcp-diagnostics/src/server.test.ts), test `an authorized MCP client prepares and publishes an Intern checkout over stdio`, crosses the real MCP stdio process, authenticated Intern HTTP fixture, Git checkout, npm package resolution, child site runtime, preview proxy, runtime/ME endpoints, preview replacement, explicit stop, validation, and publish. It asserts prepare pins the SDK, preserves the site name in the lockfile, creates no checkout `node_modules`, and keeps runtime state out of Git.
- Canonical browser proof: [`scripts/sdk-compatibility.mjs`](https://github.com/ArchAstro/intern-mcp/blob/agent/add-intern-mcp-diagnostics/scripts/sdk-compatibility.mjs) Vite-builds a real fixture importing the default `Client`, serves it through the actual preview host, runs it in Chrome under `script-src 'self'`, and observes `client.me.get()`, name mutation, profile-picture bytes, injected resolver availability, and bounded stop cleanup.
- [`src/sdk-install.test.ts`](https://github.com/ArchAstro/intern-mcp/blob/agent/add-intern-mcp-diagnostics/src/sdk-install.test.ts) verifies the public registry, online resolution, exact lock-only pinning, sandbox basename behavior, loud registry failure, and rejection of symlinked metadata without mutating its external target.
- The package smoke test clean-installs the MCP tarball, fetches SDK `0.1.0` as a normal npm dependency, and observes all 8 MCP tools. Dry-run packing reports no bundled dependencies.
- A live temporary-package probe resolved public npm `latest` to exact version `0.1.0` and produced no `node_modules`.

## Follow-ups and known issues

- Production must implement the same host resolver and ME contract against the gateway and Platform.

author: kiankinakomochi
body:
## Summary

Fixes #216 — `/diag compile-errors` reported `✓ N assembl(ies) 0 error(s) 0 warning(s)` with `ok: true` / `status: "success"` while the project was in a broken compile state, because it relied solely on an event-based compiler-message cache.

Live testing on a large real-world Unity 6000.4.0f1 project (bridge/host mode) confirmed the root cause: **the bridge's `CompilationPipeline` events (`compilationStarted` / `assemblyCompilationFinished` / `compilationFinished`) never fire in the loaded domain in this environment**, so the event cache is permanently empty and the command inferred success from it. It also surfaced a second trap: a failed compile can wedge the editor in a permanent "compilation in progress" state (`EditorApplication.isCompiling` stays true with no compiler backends running, and the pending domain reload never completes), during which every after-the-fact signal still reflects the previous clean pass.

## Changes

**Daemon (`DaemonDiagService.ExecuteDiagCompileErrors`)** — combines four signals instead of one:

1. Cached compiler messages from the event-based state (kept as before, when available).
2. `EditorUtility.scriptCompilationFailed` — authoritative for the last pass, survives domain reloads.
3. Expected-vs-actual assembly diff: every assembly `CompilationPipeline.GetAssemblies()` intends to build must have its output DLL in `Library/ScriptAssemblies`; expected-but-missing output is reported as a compile failure with a synthetic `Error` message naming the assembly.
4. `EditorApplication.isCompiling` — while a compile is running (or wedged), the command reports `compilationInProgress: true` instead of asserting success.

When any signal indicates a broken or unsettled state the response carries **`ok: false`** (failed exec status for agents/CI) while still including the diagnostic payload in `content`. New payload fields: `compilationFailed`, `compilationInProgress`, `missingAssemblies`.

**CLI**

- `/diag compile-errors` renders the failure detail (✗ + messages) from the `content` payload even when the daemon reports `ok: false`, and shows an explicit "compilation in progress" line for the unsettled state.
- Debug artifact collection keeps a diagnostic's `content` payload when the daemon reports `ok: false`, so compile-error detail from a broken project lands in the artifact instead of being dropped.

**Docs** — `docs/project-diagnostics.md` rewritten for the new contract (the old example showed per-message `assembly`/`file`/`line` fields the payload never actually had); `docs/command-reference.md` updated; `full-documentation.md` regenerated.

## Broken vs clean payloads now differ structurally

Per the issue's key observation (byte-identical output broken vs fixed), the regression criterion is that the two states must be distinguishable:

| | clean | broken (wedged compile) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| envelope | `ok: true` / exec `status: success` | `ok: false` / exec `status: error`, `E_VALIDATION` entry |
| render | `✓ compile-errors 222 assembl(ies) 0 error(s)` | `✗` / `…` + explicit failure or in-progress line |
| payload | `compilationFailed: false` | `compilationFailed: true` and/or `compilationInProgress: true`, `messages[]` non-empty |

## Testing

- `dotnet build` CLI + compatcheck (Unity 6000.2.6f2 reference set): 0 errors, 0 new warnings. The 5 pre-existing `UNIFOCL001` warnings on `main` (profiler/recorder file I/O) are untouched here and already fixed by #218 — noting to avoid a duplicate fix; happy to rebase once #218 merges.
- `dotnet test`: 128/128 pass.
- Live verification on an isolated clone of a large real-world Unity 6000.4.0f1 project via the bridge (editor launched by the CLI, `--session-seed` agentic exec):
  - clean baseline → `✓ 222 assembl(ies) 0 error(s)`, `ok: true`;
  - introduced a CS0246 script + `/asset refresh` → reproduced the exact #216 false-clean with the pre-fix bridge, confirmed the event cache stays pristine (`compilationStarted` never fires) and that the failed pass wedges `isCompiling` permanently;
  - with the fixed bridge loaded, the broken/wedged state reports non-success instead of `✓ 0 error(s)` (details in the diag output above);
  - repro script removed and the project restored byte-for-byte afterwards.

body:
The toolkit copy of `kb-article` (#131) and a copy living in a builder's `~/.claude/skills/` had diverged. The local copy gained real material the toolkit lacked, and lost the three publish-safety rules the #131 review added. Personal skills shadow toolkit skills, so the local copy was the one actually running. This merges the two, taking the toolkit as the base for anything that can cause silent data loss. ## Kept from the toolkit - **Changed-row CSV is the default publish path.** A whole-sheet overwrite rewrites the body of every row in the file, so publishing one article pushed the sheet's stored body over all ~50 articles and reverted anything edited in HubSpot since. The whole-sheet import stays, gated behind the reconcile pass, and the skill refuses "the usual import" framing when nothing has been reconciled. - **Drafts never land on the `Articles` tab.** That tab is the publish set, so a draft parked there ships the next time anyone imports, including a colleague syncing something unrelated. - **Read both tabs before adding a row.** An oversized article is invisible in `Articles!A:A`, so searching one tab appends a duplicate row for a slug that already has one. Plus: a row crossing the 50,000-char threshold gets moved, not copied. ## Added from the local copy - Internal vs external KB routing, decided before drafting. - Columns I/J (`User Name`, `User Email`) attribution, left unmapped on import. - Concrete `gws` invocations, the `--params` / `--json` split, building the row with Python rather than shell-quoting HTML, and reading the row back to catch a silent truncation or column shift. - Companion vault note pattern, house-style article structure, the em dash rule, category distribution, and the KB-article-as-standard-deliverable rule for RevOps/BI builds. ## Context This is groundwork for opening KB authoring to any builder with the toolkit, so a team can propose an article or an edit through the skill instead of routing it through one person. Two things still outstanding before that, tracked separately: a proposed-then-approved review step (the skill currently writes into the tab that gets imported), and a named owner for the KB. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) > [!NOTE] > ### Rewrite `kb-article` skill to write articles into master Google Sheet registry > - Overhauls [SKILL.md](https://github.com/thensls/nsls-builder-toolkit/pull/151/files#diff-96c7be9e06ed23707ea59232cbbebb2a5d21327975c4c108509e3dcbd3c10c91) to direct writing and overwriting articles directly into a 10-column master Google Sheet (A:J), with 8 HubSpot import columns plus 2 unmapped attribution columns (`User Name`, `User Email`), instead of building a CSV from a HubSpot export > - Default publishing output is now a changed-row CSV with import instructions; requires a post-import audience reset to Private SSO and verification of written rows > - Workflow now detects user attribution, checks both sheet tabs for existing URLs, handles oversized bodies above 50k chars by moving rows across tabs, and normalizes pasted HTML via BeautifulSoup > - Expands importer gotchas (audience resets to Public, never import raw exports, category descriptions not importable, draft handling via separate CSV) and refines house style, heading, link normalization, and no-em-dash policy for internal KB > - Behavioral Change: master sheet schema and publishing flow replace the prior export-based CSV construction; reviewers should verify the 10-column mapping and the unmapped attribution fields in [SKILL.md](https://github.com/thensls/nsls-builder-toolkit/pull/151/files#diff-96c7be9e06ed23707ea59232cbbebb2a5d21327975c4c108509e3dcbd3c10c91) > > > >

author: chokobole
body:
## Description

Opens `zorch/lnp` — the LNP proof layer (eprint 2022/284) — with the piece every protocol figure draws first: the challenge space `C = {c ∈ S_κ : σ₋₁(c) = c, ²ᵏ√‖σ₋₁(cᵏ)·cᵏ‖₁ ≤ η}`. Three choices carry the design:

- **Hashing stays caller-side.** Sampling is a deterministic function of injected transcript bytes under lattice-frx's byte-stream contract — same posture as `ajtai.py`'s caller-provided CRS, so the raw-XOF transcript seam (#622) stays a consumer decision, not a dependency.
- **The η gate is exact integer arithmetic.** At the paper's Figure-3 point (d=128, κ=2, η=59, k=32) the gate product's coefficients run hundreds of bits; a float comparison would decide a soundness parameter by rounding luck. Six negacyclic products over Python bigints cost ~5ms per candidate.
- **Rejection is pre-budgeted, never open-ended.** `ceil(-log2(fail_prob))` candidate blocks from a stated conservative 1/2 per-candidate bound (measured rejection at Figure 3 is ~1%, pinned by a test), so byte consumption is a function of the parameters alone — the discipline `uniform_from_bytes` set, lifted one layer up.

The σ₋₁-invariant embedding needs only d/2 draws (upper half mirrors negated, `c_{d/2} = 0`), and sampled challenges are checked invertible in lattice-frx's partial-split ring (`q ≡ 5 (mod 8)`) — the Lemma-2.6 property LNP soundness extraction divides by. The tests recompute the gate quantity with an independent schoolbook oracle rather than trusting the module's own arithmetic.

The lattice-frx bump rides in front: the samplers (lattice-frx#21) and the split ring (lattice-frx#23) are the two substrate pieces this consumes.

## Related Issues/PRs

Follow-up to #655 (the commitment layer); second slice of the #654 residual scope. The LNP layer item is tracked as a draft on the zorch work board — next slice there is the ABDLOP commitment class.

## Checklist

- [x] Branch name follows Branch Guideline
- [x] Commit messages follow Commit Message Guideline
- [x] Checked Pull Request Guideline

author: nitin27may
body:
Closes #25.

## What was wrong

The `Smoke (replay, deterministic, free)` eval job has been red on **every PR that ever triggered it** — disclosed-not-fixed on #21, again on #24. It was never a quality problem: live database payloads were part of the fixture cache key.

A fixture's filename is a hash of `(messages, tools, instructions)`. In a MAF tool loop, turn N+1's messages carry turn N's `function_result` — raw JSON straight out of Postgres. CI reseeds a fresh database every run, so anything in those payloads that differed between reseeds produced a different key and an unreachable fixture.

Three things differed, all inside tool results:

1. **Random primary keys** — `reviews.id` (120 occurrences across the corpus), `orders.id`.
2. **Timestamps** — every seeded timestamp is `datetime.now()` ± an offset, to the microsecond.
3. **Tied rows** — SQL leaves the order of rows tied on `ORDER BY` undefined, and Postgres genuinely returns them differently depending on the query plan, which depends on table statistics. A database seeded seconds ago and never analyzed sorts ties differently from a settled one. That is exactly the shape CI runs in, and why `product-discovery`'s trending case failed there while passing on every developer's machine.

### Two corrections to #25

- **`orders.id` is not the mechanism.** No dataset case references a real seeded order — they all use the synthetic `550e8400-…` ids that exercise "not found" paths. Random `reviews.id` and timestamps are the cause, and timestamps alone are enough to break every affected hash. That is why `review-sentiment` — which touches no order at all — fell from 100% to 40%.
- **There was never a reverted attempt at deterministic order ids.** `git log --all -S` across every ref returns zero hits for `order_id_for`; `c05747e`'s commit body and the fixtures README both record it as a deliberate, documented decision to skip.

## The fix

- **`_normalize_for_hash`** strips UUIDs and timestamps when hashing, for `role: "tool"` messages only, and ordinalizes provider-assigned `call_id`s so re-recording one turn no longer invalidates everything downstream. The fixture on disk still stores the raw request. Tool *call* arguments live in the assistant message and are hashed verbatim, so two genuinely different calls can never collide — a test guards the uuid5 product-id assumption that makes that safe.
- **`scripts/seed.py` runs `ANALYZE`** after loading. Standard practice after a bulk load; it stops the planner running blind on fresh tables.
- **`evals/rehash_fixtures.py`** re-keys the corpus offline from each fixture's stored raw request — no credentials, no re-recording. Its keeper policy is consumer-aware: collapsing two fixtures discards a whole recorded *trajectory*, and keeping the wrong sibling strands everything downstream of the discarded one. 114 fixtures → 103.

### Reporting and gating

- A missing fixture is now tracked separately from a wrong answer and **always fails the run**, whatever the threshold. CI said "review-sentiment scored 40%" when it meant "three fixtures are missing" — that ambiguity is why this stayed open across two PRs.
- The smoke job now gates on **reproducibility + baseline regression** rather than an absolute floor. It replays frozen model output, so its absolute score is a property of the recording session, not of the PR under test. The 0.7 quality floor stays on the `full` job, which drives real models.

### Bonus: a bug that amplified this one

The circuit breaker keyed on hostname, ignoring port (`shared/http_resilience.py`). All five specialists share `localhost` in CI, local dev and the eval harness, so three missing fixtures opened one shared breaker and cascaded into five failed orchestrator cases — which is what buried the real cause in #24's log. Docker production was unaffected (distinct hostnames), so it only ever bit where the evals run.

## Verification

Seeded a throwaway Postgres from scratch repeatedly and ran all seven suites against each — the condition CI reproduces and that had never been tested locally.

| Suite | Before (independent reseed) | After |
|---|---|---|
| product-discovery | 91.2% / 71.2% (flaky, 1 missing) | **91.2%, 0 missing** |
| order-management | 44.3% | 44.3%, 0 missing |
| pricing-promotions | 52.0%, 1 missing | **64.0%, 0 missing** |
| review-sentiment | 40.0%, 3 missing | **100%, 0 missing** |
| inventory-fulfillment | 66.0%, 1 missing | **82.0%, 0 missing** |
| orchestrator_routing | 0.0%, 6/6 missing | **80.0%, 0 missing** |
| safety / red-team | 100% | 100% |

Two independent reseeds now produce **identical scores with zero missing fixtures**, and every suite matches its committed baseline exactly — the baselines were already correct; nothing needed regenerating. Also confirmed the new guard works by removing a fixture and watching the run fail with a specific message, and that the breaker test fails without its fix.

`order-management`'s 44.3% is a separate, pre-existing structural issue (the dataset deliberately tests "not found" paths, incompatible with requiring `grounded: true`). It reproduces identically everywhere and is unchanged here.

Full Python suite: **776 passed**. `.NET` and `web/` untouched.

## Residuals, documented not fixed

Written up honestly in `evals/fixtures/README.md`, replacing a paragraph that claimed "this doesn't break replay itself" — which is precisely what was happening:

- **Query-time `NOW()`** still moves with the calendar. `get_sentiment_trend` buckets reviews by month within a rolling window, so a fixture can go stale on a different *day* rather than a different seed. Normalization fixes values that differ; it cannot fix a payload that changes shape.
- **Unordered ties.** `ANALYZE` makes the planner behave like a normal database, but SQL still promises nothing for tied rows. ~25 `ORDER BY` clauses lack a unique tiebreaker.
- **Eval runs mutate state** (HITL approval rows), so record and replay both need to start from a fresh seed.

author: jcsco
body:
Refs: [SYN-6894](https://splunk.atlassian.net/browse/SYN-6894), [SYN-6861](https://splunk.atlassian.net/browse/SYN-6861)

> This PR is **step 1 of a multi-step release plan** (see *Plan to v3.0.0* below). It is the history-convergence step only — on its own it does **not** produce an installable v3. Please review it as "is this the right merge, correctly resolved," not "is this releasable."

----

### Before the change?

* `main` and `v2` have been diverged since the fork point `e469511` (2023-09-08). `main` is 8 commits ahead of that base and has had no release since `v1.0.3` / `v2.0.0-beta`; `v2` is 39 commits ahead and is the actively released line (26 `v2.x.y` tags, latest `v2.8.0`).
* The two lines were kept apart only because Rigor (v1) customers and Splunk Synthetics (v2) customers had to be served simultaneously. `terraform-provider-synthetics` still imports both at once via Go semantic-import-versioning.
* `v2` — not `main` — is currently the repository's default branch.

### After the change?

* `v3` is branched from `main` and `v2` is merged into it as a true two-parent merge (parents `0953446` from `main`, `287af50` from `v2`). No commit hashes on either branch are rewritten, so existing `v2.x.y` tags, open PRs, and forks pinned to v2 SHAs all remain valid.
* 109 files changed, +10,341 / −349.

#### Conflict resolution

13 files conflicted, all confined to `syntheticsclientv2/`: `common_models.go` plus 12 `*_test.go` files. The legacy `syntheticsclient/` (v1) package had zero conflicts. All 13 were resolved in favor of `v2`.

#### The resulting tree is byte-identical to the v2 tip — this is intended

```
$ git rev-parse origin/v2^{tree} origin/v3^{tree}
5cd6d1695cd7639c1131bcabb023f8958059593e
5cd6d1695cd7639c1131bcabb023f8958059593e
```

Worth stating explicitly, because it looks alarming and a reviewer should scrutinize it. It is arithmetic, not accident: all 13 conflicts resolved to `v2`, plus the two files `v2` had deleted (`sonar-project.properties`, `coverage.txt`) staying deleted, is exactly a copy of v2's tree.

**The merge's value is the history, not a novel tree.** v2's 39 commits become reachable from `main`, which is what lets `main` be tagged `v3.0.0` and become the default branch. A rebase or squash would have produced the same tree with a worse history.

So the question that matters is *"was anything unique to `main` lost?"* `main` changed 18 files since `e469511`; audited individually:

| `main`-only change | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `.github/workflows/cla.yaml`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` | byte-identical on `v2` — nothing to lose |
| `.gitignore` | `v2`'s version is a strict superset (adds `integration.jsonl`, `.env.testacc`, …) |
| `README.md` | 2 superseded lines only: a reworded tagline, and the pre-`/v2` import path (which becomes `/v3` anyway) |
| `common_models.go` + 12 `*_test.go` | resolved to `v2`; feature audit below |

Symbol coverage for `main`'s two substantive features, counted across `syntheticsclientv2/`:

| Symbol | on `main` | on `v3` |
|---|---|---|
| `customProperties` (SYN-3197) | 31 | 47 |
| `CustomProperties` | 10 | 29 |
| `lastRunAt` (SYN-3798) | 9 | 13 |
| `lastRunStatus` | 9 | 20 |

`v2` reimplemented both independently with strictly broader coverage — neither was lost.

A JSON-tag audit of `common_models.go` found 93 tags on `main` and 144 on `v2`. Only three `main` tags are not present verbatim in `v2`, and all three are deliberate `v2` restructurings rather than regressions:

* `selectorType` + `selector` (flat scalars) became `Selectors []Selector{Type,Value}` — a structured, strictly more expressive locator.
* `device` (embedded `Device` object on `BrowserCheckV2Response`) became a flat `deviceId int` on the restructured `BrowserCheckV2ResponseTest`. The `Device` struct itself still exists, used by `DevicesV2Response`.

#### Also merged in (tooling drift, no conflicts — worth a deliberate ack)

* Added from `v2`: `.github/CODEOWNERS`, `.github/pull_request_template.md`, `ci.yml`, `integration-test.yml`, `pr-metadata.yml`, `.testcoverage.yml`
* Deleted, because `v2` dropped them: `sonar-project.properties`, `coverage.txt`

----

## Plan to v3.0.0

Goal: **one client, released as `v3.0.0` from `main`.** Rigor/v1 is decommissioned and goes away; the v2 module line stops receiving releases but keeps working for existing consumers.

Worth stating up front, because it will come up in review: deleting the Rigor client is **not** what forces a major bump. The v1 client lives at a *separate* module path (`github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient`), so removing it does not break anyone importing `/v2`. The breaking change is the **module path itself moving `/v2` → `/v3`**, which is what buys a single `main`-based source of truth.

| # | Step | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Converge `v2` into `main`'s history | **this PR** |
| 2 | `go.mod` → `module github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v3` | required — see below (SYN-6865 for the optional toolchain bump) |
| 3 | Delete the legacy `syntheticsclient/` (Rigor) package | SYN-6862 — **must precede the tag**, see below |
| 4 | Tag `v3.0.0` from `main`; flip default branch `v2` → `main` | after 2 + 3 |
| 5 | Point `terraform-provider-synthetics` at `/v3`, drop the v1 dependency | SYN-6863 |
| 6 | Ship final `v2.8.1` marking the v2 line deprecated; protect the `v2` branch | after 4 |

### Step 2 is a hard gate, and this branch does not satisfy it yet

`main` never touched its module line after the fork; only `v2` did. Because just one side changed it, git resolved `go.mod` **without a conflict** — so this merge currently leaves the module path at `github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v2`.

This was left exactly as git resolved it rather than quietly renamed, so the reviewer can see the raw merge. It **must** be fixed before any tagging. Tagging `v3.0.0` while the path says `/v2` produces a release that is dead on arrival in both directions: `go get .../v3@v3.0.0` fails with `invalid version: major version must be included in module path`, and the tag is equally invisible to the `/v2` path because `v3.0.0` is not a valid version for a `/v2` module.

**Verified: the fix is genuinely one line.** There are **zero** references to the module path in any `.go` file in the repo (the `syntheticsclient` and `syntheticsclientv2` packages do not import each other), so no import rewrites are needed anywhere. Only `go.mod` and `README.md` mention the path at all. Confirmed by applying `go mod edit -module=github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v3` to this branch in a scratch worktree:

```
$ go build ./...                  # OK
$ go vet ./...                    # OK
$ go vet -tags integration ./...  # OK (type-check only, not executed)
$ go test ./...
ok  	github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v3/syntheticsclient	0.591s
ok  	github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v3/syntheticsclientv2	1.462s
```

No existing ticket covers this rename (SYN-6862 deletes v1 but never states it) — recommend adding it as an explicit acceptance criterion there.

### Step 3 must land before the tag, for semver reasons

Deleting the Rigor package isn't a tagging blocker, but it is a semver one: if `v3.0.0` ships with `syntheticsclient/` still present, removing it later becomes a breaking change *inside* a major version. SYN-6862 therefore needs to land before the tag, not after.

### Decided: the `syntheticsclientv2/` directory keeps its name

Under the `/v3` module path the public import becomes:

```go
import "github.com/splunk/syntheticsclient/v3/syntheticsclientv2"
```

Yes, that reads oddly ("v3/…v2"). Renaming the directory to `syntheticsclient/` (free once Rigor is deleted) was considered and **deliberately rejected**, for two reasons:

1. **Backports would stop cherry-picking cleanly.** We expect to backport fixes from this line to `v2` (see below). Renaming the directory *and* its package clause across 102 files would make essentially every cherry-pick conflict — a recurring cost paid under customer-driven time pressure

author: naingthet
body:
Part of epic #2335. Stacked on #2366 (session browser authority) — the base branch is `thet/browser-session-authority`, so this diff shows only the route-seam slice.

## What this adds

**`BrowserRuntime` trait** (`crates/tidebreak-server/src/code/browser_runtime.rs`)
A server-private `async_trait` seam with `list` / `navigate` / `snapshot` / `wait_for` / `screenshot` / `act`, each taking the `BrowserSubject` derived from the caller's capability token plus already-validated args from `tidebreak-core::browser`. Typed `BrowserRuntimeError` variants map to stable statuses: `UnknownBrowserId` → 404, `SessionEnded` → 403, `StaleTarget` → 409, `Unsupported` → 501, `Failed` → 500. The desktop's engine adapter implements this in the native-driver slice; until then `AppState.browser_runtime` is `None` and every route answers 501.

**Six POST routes** (`crates/tidebreak-server/src/routes/code/browser.rs`)
`/code/browser/{list,navigate,snapshot,wait,screenshot,act}`, registered as a separate router merged into the API *after* `route_layer(require_token)` wrapped the launch-token routes, so they stay under `require_app_origin` + CORS but never see the launch bearer. Each handler resolves its own `Authorization: Bearer` header through `BrowserTokenRegistry::subject_for_token`, then walks a fail-closed ladder: missing/unknown/revoked token → 401; session gone, ended, or fenced, or workspace inactive → 403; session/workspace mismatch or missing workspace → 404 (indistinguishable from a missing target). Owner, workspace, and session identity come only from the token — the deny-unknown-fields bodies make a payload naming `workspace_id`/`session_id`/`owner_id` a 400, and the token never appears in a path, query, or response body.

**Synchronous revocation hook**
`BrowserTokenRegistry::revoke` now fires an optional observer (installed at bind time when a runtime is attached) after dropping in-memory authority, calling the new `BrowserRuntime::revoke_session` — so the native capability is revoked before the session-end call returns, not on a later poll. Fires once per actually-removed entry; repeated revokes stay silent.

**Core contracts** (`tidebreak-core/src/browser.rs`)
Adopts the wait/screenshot/act contracts (`BrowserWaitArgs`/`Result`, `BrowserScreenshotArgs`/`Result`, `BrowserActArgs`/`Result`, `BrowserAction`, statuses, validators, tool specs) byte-for-byte from `thet/browser-native-driver`, so the two branches converge without conflict.

**Plumbing**
`AppState.browser_runtime: Option<Arc<dyn BrowserRuntime>>` mirrors the `LocalVoiceRunner` posture and threads through `bind_inner`; the public bind functions pass `None` until the desktop adapter lands (the trait is `pub(crate)` for now, so it deliberately cannot appear in the public bind signatures yet). New `ServerError::forbidden` / `not_implemented` helpers.

## Tests

`crates/tidebreak-server/src/tests/code_browser.rs` drives the full router over loopback HTTP with a `FakeBrowserRuntime` and directly-seeded workspace/session rows: valid token lists (and the runtime sees exactly the token's subject), missing/unknown/app-launch token → 401, ended session → 403, cross-workspace token → 404, revoked token → 401 with the hook observed synchronously, missing runtime → 501, stale snapshot → 409 `stale_browser_target`, ill-formed URLs → 422 before the runtime, subject identifiers in bodies → 400, and no error body echoes the token.

## Validation

Rust builds and tests are CI-only per repo policy; `git diff --check` is clean locally. Keeping this draft until CI is green and reviews converge.

author: longcw
body:
**Problem**

The watchdog was set to 20 seconds, below every deadline in the video loop, so it answered first for stalls the loop already handles.
It caught a blocked write into FFmpeg on 2026-08-21, five seconds before the loop's own 30 second timeout, and that path is the better one: it reports the stderr of FFmpeg, which says why FFmpeg stopped reading, where a stack dump says only that the write is stuck.
The comment in `main` also gave the wrong way to send SIGUSR1.

**Fix**

The two video deadlines now have names, so the order is legible, and a test holds the watchdog above both.
Its job is the freeze where no deadline fires at all, which ran for 148 seconds before the watchdog existed, so 75 seconds loses nothing.
`docker kill -s USR1` does print the stacks, but it marks the container manually stopped whatever signal it carries, and dockerd then refuses the restart policy for the rest of the life of that container, so the comment now gives `docker exec <name> kill -USR1 1`.

Caveat: the reason FFmpeg stopped reading its stdin is still unknown, and its stderr is what names it next time.

author: adityamukho
body:
## What

`monkeypatch.setattr(instance, name, value)` **restores** rather than deletes an attribute the instance did not own — undo captures the inherited value first, then plants it as a real entry in the instance's `__dict__`. On the module-level `_lease_manager` singleton that shadows the class method for the rest of the session, so every later class-level patch of the same name is silently ignored.

`test_ingest_status_acquires_only_when_not_running` was doing exactly that to `try_acquire`. Both it and its victim — PR #269's ablation `test_disabling_try_acquire_reuse_reproduces_the_failure`, which worked around the shadow by patching the instance too — now patch `_DbLeaseManager` itself.

## The guard

The autouse `reset_mcp_server_db` fixture now fails, at teardown, any test that leaves a class-shadowing name in `_lease_manager.__dict__`, and strips it so one offender cannot poison the rest of the run. This catches the cause at the source, which the order-dependent failure mode otherwise hides.

## Evidence

- **Mechanism confirmed directly**: after `setattr`/`undo` on the instance, `'try_acquire' in mgr.__dict__` is `True` and a subsequent class-level patch is not visible through the instance.
- **Guard watched red** against the unfixed test before the fix landed, naming `['try_acquire']`.
- **The guard found the second offender itself** on the first full-suite run — the #269 ablation — which was not in the issue's scope.
- **The ablation's counterfactual still holds**: deleting the class-level patch line makes it fail on "the ablation did not reproduce the #255 failure", so the patch is load-bearing rather than incidentally green.
- **AST sweep** of `tests/`, `evals/`, `hooks/` found no other instance-level patch of a class attribute. `strict_leak_detection` is set in `__init__`, has no class counterpart, and is correctly ignored by the guard; the `mcp_server._subprocess` patches target a module, where undo restores into the namespace the name already lived in.

Full suite: **1578 passed, 1 xfailed**.

`docs/testing-conventions.md` gains a "Patch the class, never the module-level singleton" section.

Closes #272

author: pablog55
body:
Design only — no code, nothing built. `docs/mobile.md` plus a ROADMAP entry.

## Why it is smaller than it looks

Two thirds exists. `fleet-grid.mjs` already computes every field a phone needs, and fast enough that polling is not a design problem — **0.39s** for the busiest fleet (superkey, 6 live sessions), **0.17s** for all 14 projects. `mcp/fleet-mcp.mjs` is already the complete verb set, already `project`-aware, and since #38 refuses a call with a missing argument rather than shelling out with `"undefined"` — the property you want before putting it behind a network.

Missing: a machine-readable output, a transport, a client. Not a second implementation of the grid.

## The two measurements that changed the design

**This endpoint is RCE by design.** `fleet_spawn` runs shell commands; `fleet_send` injects prompts into agents running `--dangerously-skip-permissions`. And the data is live — the grid's `LAST MSG` renders conversation text, and these transcripts hold a hosted-Neon `DATABASE_URL`, Clerk keys, and real insurance records. So: never publicly routable, and v1 executes nothing. Tailscale over Cloudflare Access because it fails closed. Quick tunnels (`cloudflared --url`, `ngrok http`, both installed here) rejected — a random public hostname in front of a process spawner is a breach with a delay.

**`pmset` says `sleep 1` on AC as well as battery.** The fleet survives today only because `ttyskeepawake` holds the machine up while tmux ttys are active — incidental, not designed. `pmset -c sleep 0` plus a held `caffeinate` is a precondition, not polish.

## No redesign

`renderGrid()` derives its column count from width, so a phone is `nc = 1` and the card is the same five lines `cardLines()` emits. The JSON schema is specified as *exactly what `cardLines()` consumes*, so the surfaces cannot drift — including the three ways the summary could lie: all nine status values survive, `unknown` is not `idle`, and `limit` is never folded into `ready`.

PWA rather than React Native, decided on the repo rather than preference: no declared dependencies, no `node_modules`, nothing imported outside node builtins. The Apple Developer account is available, so cost is explicitly not part of that argument; if push reliability proves to be the blocker the migration is cheap, because the server API does not change.

## Decisions this PR is asking for

1. Tailscale or Cloudflare Access — recommendation Tailscale
2. Is v1 strictly read-only — recommendation yes
3. Redaction scope — recommendation: serve the card's sentence, never the scrollback
4. Single-user assumption, stated throughout — confirm

§11 and §12 list these with the reasoning, and §12 is deliberately risks rather than plans.

author: dapiced
body:
## Quoi

Correctif du CI rouge sur main (run #44, commit 9bff950) : le test `calibrationCurve > bins predictions and scores them with Brier` portait une **attente erronée** — le moteur, lui, calcule juste.

Pour `y=[1,0,1,0]` et `p=[0.95, 0.85, 0.15, 0.05]`, le troisième terme du Brier est `(0,15 − 1)² = 0,7225` (la ligne est un positif prédit à 0,15), pas `0,0225`. Le Brier exact vaut **1,45/4 = 0,3625**, exactement ce que `calibrationCurve` renvoie. L'attente du test est corrigée (2 lignes).

## Pourquoi c'est passé localement

Ma validation locale pipait la sortie de vitest (`| tail -3`), ce qui **avalait le code de sortie et masquait la ligne d'échec**. Le CI, lui, lit le vrai code de sortie — il a bien fait son travail. Je durcis ma routine de validation en conséquence (lecture explicite du résumé `Tests … passed` + code de sortie).

## Preuves

`vitest run threshold.test.ts` → **11/11, exit 0** (vérifié explicitement cette fois).

Une fois mergée, main redevient vert et le **deploy V16** (bloqué par le run rouge) part.

> **High Risk**
> One-org production data repair that remaps stock, variants, and transactional FKs. Unique-conflict handling and leftover soft-deletes can silently fold SKUs if matching is wrong.
> 
> **Overview**
> Hardens the one-off KS Footwear duplicate-product repair so variant merges survive unique constraints and leftover SKUs instead of aborting mid-run.
> 
> Matching now treats **NULL size/color as equal** (`COALESCE`). When folding a source SKU into a target, `batch_stock`, `customer_product_prices`, and open `stock_alerts` are merged/deleted first so unique keys do not block FK remaps.
> 
> Reassigning a variant onto the canonical product is wrapped in a unique-violation handler that folds stock and remaps line items, then leftover active variants on the source are force-soft-deleted. The orphan assertion only fails for products this run deleted; historical orphans are NOTICE-only.
>

author: braelyn-ai
body:
The control plane's store moves from a SQLite file on the Railway volume to the project's managed Postgres service. A verbatim port — same tables, same semantics, no behavior change — as the foundation for the users-table work stacked behind it.

## Why this is safe

- **Every guard already traveled inside a single statement** (the store's own repeated design point), so the pool replacing the one `Mutex<Connection>` weakens no guarantee — the statements were written for racing callers all along.
- **Timestamps stay RFC3339 TEXT**, written by the same `stamp()`, parsed by the same `parse_ts()` — with `COLLATE "C"` on every timestamp column (including the ALTER-added ones), because the expiry comparisons are memcmp by promise and a locale collation of `-:.TZ` must not be a latent bug.
- **Identity sequences never rewind on DELETE**, preserving the never-reuse property the soft pointers (`waitlist.invite_id`) rely on.
- `insert_tenant`'s message-sniff becomes SQLSTATE 23505 + a **named** constraint (`tenants_label_key`), same conservative fall-through (unknown constraint reads as AccountTaken).
- `init` runs on every connect under a transaction-scoped advisory lock, so overlapping deploys and the CLI can't race the catalog.
- `list_waitlist`'s two SELECTs ride one `REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY` transaction — the Mutex used to be that single-snapshot guarantee.

## Cutover

`squelch-control import-sqlite /data/control.sqlite3` copies the live file over once: read-only open, refuses a non-empty target, ids preserved via `OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE`, sequences re-armed with `setval` (asserted in its test by inserting, since `last_value` reads NULL until the first nextval). Full runbook in `deploy/hosted/PRODUCTION.md`, with its own deletion clause. `rusqlite` stays only until the volume is retired.

## Tests

The suite now dials a real Postgres (`SQUELCH_TEST_PG_URL`), one throwaway schema per test, reaped after an hour — the production `connect()` path exercised verbatim, no test-only constructor. CI grows a `postgres:16` service container. Unset locally, the tests panic with the docker one-liner rather than skipping: a suite that can be silently skipped is a suite CI could silently skip too.

159 unit + 76 integration tests green; workspace clippy clean.
