author: marvinvr
body:
The cloud module's tailnet vantage was sourced from this host's own `tailscale serve` config. That only ever says **"this host believes it is serving."** It cannot see:

- a service **awaiting admin approval** in the Tailscale console,
- a service **definition that was deleted** from the tailnet,
- an **advertisement the control plane never registered**.

In every one of those the host looks perfectly healthy and nobody can reach the service — the exact failure the cloud product exists to catch. The control plane is the authority; the local serve config can lie.

## What this does

Reads the **Tailscale control plane** (`api.tailscale.com`) using the credentials DockTail already holds (`TAILSCALE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`/`SECRET` or `TAILSCALE_API_KEY`), and answers a cloud-issued `tailnet_probe` with a `tailnet_control` report.

**The credential never leaves the host.** The cloud sends a list of service names this agent itself published and receives metadata back. There is nothing to execute and no destination to choose — the metadata-only non-goals (no exec, no deploy, no shell) are unchanged.

**The cloud drives the polling, not the agent.** One credential covers a whole tailnet, so per-agent polling would scale Tailscale API load with host count. The agent still enforces `proto.MinTailnetProbeIntervalMS` (60s) between control-plane reads *regardless of what the cloud asks* — the quota being spent is the customer's, so a buggy or hostile control plane must never be able to turn it into a rate-limit incident.

## Notable

- `tailscale/control.go` — `ServiceControlState` + `APIEnabled`, with a typed `APIStatusError` so **404** (no such service definition — itself a real answer) is distinguishable from **401/403/429** without matching on error strings. `listServiceHosts` now returns that typed error; `deleteUnusedServiceDefinitions` still treats it as "skip deletion" and `Error()` reproduces the previous message text.
- **Unrecognized `approvalLevel`/`configured` vocabulary normalizes to `unknown`, never to a failure.** The raw API value strings could not be verified against a live tailnet, so matching is case-insensitive and by substring, explicit negations are tested *before* `"approved"` (so `"unapproved"` can't substring-match into a false healthy), and anything unfamiliar falls through. A monitoring agent that invents an outage from a vocabulary change is worse than one that admits it doesn't know. The raw strings travel alongside for display.
- The probe handler runs **off the websocket read loop** — a hanging Tailscale API would otherwise block heartbeats and drop the connection.
- `CapTailnetControl` is advertised **only** when credentials exist, so an agent that cannot answer is never asked.
- `tailscale/status.go` now parses the tailnet name, which is what lets the cloud group hosts sharing a control plane.

## Without credentials

Inert. Reports `no_credentials` rather than a fault, and the cloud renders "here's what to configure" instead of a phantom outage. Local monitoring is unaffected. Peer liveness (`TypeTailnet`) is untouched.

## Compatibility

`ProtocolVersion` stays 1; `cloud/proto/messages.go` is hand-synced and verified wire-identical with the cloud repo's copy. Pairs with marvinvr/docktail-cloud#23 — **deploy order between the two does not matter**: an old agent against the new cloud is never probed and degrades to a "no data" vantage, and this agent against an old cloud simply never receives a probe. Same outcome either way.

## Follow-up (not blocking)

Each inbound probe spawns a goroutine that queues on `probeMu`; a misbehaving control plane could pile them up behind a 60s in-flight read. They drain to the cached answer, but `TryLock` would be strictly better.

## Testing

Not run, per repo convention — `go build ./... && go vet ./...` and `gofmt` are clean.

author: andreolf
body:
## Motivation

Closes #467. Requested in https://github.com/ChainSafe/lodestar-z/pull/462#discussion_r3529291103: reading a slice of a composite list/vector view currently requires one `getValue`/`getReadonly` call per index, each of which walks the tree from the root.

## Description

- Adds `CompositeChunks.getReadonlyByRange(allocator, start_index, count)`: fetches the committed nodes for the range with a single `getNodesAtDepth` traversal, then materializes element views through the same cache as `getReadonly()`, so borrow rules and visibility of staged (uncommitted) writes are unchanged. The name and shape mirror `getReadonlyByRange` in the TypeScript ssz package.
- Exposes it on `ListCompositeTreeView` (runtime length bounds check) and `ArrayCompositeTreeView` (comptime length bounds check). Out-of-range requests return `error.IndexOutOfBounds` rather than clamping, following existing accessor conventions.
- `getAllReadonly` now delegates to the range variant and gets the same single-traversal speedup.

## Tests

- New unit tests cover range contents, bounds errors, empty ranges, cache identity with `getReadonly`, and visibility of an uncommitted `setValue` inside a fetched range.
- `zig build test:ssz`: 244/244 pass
- `zig build test`: full unit suite passes

author: bpintea
body:
The splitAndConvertDirect method in CsvBatchIterator previously dispatched every quoted-dialect CSV row through splitAndConvertQuoted, even when the row contained no embedded quote or escape character (the common case). This added per-row StringBuilder allocation and extra per-character checks over plain data rows, causing the ~7–9% wall-clock regression on sort_google_url_by_time observed since the direct-to-block rewrite.

Fix: scan each row buffer for the configured quote char and (when escaping=true) the escape char before dispatching. Rows with no special bytes are routed directly to the cheaper splitAndConvertPlain, which calls the same emitPlainField helper and produces identical output. Rows that do contain a quote or escape char continue through splitAndConvertQuoted unchanged.

Closes https://github.com/elastic/esql-planning/issues/1215

author: bygmedai-haruki
body:
To af Sirius' syv port-punkter. **Bevidst uden performance-gulvet** — begrundelsen står nederst og er det vigtigste i PR'en.

## 1. Node 24 overalt

```
Vercel-projektet bygger paa   24.x   ← verificeret i projekt-API'et
CI koerte                      22     ← min egen #150
Lighthouse koerte              20
```

Vi testede i to runtimes og deployede i en tredje. **Jeg lavede selv den tredje version i dag** ved at bumpe CI fra 20 til 22 og efterlade Lighthouse på 20.

Nu: `ci.yml`, `lighthouse-ci.yml`, `.nvmrc` og `engines` — alle 24, som Vercel.

## 2. Pessimistisk aggregering

Jeg påstod i #151 at LHCI aggregerer på median. **Det var forkert.** Sirius' bevis er koldt:

```
maalinger:   0,68 · 0,72 · 0,76
rapporteret: 0,76          ← den bedste, ikke medianen (0,72)
```

Default er `optimistic` — den vælger den kørsel der lettest består. Det er også derfor `total-blocking-time` med `["error", 650]` var grøn, mens én af tre kørsler målte **878 ms**: de 527 dækkede over den.

`aggregationMethod: "pessimistic"` gør at den dårligste kørsel er den der tæller. En grænse man kan gemme sig bag er ikke en grænse.

## ⚠️ Hvorfor gulvet IKKE er med her

Sirius' ruling siger `minScore: 0.68, aggregationMethod: pessimistic, level: error`. Jeg sætter kun det andet led nu, og det er med vilje:

**De 0,68 er målt på node 20 med optimistisk aggregering.** Denne PR ændrer begge dele. At gate på et tal fra en konfiguration der ikke længere findes ville være at gentage præcis den fejl vi lige har brugt en dag på: et tal uden sin kontekst.

Rækkefølgen bliver:

1. **Denne PR** → node 24 + pessimistisk. Performance er stadig `warn`, så intet går uventet rødt.
2. **Læs det første pessimistiske tal** denne konfiguration selv producerer.
3. **Næste PR** → `["error", { minScore: <det målte tal> }]` som spærreklinke.

Måle først, gate bagefter. Og Sirius' formulering står ved magt: **0,68 (eller hvad tallet bliver) er et regressionsgulv, ikke en ny definition af godt.** Krogs ≥0,90 er uændret.

## Ikke testet

Om node 24 flytter Lighthouse-tallene, og i hvilken retning. Det er hele pointen med at måle bagefter. Hvis CI på denne PR går rødt på noget uventet, siger jeg det med det samme.

## Verifikation

`typecheck` rent · **59/59** · build **18/18 sider**. Bemærk: kørt lokalt på node 22 — CI på denne PR er den første kørsel på 24, og den er den rigtige prøve.

## Rollback

Sæt versionerne tilbage og fjern `aggregationMethod`. Ingen tilstand.

— Haruki, S568 · Sirius' port-punkt 2 (delvist) og 3

author: sebe585
body:
The GIS export shipped in v1.0.5 was written for one deposit, at the request of the first outside user of the bench. Nothing in it was specific to elephants except the file name. This makes it a function of the bench rather than a favour to one reader.

## What changes

**`export_gis.py` moves to `ichnos/common/` and reads `out/<source>_pivot.parquet`.** It now runs on every dataset an adapter has converted, six of them today:

```
python3 -m ichnos.common.export_gis --list
python3 -m ichnos.common.export_gis --source storks_gps
make gis SOURCE=kruger
```

It carries whichever quality column the source actually has (`h_accuracy_m`, the e-obs fix type, the Movebank manual-outlier mark), on the rule the capability descriptor already follows: report what is there, invent nothing.

**`fence_crossings.py` takes `--source`, `--polygon` and `--zone-cm-deg`.** The control is no longer tied to this deposit. Etosha stays the default because it is the only case here that ships a boundary.

**The `make gis` and `make fence` target names do not change.** They were given to an outside user in writing on 21 August, and a renamed target would have broken that. Only what runs behind them moved.

## Two guards that came out of the move

- Above five million fixes the points layer is skipped rather than written as several gigabytes no GIS opens comfortably. The skip is printed, never silent, and the line layers are written regardless. Without it, `--source baboons_gps` writes 19.2 M points.
- The pivot files carry `bool[pyarrow]` and pandas string columns. Neither `cumsum` nor the OGR drivers accept them, and both fail late with a message about a dtype rather than about the data. The frame is brought back to numpy dtypes once, at the door.

## One declaration in the README

The export drops the rows a source marks `visible = false`. It is the only place in the bench that drops anything, and that deserved saying out loud rather than leaving to be discovered:

> Everything else here measures the file as delivered, hidden rows included, because that is what a reader who downloads the CSV actually gets. The export is the exception because a map is not a count: an outlier that is one speck among millions of points becomes the longest line on the same data.

## Verification

Regression on Etosha, pivot path against the CSV path of v1.0.5:

| | v1.0.5 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| fixes | 2,930,263 | 2,930,263 |
| flagged | 29,446 | 29,446 |
| hidden rows dropped | 5 | 5 |
| tracks | 258 | 258 |
| day paths | 10,658 | 10,658 |
| `out/etosha_fence.json` | 22 counts | identical |

Also run end to end on `kruger` (283,688 fixes, 623 tracks) and `laikipia_gps` (151,104 fixes, 35 tracks), which have no flag list: the `flagged` column stays false and the script says so.

No figure and no count of the paper changes.

## Note on this branch

The public repository is the package built by `build_release.py` from the private source, so this branch is that build, not a hand edit. Merging it is what a release does; the source-side change lives in the private repository and the two are checked identical before publishing.

## Not in this PR

Counting the `visible = false` rows across the corpus, so that the quality sheet carries the number per dataset. It is a one-line change to `corpus.py`, but it only produces anything after a full `make corpus` over 27 GB, and a sample of 12 datasets suggests hidden rows are rare (6 carried the column, none had a hidden row). Worth doing on the next corpus run, not worth one of its own.

author: vbp1
body:
## Problem

`codex-review.sh` passes the built prompt as the last argument of `codex exec`, so its
size is capped by `MAX_ARG_STRLEN` — 128 KB on Linux, regardless of what `ARG_MAX`
reports. A plan that grows over a long review cycle crosses that cap and the exec fails
with `/usr/local/bin/codex: Argument list too long` (exit 126) **before codex starts**.

It surfaces late and looks like the wrong thing: twelve rounds succeed, the thirteenth
dies, and the output reads as a codex crash rather than a size limit. Non-ASCII plans hit
it sooner than the character count suggests — Cyrillic text is two bytes per character in
UTF-8, so the cap lands near 64k characters.

`--plan-file` / `--description-file` do not help: they read the file into a variable that
is still spliced into the command line.

## Change

Both call sites — `cmd_init` and `cmd_review` (which serves `plan` and `code`) — write the
prompt to a file next to the attempt's log and pass it on stdin with `-`:

```
codex exec ... - < "$prompt_file"
codex exec ... resume "$SESSION_ID" - < "$prompt_file"
```

The previous `</dev/null` (added in #104 for the hang in #103) is no longer needed: stdin
is now a regular file, which ends at EOF, so codex cannot wait on it the way it waited on
an inherited pipe.

The prompts are archived alongside the logs and requests they belong to.
`codex-init.prompt.md` has a fixed name, so one left in the active state directory would
be overwritten by the next session instead of kept.

`.prompt.md` is added to the gitignore list the skill's README tells a project to adopt,
and to the state-directory tree in the same README.

## Coverage

`test-description-file.sh` grows from 75 to 81 assertions, all offline:

- a 183 KB plan and a 183 KB task each reach the stub whole — asserted on the **last**
  line of the text, so a truncated prompt cannot pass;
- `init` is covered separately from `plan`/`code`, since it builds and sends its prompt on
  its own path;
- the archive scenario asserts no prompt is left behind, and that the replaced session's
  init prompt lands in the archive rather than being overwritten.

Each new assertion was checked against the unpatched script and fails there.

Verified against codex-cli 0.148.0: `codex exec -` and `codex exec resume <id> -` both read
the prompt from stdin (for `resume`, `-` is the only documented form), a 132 KB argument
fails with exit 126 while the same text on stdin succeeds, and a 155 KB plan sent through

author: energee
body:
## Why

User-visible loading jank: /dashboard's route fallback was shaped like a list page under a card-grid dashboard, and /production/batches flashed blank → wrong rows → dimmed swap with a too-short table skeleton. The audit (`docs/plans/2026-08-21-loading-pattern-audit.md`) traced it to the 2026-07-15 sitewide loading plan stalling at Phase 0: seven disagreeing skeleton implementations, and a server prefetch whose payload was discarded on every default visit.

## Root causes found

1. **The default "Active" quick filter never actually applied.** It was written by a mount-time `setUrlFilters`, which races hydration — nuqs applies it optimistically and then reverts it. The page always landed unfiltered with a wasted refetch.
2. **The prefetch page size was wrong** (literal 10 vs the client's `DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE` 25), so the hydration key never matched even before filters.
3. Seven skeleton shapes with different heights chained on every cold navigation.

## What changed

- **One skeleton vocabulary** (`src/components/ui/skeletons.tsx`): the private copies in entity-data-table / entity-detail-unified / entity-relation-table / report tables are gone; dashboards and their route fallbacks compose a shared `DashboardTrendsSkeleton`; table skeletons are fold-capped and column-accurate.
- **Default quick filter = the nuqs filters-parser default** — single source of truth. Clean URL ⇒ Active view, prefetch key matches first render (verified: **zero client list fetches** on navigation), "All" writes a shareable `?filters=[]`. `DataTableFilterList`/`MobileFilterSheet` share the same parser default. The preset→filter mapping exists once (`quickFilterColumnFilters`), `DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE` lives once in `src/lib/constants.ts`, and a default preset's `sort` mirrors into the server ORDER BY (tests: `list-query-prefetch-key.test.ts`).
- **Prefetch is skipped when the URL carries explicit `?filters=`/`?sort=`** (batches, brands) instead of blocking TTFB on a query the client discards.
- **quickFilters moved to entity core** (pure data) so server prefetch can see them.
- **GettingStartedChecklist** reserves its space while loading via `usePersistedFlag` (and renders nothing on query error) instead of inserting itself after first paint.
- `/production/batches` `loading.tsx` null-hack reverted; `/settings/brands` loading is a Server Component; `/dashboard` + `/dashboard/inventory` get shape-matched fallbacks.

## Verification

- `make check` green after each commit (lint, typecheck, 3,042 vitest, build, DB checks).
- Driven live against the local stack: batches default view hydrates with zero client fetches, Active tab selected from first paint, clean URL; All ⇒ one fetch + shareable `?filters=[]` that reloads correctly; filter panel agrees with the table; dashboard fallback matches the page; no console errors.

## Follow-up

- #859 — persisted page-size restoration has been dead since before this branch (stored, never re-applied on mount).

Audit + implementation log: `docs/plans/2026-08-21-loading-pattern-audit.md`

author: skifahrer
body:
> Nezávislé od #178 (stoh vrstiev) — obe sedia na `master`, každá siaha do inej časti `devmode.js`.

## Čo sa zmenilo vecne

**1. Vzor je vidieť ako obrázok, nie ako meno.** Vyberal sa z rozbaľovačky („Šrafovanie /", „Šupiny (skaly)") a to je pri vzore ešte horšie než pri ikone: meno nepovie ani ako je hustý, ani ako hrubý, ani ako vyzerá nad farbou, ktorú tá plocha má. Teraz je pri vrstve **náhľad terajšieho vzoru** a po rozkliknutí **mriežka s náhľadmi** — kreslená tým istým rasterizérom (`renderPattern`), aký vyrobí obrázok pre mapu aj pre sprite, takže je to presne to, čo v mape bude. Kreslené vzory sa v mriežke ukazujú s TERAJŠOU farbou, veľkosťou a hrúbkou, lebo prepnutie vzoru tie tri hodnoty nemení.

**2. Náhľad sa kreslí nad farbou podkladu — a tá je hneď vedľa na zmenu.** Vzor je vždy DRUHÁ vrstva nad plochou (`fill-pattern` sa nedá kresliť do tej istej vrstvy ako výplň), takže sám o sebe nehovorí nič: to isté šrafovanie vyzerá inak nad tmavozeleným lesom a inak nad svetlou lúkou. V sekcii vzoru je preto „Podklad" — farba výplne tej vrstvy, aj s „bez výplne" (plocha stratí farbu, vzor a okraj na nej ostanú).

**3. Vlastný obrázok ako vzor.** Nahraný PNG/JPG/SVG sa uloží ako **vlastná ikona** (`own:…`, PNG v `data:` adrese) a nasadí sa ako `fill-pattern`. Nie je to obchádzka, ale celá pointa: taký obrázok sa nesie priamo v úpravách (funguje offline aj v balíku pre mobil), prehliadač ho dokreslí cez `styleimagemissing` a do každého spritu ho dopečie `workers/assets/custom-icons.mjs` — **pipeline teda netreba meniť ani riadok**. Druhá pečiaca cesta pre „obrázky, ktoré sú vzory" by bola druhé miesto, ktoré sa raz rozíde s prvým.

**Veľkosť dlaždice sa vyberá pri nahratí** (16–96 px) a obrázok sa na ňu rovno prevzorkuje. `fill-pattern` sa v MapLibre neškáluje — dlaždicuje sa tak, ako je obrázok veľký —, takže „veľkosť až pri kreslení" by musel rovnako spraviť aj sprite; čo je uložené, je to, čo mapa kreslí. Inú veľkosť dostaneš nahratím znova.

Farba, veľkosť a hrúbka ostávajú len pri kreslenom vzore (obrázok ich má v sebe — boli by to tri políčka, ktoré nič nerobia); krytie platí pri oboch.

## Ako sa to overilo

- `node workers/lint/icons.mjs` — 0 chýb, pribudla **šiesta sekcia** na dve tiché veci: meno obrázka, ktorý v úpravách NIE JE, sa nesmie dostať do štýlu (nemal by ho kto dopiecť a MapLibre neznámy `fill-pattern` ticho preskočí), a `collectPatternNames` ho nesmie vrátiť medzi kreslené vzory — `workers/styles/patterns.mjs` by cezeň v atlase nakreslil šrafovanie a prepísal obrázok, ktorý tam dal `custom-icons.mjs`. Overené aj **naopak** (po vypnutí kontroly mena lint spadne).
- `node workers/lint/overrides.mjs` — do sady, ktorou preháňa `workers/styles/overrides.mjs`, pribudla vrstva so vzorom z obrázka: do repozitára sa musia dostať OBE polovice (meno vo vrstve aj samotný PNG), inak by mapa ostala bez vzoru.
- V node overený hotový štýl: `landcover-wood__pattern` má `fill-pattern: own:…` aj vtedy, keď obrázok v sprite ešte nie je (stav hneď po nahratí), a vzor s neznámym menom normalizácia odmietne s hláškou.
- `node workers/lint/*.mjs` (všetkých osem) a načítanie modulov v node — bez chýb.
- V prehliadači overené nebolo (bezhlavé prostredie) — treba pozrieť okom, či nahratý obrázok v tej veľkosti dlaždicuje pekne (švy pri fotke budú vidieť; na vzory sa hodia obrázky, ktoré nadväzujú).

author: wixely
body:
## What

The **Start** button now reads **Restart** whenever the service is up, and does the stop and the start as one action.

```
Stopped:   [Install] [ Start ] [ Stop ] [Config] [Logs]
                      enabled   greyed

Running:   [Reinstall] [Restart] [ Stop ] [Config] [Logs]
                        enabled   enabled
```

## Why

Picking up a config change meant clicking **Stop**, waiting for the row to settle, then clicking **Start**. Start was disabled the entire time the service was running — the exact moment you most want it.

## Behaviour

- "Restart" shows when the service is `Running`, `Starting` or `Unhealthy`; "Start" when it's `Stopped` or `Faulted`.
- An `IsRestarting` flag disables the button and shows `…` in between, so the brief window where the service is genuinely `Stopped` can't be clicked into a second overlapping restart.
- **If the stop leaves the service unable to start** — faulted, or the process wouldn't die — the command returns instead of blindly calling `StartAsync`. The row then shows the real state rather than a restart that silently half-happened.
- **Stop stays a separate button.** Stopping without starting again is still something you want.

The Actions column grew 344 → 354px to fit the wider label; both the header and the row template use the same definition, so they stay aligned.

## Testing

`dotnet build -c Release` clean, **76/76 tests pass**.

No unit test for the restart itself: it's view-model logic and `MCPHub.Tests` references only `MCPHub.Core`, so covering it would mean pulling Avalonia into the test assembly. `AvaloniaUseCompiledBindingsByDefault` is on, so `StartButtonText`, `CanStartOrRestart` and `StartOrRestartCommand` are all verified against the view model at build time.

Worth a click-through on a running service before merging, since the state machine is the interesting part.

Fixes two defects found during the TICKET-064 real validation.

## TICKET-067 — ci check resolves the project's git repo via proj/
The ci check ran git in the raw project dir, so a fleet-style layout (a proj/ git repo with an origin remote next to an ai/ dir) was wrongly SKIPped as 'no origin' and never verified CI. body:
This repository is a derivative of an MIT-licensed php-collective project, and the MIT terms require the original copyright notice to be retained in derivative works. The notice was correct - what was missing was a second one covering the Carve work built on top of it.

So this **adds** a line rather than changing one:

```
Copyright (c) 2024 php-collective
Copyright (c) 2026 Mark Scherer
```

Replacing the upstream holder would have stripped a notice the license requires to be kept.

The license body is untouched and still byte-identical to the MIT text, so GitHub's detector continues to report MIT. (The recent `NOASSERTION` on vim-carve was caused by prose appended *after* the license body, not by the copyright header - a different edit.)

author: xiaokangwang1992
body:
## D1 — the input lock is removed outright, not repaired

Owner decision: option (iii). Idle-release (i) and fixing the client id so re-entry works (ii) were both rejected.

The lock did not hold up on its own terms:

- `handleWTShell` minted a **fresh random client id on every connection** and never read one from the request, so `SessionLock.Acquire`'s "same client may re-enter" branch was **unreachable in production** — and that branch is exactly what a force-takeover's own follow-up connection needed. The taker would have been locked out by the lock it had just taken.
- Keyboard input never touched the lock. The 60s `time.AfterFunc` armed once at connect time, so a user who was **still typing** at t=60s had the PTY killed and was told `session taken over` — naming a client that did not exist.
- `lock/force`, `lock_held`, `lock_taken`: **zero** references in the SPA. The endpoint was reachable only by a hand-built authenticated request.
- Zero test coverage.

Removed:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| `internal/session/lock.go` | deleted outright |
| `Registry.locks`, `Registry.GetLock` | `internal/session/registry.go` |
| `handleLockForce`, `newShellID` | `internal/server/wt_shell.go` |
| route `"/api/v1/session/"` (singular PREFIX) | `internal/server/mux.go` |

**Consumer enumeration at `2c85d9a`** (re-done, not inherited from the ticket): `SessionLock`'s only call sites were the four in `wt_shell.go` the ticket named, plus `Registry.GetLock` — a lazy factory — and the `locks` map behind it. Nothing else in `internal/` or `cmd/` touched it. Deleting `lock.go` therefore **forces** the `registry.go` edit; that is the only reason a file outside the declared scope is in this diff.

**The route was safe to unregister.** `/api/v1/session/` (singular) served nothing but `{sid}/lock/force`; `handleLockForce` 404'd every other path under it. So this removes a prefix, not an endpoint. Requests to the old path now reach the `/api/v1/` 501 stub, pinned by a routing test against the real `buildMux`.

## C1 — a shell that ends normally no longer leaks

The `case <-done:` arm — the single most ordinary way a shell ends, a user typing `exit` — had an **empty body** and fell through to a bare `stream.Close()`. For as long as the browser held its QUIC connection that left three things alive:

- **the PTY master fd**, never closed. ~1024 shell opens exhaust the daemon's descriptor limit, and what breaks then is not the shell — it is the next cert load and every listener with it.
- **the WT→PTY pump goroutine**, parked in `io.Copy` forever. `Stream.Close()` closes the **send** direction only (`stream.go:404`: "It does not close the receive-direction"), so closing the stream cannot wake it.
- **the WebTransport session**, still registered. `Server.Upgrade` builds it with `context.WithoutCancel(r.Context())` (`server.go:379`) over a CONNECT stream hijacked from http3 (`server.go:366`) — precisely so the handler returning does *not* end it.

All three library facts re-verified in `webtransport-go@v0.10.0` for this change.

Teardown is now unconditional across both remaining arms and lives in `pumpShell`, extracted so a test can reach it (the handler needs a real QUIC connection). `/wt/shell` was the only WebTransport route in the package without a session close — `serveChat`, `serveControl` and `serveEvents` all open with `defer CloseWithError(0, "")`.

## Known regression, left standing on purpose

The resize lane (tether#68) routes by **sid alone**, and the removed lock was what made two live shells on one sid impossible. Two panes on one sid now both connect, and `Registry.shellResize` holds whichever registered last: the older pane's resizes reach the newer pane's PTY, and the newer pane's exit unregisters the sid out from under the older one.

Fixing it means keying `shellResize` by shell instance instead of by sid — a change to `Registry`'s shape, not to the shell handler. Documented at both ends (`attachShellResize` and `RegisterShellResize`) rather than patched at the call site where it would only look fixed. **Needs its own ticket.**

## Verification

`GOWORK=off` throughout; `make build` first (web/dist is not in git).

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `make build` | pass, SPA embed verified |
| `go vet ./...` | clean |
| `go test -count=1 ./...` | **1254** pass/skip, 0 fail, 0 `[setup failed]` |
| `go test -count=1 -race ./...` | **1254**, 0 races |
| cross-compile + vet, all 5 released platforms | clean |
| `check-artifacts` / codegen drift | clean |
| web suite | 936 (934 + the 2 known skips) |

**Test count 1243 → 1254. Bidirectional name set diff: zero tests removed**, 11 added (6 top-level + 5 subtests).

### Red before green

`pumpShell` was first extracted with the leaky teardown verbatim. Against it, all three assertions failed on the `exit` path — and only two failed on the disconnect path, independently confirming the ticket's claim that the `<-ctx.Done()` arm already closed the PTY. Suite time 10.27s (timeouts hit) → 1.27s after the fix.

### Why these quantities are the determinate ones

- **fd**: measured **per-object**, not as a count. After `pumpShell` returns, writing to the PTY master must report `os.ErrClosed` — an answer that comes from `os.File`'s own state before any syscall, so it is a two-valued fact about *this* descriptor decided at the moment of return. A `/proc/self/fd` delta would be a global count in a process where the runtime, the netpoller and other tests open and close descriptors. A still-open master answers `EIO` instead, so the two outcomes cannot be confused. The PTY is a **real** `pty.Open()`, not a mock counting a method call.
- **goroutine**: the pump's only blocking call is `stream.Read`, so "Read returned" is necessary and sufficient for it to run to completion. The fake stream records that edge. Bounded wait on a channel close, not a sleep.
- **the guillotine's absence**: cannot be proved behaviourally in bounded time — watching an idle shell survive 200ms says nothing about 60s. So it is proved **structurally**: `lock.go` is gone, none of `SessionLock` / `ForceAcquire` / `lockTimeout` / `GetLock` / `handleLockForce` survives **as an identifier** anywhere in `internal/` or `cmd/` (AST, not grep — so comments naming them are allowed and a declaration is not), and `pumpShell` has exactly one `select` with exactly two cases and no reference to `time` at all. A deadline needs a clock; the shell's lifetime has none.

The fake stream deliberately encodes the two library facts: `Close()` does **not** wake a blocked `Read`; only the session going away does. A fake that woke `Read` on `Close()` would make the buggy code pass.

### Guards on the guards

- The symbol walk fails if it collects fewer than 60 files (a walk that stopped finding files would pass against anything).
- `funcShapeOf` is asserted against the reconstructed pre-tether#121 shape (3 cases, `time.AfterFunc`) and against a function name absent from the source, so neither the case count, the clock check, nor `found` can silently stop measuring.

### Mutants — each reverted individually, each killed

| # | Mutant | Compiles | Killed by | Isolation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | re-register `/api/v1/session/` with the old handler shape | yes | `TestShellLockForceRouteIsGone` | 405 vs 501, 2 rows |
| M2 | restore `internal/session/lock.go` | yes | `TestShellLockSymbolsAreGoneFromTheDaemon` | file-exists + 3 identifiers |
| M3 | 60s `time.NewTimer` + third select arm | yes | `TestShellLifetimeHasNoClock` | both case-count and clock |
| M4a | delete both `closeSession()` calls | yes | `TestPumpShell_*` | **only** (b) + (c) fail; fd assertion still passes |
| M4b | delete the unconditional `closePTY()` | yes | `TestPumpShell_*` | **only** the fd assertion fails, 3/3 runs |

M4a and M4b together show each of the three assertions is individually load-bearing. Reverts were done with `cp` from `/tmp` backups and checked by `sha256sum`, never `git restore`.

author: lksndrtmlkv
body:
Addresses items 4 and 5 of #148 — the last of the five. **Stacked on #152**
(which is stacked on #151); review those first.

Verified against a node built from this branch, running on a throwaway
Postgres — not against the published image, which predates `/whoami`.

## Item 4 — three endpoints with no CLI route

**`odal whoami`.** New top-level command. Verified with a real `read`-scoped
key, which is the whole point of the endpoint:

```
$ ODAL_API_KEY=<read-scoped> odal whoami
user  : api-key
scope : read
key   : 01a024e0-bba0-7573-9d66-79fe7557b187

$ ODAL_API_KEY=<read-scoped> odal key list
Error: failed to list keys: Forbidden — API key management requires an admin-scoped credential.
```

The second command was previously the only way a read-only key could learn what
it was.

**`odal passport validate <file>`.** The file argument is optional, so the
no-arg form still checks stored drafts and nothing existing changes.

A rejection comes back as the identical response `create` would have sent, so a
non-2xx is the verdict. `401`/`403` are the exception — they mean the caller was
not entitled to ask, which says nothing about the file:

```
$ ODAL_API_KEY=<read-scoped> odal passport validate good.json
Error: cannot validate: Forbidden — Validating a passport body requires a write-scoped credential.
```

**`odal status` surfaces the trust posture**, so `seal: ghost` is finally
visible. The CLI's `NodeState` was dropping `profile`, `trustMode` and
`rulesetVersion` on the floor.

## Item 5 — two kinds of check in one table

Probes have a URL and a latency; containers have a name and a state and no
latency. They are now two tables, and the probe failure reason moved out of the
fixed-width status column where anything over eight characters broke every row
below it.

```
SERVICE      URL                                    STATUS   LATENCY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
vault        http://localhost:8011/vault/health     OK       323ms
resolver     http://localhost:8013/health           FAIL     2345ms  unreachable

CONTAINER    NAME                                   STATE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
postgres     odal-node-postgres-1                   OK

TRUST
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
profile             development
seal                ghost
ruleset             baseline

! Running on a stand-in: archive, credential_issuers, registry_sync, seal.
  Anything depending on them carries no legal weight.
```

`compliance: sandbox` is deliberately not warned about — sandbox is a real
service in a test tier, and crying wolf teaches operators to ignore the line
that matters.

The posture is authenticated while the probes are not, so an unreadable posture
renders as absent rather than failing the command. Verified: `odal status` on an
entirely unconfigured machine still prints both tables and omits the trust
section.

## One finding worth a separate look

**`publishValid: true` from `POST /api/v1/dpp/validate` does not mean publish
would succeed.** `publish_readiness` is `validate_sector_data` +
`validate_schema_for_publish` — it never reaches the registry-identity check or
the category-mandatory-content gate, both of which run at real publish time.
Demonstrated on a live node: the dry run returned `publishValid: true` for a
body that publish then refused with `422 — missing required registry identity`.

That is the endpoint's behaviour, not this CLI's, and is left alone here. But
rendering it as "publish would be accepted" would have been this CLI telling the
operator something false, so the label says what was actually checked:

```
✓ create   would be accepted
✓ publish  passes the sector-data schema gate

Publish applies further checks this preview does not run (registry identity,
category-mandatory content).
```

## Verification

`just check` green (809 tests, 5 new). The new unit tests cover the pure logic —
ghost-vs-sandbox classification, the no-posture case, and that `all_ok` still
counts both halves of the split report. Command behaviour was verified by
running the binary against a live node, as this repository has no CLI
integration harness.

author: mynjj
body:
Adding public codeunits for creating "Matched Order Line" records. The first consumer of this API will be the E-Documents app to allow for creating 1-M matches and that can be received on invoice from the Payables Agent flows.

All the changes are additive and no existing BaseApp flow with the existing logic has been disturbed. We have yet to decide whether to update our own existing `MatchedOrderLineMgmt` with it. In essence, this change is only a facade for inserting "Matched Order Line" records.

The one novel bit, is an internal usage of this new API in the codeunit `PO Matching`, where we add a surface to suggest receipts in a match: given the order and the proposed match, if there are receipts that could cover the remaining amount to invoice, they are suggested in the match. This new procedure is not uptaken internally in the BaseApplication, but it will be used in the E-Document app (see second PR on the stack) as a convenience when receiving invoices from that flow that didn't have receipts specified for matching.

The new public API encapsulates a new match under the `PO Matching Group`, that holds a buffer of the matches to be inserted. At every point in time that a new match is added to the buffer, we run validations to ensure that it makes sense quantity-wise, and the other validations we have (like no prepayment, or partial receipts for item-tracked), additionally we discover the already existing matches that have been persisted in the database and load the whole match as well so that the validations are applied considering those as well. The edges to be loaded are discovered in a BFS fashion, and appended running the validations.

A iterator is implemented for `PO Matching Group` to allow consuming the matches, additionally, another iterator to encapsulate the possible receipts to suggest (`Invoiceable Receipts`) was also added. See how they are used to suggest the receipts on the match.

Fixes [AB#625392](https://dynamicssmb2.visualstudio.com/1fcb79e7-ab07-432a-a3c6-6cf5a88ba4a5/_workitems/edit/625392)

author: clarejor
body:
Follows #101, which reshaped recurring schedule storage into a recurrence plus two independent bounds, and #104, which moved the add/edit dialog into its own component. This is the user-facing half of that reshape: the two rows that set the bounds, the dialog chrome around them, and the run window's exposure on the Zones panel.

## Start and Finish rows

The dialog carried one anchor: a single clock time or solar event, plus a flag saying whether that time meant the start or the end of watering. A window has two ends and only one of them could be expressed.

Each end is now its own row, independently `No limit` / `At a time` / `At sunrise` / `At sunset` / `At solar azimuth`, with the one stepper that mode's quantity needs: a clock for a time, signed minutes for a solar event, degrees for a bearing. What the schedule does follows from which ends are bounded, and the row's help line says it:

- Start only: the run begins then and every due zone runs to completion.
- Finish only: the run starts early enough to end at the target.
- Both: the run is fitted to the window, the finish is a deadline, and a third row asks whether to water as early or as late as possible inside it.

Neither bounded describes no time at all, so it blocks Save; the backend rejects the same shape, and the dialog now reads that rejection rather than closing on it. A rejected save arrives as a successful websocket result carrying `success: false` rather than as an exception, so without the check an edit the backend refused would vanish silently on the next reload.

`schedule-rows.ts` holds the mapping between the stored fields and the rows, so both ends go through one piece of logic instead of the Start end being the general case and the Finish end a flag on it. Changing a row's mode replaces its value with that mode's default in the same step, and the rows-to-fields direction always writes every field so a stale `start_azimuth` cannot hang off a mode that has no bearing. Its test drives every mode and anchor pair and includes a rows to fields to rows identity check.

## Dialog chrome and the summary sentence

The dialog gained enough fields with the second bound that an ungrouped list stopped being readable, so it groups into When, Zones and Season, and the day and zone pickers render as chips rather than a row of checkboxes.

`schedule-summary.ts` builds a plain-language sentence restating the whole schedule. The same sentence heads the dialog and each card in the schedule list, so the two cannot word it differently, and it describes the schedule's own configuration only, never live bucket or weather state: a sentence that changed because tonight's forecast changed would be describing something nobody configured.

`schedule-shape.ts` translated the stored two-bound schedule into the old single-anchor shape for the dialog to render. The dialog reads the stored shape directly now, so it and its test are removed.

One other state in `schedule-rows.ts` is reachable by its callers but not by this UI. `describeWindow` takes an optional set of ends that cannot be resolved to a time, and returns warning help for them; only a solar azimuth bearing can be unresolvable, and only at a latitude where the sun never crosses it. Resolving a bearing needs solar geometry that is not part of this change, so nothing here passes that argument and the two warning strings do not render yet. The help vocabulary is complete in one place rather than split across the module and its later caller.

That missing geometry is also why the When card carries no run window dial: drawing the window on a 24 hour clock needs the same solar positions, and it is a large enough piece to be worth reading on its own, so it comes separately rather than on top of this.

## Zones panel

Two things a windowed run does were invisible from the panel, and both read as defects when they are not.

A finish-anchored run is sized from the water demand read shortly before it begins, so the start time shown for it moves until that moment. The next-run line and the at-a-glance decision carry an "estimated" marker with the reason on hover, which clears once the run is armed. `UpcomingRun.estimated` and `start_bound_utc` are optional, and the scheduler does not publish either yet, so on this branch the marker is inert: it renders nothing until the resolver that computes a decision point lands. It is here rather than with that resolver because it is panel copy, and putting it there would pull the frontend bundles into a backend change.

A zone whose computed duration hits its maximum duration emits nothing at all: the shortfall is simply never watered, so deepening the bucket threshold past what the cap can deliver is silently ignored and the zone drifts drier every cycle. The zone card now says so. The condition is derived from the stored duration rather than reported, because the clamp is unambiguous there: `calculate_module` clamps first and adds lead time afterwards, so a run that hit the cap is exactly lead time plus the cap. Only automatic zones go through that path, and a manual zone's hand-set duration is excluded.

## Translations

Fifty-two new keys ship in all eight catalogues in this PR, and thirteen keys the old anchor left behind are removed from all eight. Each string is built from that catalogue's own existing wording rather than translated from the English afresh, so the German bucket stays `Vorrat`, the French one `seau (bucket)`, and so on. Every interpolated string was compiled and formatted with the same message formatter the panel uses, in its own locale, including the Slovak plural categories.

## Verification

Against the head commit of this branch:

- 1798 passed, 9 skipped; ruff and black clean on `custom_components/`.
- 451 frontend tests across 13 files; `tsc --noEmit` and eslint clean on the changed sources; `dist/` reproduces byte-identically from a fresh build.
- Live on a Home Assistant instance running this branch, with the panel bundle it served confirmed byte-identical to the one committed here. Each bound mode was set through the dialog and saved, and every schedule round-tripped through storage unchanged: a clock start, sunrise with a negative offset as the finish, both ends bounded with a sunset finish on a weekly recurrence, a solar azimuth start, and an interval schedule. The both-unbounded shape was refused by the backend and the dialog blocked Save on it.
- Each of those resolved to the expected occurrence. The sunrise finish with a thirty minute offset resolved to sunrise minus thirty, with the start placed one run length earlier; the both-bounded weekly resolved to the next Monday, finishing fifteen minutes after sunset and starting as late as the window allowed; the azimuth start resolved to the sun's crossing of due west.
- The duration cap warning was confirmed on a real clamped zone, and left off the six zones that were not clamped.
- The German and Slovak catalogues were confirmed to be served from the integration's static path with their own strings for the new keys, not an English fallback.

author: patrick-hermann-sva
body:
Closes #12. Part of #7. Based on `main` — no stacking this time.

The plain roster becomes a ranking, and every name links to a profile.

## Counting in SQL, ranking in Go

The split follows what #12 asks for: the repository returns rows, a package turns them into a table.

`PlayerRepository.Records` counts confirmed matches per player **in one statement**. Answering "how many has she won" with a Go loop over every match is the shape the repository interface exists to avoid, and it is the aggregation Postgres was chosen for (ADR-0001).

The winner comes from the **set scores**, not from the rating history. A strong favourite who wins can move by zero points — "did the rating go up" is a different question from "did they win", and AP5 already had one bug from confusing them.

`internal/standings` owns the part that is easy to get quietly wrong: two players on the same rating share a rank, and the next distinct rating skips the ranks they used up.

| | 1100 | 1100 | 900 |
|---|---|---|---|
| correct | 1. | 1. | **3.** |
| tempting | 1. | 1. | 2. |

Rank 2 there promotes somebody nobody beat. Every fresh pair of players hits this on day one, since neither has played.

It sorts its own input rather than trusting the order it arrives in. The repository does sort — but a ranking that silently depends on that is one refactor away from being wrong, and a few dozen rows cost nothing.

## The chart, and why it looks the way it does

A stat tile: the current rating as the number people came for, what the last match did to it, and the history as an inline SVG line. Each decision is a way it could have gone wrong:

- **The series opens with the rating *before* the first match.** Otherwise a first win reads as the starting position rather than as a rise.
- **The vertical range is the data's own, not zero-based.** Ratings sit around a thousand; a zero baseline would flatten every match ever played into one straight line. That is only honest because the range is printed beside the chart — `Verlauf 1000 bis 1008`.
- **One series, so no legend.** The label above the number says what the line is. The line stays recessive and only the current rating carries the accent, which is the point a reader is looking for.
- **A flat history sits in the middle** rather than dividing by zero or hugging an edge, and a player with no matches gets no chart at all — one point is a dot pretending to be a trend.
- **The match table underneath is the same data in numbers**, for anyone the line does not serve. It also marks what does not count: a pending result reads `offen`, a contested one `strittig`, neither with a rating change.
- **No hover layer.** A crosshair needs JavaScript, and invariant 7 says HTMX or nothing. The table carries what a tooltip would.

Columns get `tabular-nums` so they stay aligned while ratings move. The large number on the profile deliberately does not — tabular digits are all the width of a zero, which reads loose at 2.5rem.

## Replaced, not added

The standings replace the old player list everywhere — index, the out-of-band refresh after a join, and after a confirmation. Two renderings of the same players would drift. `/fragments/players` is now `/fragments/standings`.

## Verified

- `go build`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint`, `go test -race -p 1`, generated-code check — green.
- **Sparkline geometry has its own tests**: the extra opening point, both ends spanning the box, the highest rating at the top and the lowest at the bottom, the flat-history division-by-zero case, and the marker sitting on the last point.
- `Records` tested against **PostgreSQL 18**, including that a pending match and a disputed one are both excluded, and that a player with no matches comes back as a row of zeroes instead of vanishing from the ranking.
- Image built, run, full verify script executed against it. Rendered output read back:

```
1.  Verify Anna  1008  1  1:0
2.  Verify Bodo   992  1  0:1

<polyline points="6.0,42.0 234.0,6.0">   Verlauf 1000 bis 1008
```

`verify` now follows the profile link **out of the rendered markup**, so it also proves the ranking links anywhere at all.

## That leaves AP7

#13 is the last work package, and the one the Definition of Done most depends on — without the QR code, entry friction is the likeliest reason nobody logs anything. It has an open point to settle first: the MVP schema has no table entity, so the QR code needs either an opaque string in the URL or a minimal `tables` row. My reading is still the former.

author: elizafarley
body:
## Summary
- **Grasp by descending in the gripper frame**: instead of computing a second camera-frame grasp pose (and transforming to `world`), the pick now moves above the block in the camera frame while the arm is still at home, then descends the remaining distance straight down in the gripper's OWN frame (`Pose(z=grasp_distance)` in `reference_frame=gripper`). Since `cam-1` is wrist-mounted, its frame shifts as soon as the arm moves for the approach; resolving the descent relative to the gripper avoids that drift. The remaining descent is `(APPROACH_MM - GRIPPER_LENGTH_MM)` as a positive value. Applied consistently across `module-reference.py`, `reference-solution.py`, and the `starter-script.py` TODOs.
- **Drop the `LinearConstraint` descent** (`reference-solution.py`): removes the `Constraints`/`LinearConstraint` import and the optional Phase-5 straight-down follow-up, plus the related NOTE in the docstring — the gripper-frame descent already comes straight down, and this isn't covered in the companion tutorial.
- **`module-reference.py` config/type cleanup**:
  - Swaps the motion dependency from `Motion` to `MotionClient` (import, `motion: MotionClient` field, and the `builtin` lookup).
  - Renames the pose config attributes to hyphenated names (`home-pose`, `travel-pose`, `place-pose`) with matching required-attribute validation, and renames the switch fields to `home_pose`/`travel_pose`.
  - Resolves and stores `gripper_name`/`camera_name` from attrs and uses them in the pick flow instead of hard-coded resource names.
  - Replaces the concrete `MODEL` triplet with the `<auto-generated-namespace>`/`<unique-id>` placeholder so the reference doesn't ship a real module identity.
- **Starter-script guidance** (`starter-script.py`): rewrites the TODO 6/7 walkthrough to teach the gripper-frame descent (approach in the camera frame, then descend in the gripper frame) instead of the old world-frame transform, and comments out the `machine.resource_names` debug print.

Companion tutorial changes: https://github.com/viamrobotics/docs/pull/5277

## Why
Testing showed the wrist-mounted camera's frame shifts once the arm moves for the approach step, so a grasp pose computed relative to the camera drifted off target. Rather than transforming poses to the `world` frame at detection time, the approach is resolved from the camera frame while the arm is still at home (accurate) and the final grasp is a fixed straight-down descent in the gripper's own frame (drift-free) — simpler and more reliable than the transform-to-world approach.

## Test plan
- [x] Run a full pick cycle against a real/simulated arm and confirm the grasp lands on the block after the approach move (no drift)
- [x] Verify config validation rejects machines missing any of the `home-pose`/`travel-pose`/`place-pose` switches
- [x] Confirm the inline module loads with `MotionClient` and completes a `pick_cycle` do_command
- [x] Work through the starter-script TODOs end-to-end as a student would

Adds `research/reports/report088-windows-update-lifecycle-2026-08-21.md`. Report only — the batch provenance for the three issues in #7, #8 and #9, branched off `main` at `7f03345`.

Per `reqts/issues/README.md`, the issues are canonical for the findings and are not restated here; this carries method, coverage, threats to validity and the command log, and links both directions.

## Two arms

**Arm A — the update lifecycle.** `install → test → uninstall → reinstall` on the box exactly as report 086 left it: a **pre-manifest v0.10.0 install**, which is the input issue 039's fallback path exists for and which disappears once everyone has upgraded. All three new issues come from this arm.

**Arm B — re-verification of the nine issues from #2 against v0.10.2 on Windows.**

> **8 of 9 confirmed fixed. The 9th (019) is correctly absent from the release.**
> **Issue 022's full real-Windows checklist — found / entry-count / drive-letter / kind / not-found — now passes on hardware**, which is the outstanding condition the v0.10.2 release notes name for closing it.

Arm B produced **zero** new issues. Worth stating plainly, because a re-verification that finds nothing is both the outcome you want and the one that looks like idle work.

| issue | verdict | evidence in brief |
|---|---|---|
| 014 | **fixed** | `--type d --max-depth 0/1/2` → 1/5/6 on a 4-subdir fixture; the triage's bonus defect (dirs leaking into `--type f`) fixed too |
| 015 | **fixed** (tier-1) | recovery hint on **both** `skillcheck` and `skillgrants`; exit 2 kept by design |
| 016 | **fixed** | `--cap`, uncapped default, `=== truncated: showing 40 of 1498 lines` with the true total, clean bad-value error |
| 017 | **fixed, both halves** | 086's misleading `1 matches → the only hit is a build artifact` is now `0 matches (3 excluded: node_modules, target)` |
| 018 | **fixed, both halves** | the three byte-identical outputs 086 recorded are now three distinct verdicts; `--require-markers` exits 1; `0 tests passed` scores 0 |
| 019 | **not in this release — correctly** | `7add972` closed it 2026-08-16, after the 2026-08-11 cut. Gap still present verbatim: 71 lines, `tt which` 0× |
| 020 | **fixed, all three** | help exits 0 on `help`/`--help`/`-h`; gitinfo hint present; digest names `tt find` + the division of labour |
| 021 | **fixed** | every carrier reads `0.10.2` at the tag; CHANGELOG section exists; the honest note about v0.10.0 stands |
| 022 | **fixed, verified on hardware** | all five checklist items; entry count 36 == ground truth 36, single-entry PATH → `1 dirs` |

For 017 the fixture is a deliberate byte-level replica of the one report 086 recorded, so the before/after comparison is direct rather than analogous.

**The 019-after-022 ordering constraint held.** Report 086 warned that landing 019 first would teach Windows users to trust a broken check. 022's fix shipped in v0.10.1 and 019's doc lands in v0.10.3, so a Windows reader meets the prescribed `tt which tt` ritual only once it works — honoured across three releases and two reports.

## What the report adds beyond the issues

- **The full command log**, 57 commands with the reason each was run and what it settled — requested by @hmiddelk as part of this follow-up.
- **Coverage stated honestly: 8 of 45 tools invoked for real, 37 untested on Windows.** One more than 086's 7, same denominator. The Windows sweep in report 085's style remains undone and is named as still owed.
- **Six corrections withdrawn during the run**, including two that changed what got filed:
  * the **numbering and two of five findings** — the duplicate check was run against `reqts/issues/` on `main` (highest 039) but **not against open PRs**, where #4, #5 and #6 already claimed 040-042 and had already filed two of my findings. On a repo where issues arrive *as* PRs, `main` is the wrong denominator. Report 087's lesson recurring in a new place; @hmiddelk caught it by asking.
  * **issue 043's severity and placement** — first drafted as the "aggravating half" of 044 with the prediction that it would *"close when v0.10.3 ships"*. Both wrong, and the reframing came from the human asking why downloading the script had not been enough.
  * three tooling errors of mine (a `>`-redirect that line-wrapped a downloaded file and inflated 360 lines to 873; a regex-escaped pattern passed to `-SimpleMatch`; a mojibake blamed on the tool that was PowerShell's ANSI-default reader).
- **Threats to validity**, including that arm B is confirmation-shaped in the direction where a tester stops looking early, that 022's entry-count check is one bit weaker than 086's asymmetric case, and that these confirmations are cross-platform but **not cross-observer** — same human, same agent model as 085–087.

## Also recorded

A **prediction registered before the deletion** in arm A: the uninstaller listed 29 files against 30 on disk, and the gap was named as `reqts/PRD.md` *in advance*. It held exactly. That is the Windows confirmation for issue 040 (#4) — held rather than pushed into your open branch. Same for issue 042 (#6), where both halves reproduced independently before I had read that PR. Happy to open those as `## Discussion` comments once #4 and #6 merge.

Two notes that belong to issue 022's eventual closing comment rather than to any new issue: the printed filename carries the PATHEXT probe's casing (`tt.EXE`, `git.EXE`) rather than the file's, and the single-entry case reads `1 dirs`.

## Numbering

Report number 088 continues the series after 087; the filename matches the path the three issue files already cite, so the cross-references resolve on merge. The issues assume #4, #5 and #6 land first — per `reqts/issues/README.md` the later PR renumbers if not, and the report's *Duplicate check* section explains the dependency.

Agent disclosure: an AI agent (Claude Opus 5) ran both arms, made the pre-deletion prediction, measured the ground truth for every verdict, and drafted this report under my direction. I supplied the uninstall command under test, redirected the work from #3 to #2, hit issue 043 by following the documented procedure, and asked for the duplicate check against #4–#6 that corrected the findings list. Six claims the agent made were withdrawn during the run and are recorded in the report.

author: helix-nine
body:
## Summary

Bumps Forgejo **16.0.2 → 16.0.3** and the StartOS version **16.0.2:0 → 16.0.3:0**.

16.0.3 is a current-line patch release carrying Forgejo's [2026-08-20 consolidated security patches](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/security-announcements/issues/58) (PR [13985](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/pulls/13985)), plus a batch of backported fixes.

Only two files change: the `dockerTag` in `startos/manifest/index.ts` and `startos/versions/current.ts`.

## Artifact verification

`codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:16.0.3` is published and resolves, with both arches the manifest declares:

| platform | present |
| --- | --- |
| `linux/amd64` (`x86_64`) | yes |
| `linux/arm64` (`aarch64`) | yes |

Picked `16.0.3` over `v15.0.7`, which was published three minutes earlier the same day on the **LTS** line — `UPDATING.md`'s selection rule is highest version, not newest by date.

Registry currently has `16.0.2:0` as its only `best` entry and there is no `v16.0.3_0` tag, so `16.0.3:0` is free.

## Version graph

The departing `16.0.2:0` carried an empty `up`, so `current.ts` is edited **in place** rather than spun off into `other[]`. `other: []` and `down: IMPOSSIBLE` are unchanged.

## Release notes

Written against the upstream **security PR bodies** rather than the auto-generated release-notes summary lines. That changed three claims a summary-line reading would have gotten wrong:

- **Actions commit drift.** Upstream issue [12572](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/issues/12572) is a *wrong-commit* race — a delayed run executing a newer commit than the one that triggered it — not a wrong-pull-request one. The bullet says so, and covers both halves of the fix (PRs [13706](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/pulls/13706) and [13752](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/pulls/13752)) rather than only the `pull_request` half.
- **`pull_request_target`.** Now names the defect — workflows expanded local reusable workflows from the pull request's untrusted **head** branch instead of the trusted base branch — instead of only stating post-fix behaviour. An operator reading a `**Security**` bullet needs to know what was exposed. Described as "a vulnerability", matching upstream's own wording, which reserves "privilege escalation" for the collaborator issue.
- **Collaborator → owner.** Records that a repository administrator could promote **themselves**, which is the impact PR 13985 states.

Also added the 401 fix (PR [13740](https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/pulls/13740)): besides returning 401 instead of a login redirect, it stops those requests from invalidating a valid web session — self-hosters see that as spurious logouts, so it is worth a line.

All five locales (`en_US`, `es_ES`, `de_DE`, `pl_PL`, `fr_FR`) carry the same 4 Security + 7 Fixes bullets in the same order.

Note PR 13985 adds a `workflow_source_commit` column to `action_run`. Forgejo applies this itself through `forgejo_migrations` at startup, so no package migration and no user action is needed.

## No SDK or dependency changes

- `@start9labs/start-sdk` is already pinned at `2.0.9`, the latest published — no bump, and `package-lock.json` is untouched.
- The package pins no `*-startos` git dependencies, so there is nothing to re-resolve. No nested SDK copies in the lock.

## No package code changes needed

I read the full upstream 16.0.3 notes against this package's integration surface. Nothing in the release touches a `FORGEJO__*` config key, the `forgejo admin user` CLI the actions drive, the `SSH_PORT` / `ROOT_URL` derivation, or the healthz check. I specifically checked PR 13740 since a 401 change could plausibly affect the health check — its diff touches the web auth path only, and the check is an unauthenticated GET to the API healthz route.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run check` (`tsc --noEmit`) clean.
- [x] `prettier --check` clean on both changed files.
- [x] `codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:16.0.3` manifest resolves with `linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`.
- [x] Every release-note bullet traced to a specific upstream PR.
- [x] Locale parity: 11 bullets each, version `16.0.3` in every opening line and Full-notes URL, zero residual `16.0.2` repo-wide.
- [x] `16.0.3:0` free on the registry; no `v16.0.3_0` tag.
- [ ] `make` / s9pk pack and install — not run; per the monitor cycle this ships on a green typecheck, fuller verification happens here in review.

## Proposals, not implemented

- `UPDATING.md`'s "Applying the bump" section documents only the `dockerTag` edit. It never mentions `startos/versions/current.ts`, the version-string move, or that release notes are required in five locales. Following it verbatim would ship a new image under the already-published `16.0.2:0`. Worth extending — happy to do it here or separately.
- `UPDATING.md`'s worked examples use `15.0.3` / `15.0.x`-as-current, which is now the LTS line, directly under the paragraph warning not to pick the LTS line.

**Merge with a merge commit — do not squash.** `next` is long-lived: a merge commit leaves it a true ancestor of `master`, so it fast-forwards cleanly afterwards. A squash re-lands the same content under a new commit, so the branch is left carrying history `master` will never contain.

body:
There are many cases where commercial use of YouTube-derived data is legally problematic, even when the underlying video carries a Creative Commons licence and even when the transcripts have been manually cleaned, annotated, or corrected. 

The reason is that the licence on the content and the terms governing the method of retrieval are separate concerns: YouTube's Terms of Service restrict programmatic downloading regardless of how the video itself is licensed, so a CC licence on the content does not by itself clear the acquisition path. Separating these documents into their own files means the rest of the test set can be used in industrial settings without that ambiguity, while the YouTube-sourced portion remains fully available to anyone whose use case permits it. 

We'd be grateful if you would consider merging this, and we're happy to adjust the approach if you'd prefer it structured differently.

author: hawkynt
body:
Seventeen rows of §11 and eleven of §83 were open. This closes fourteen and seven of them; the rest
are left unticked or amber with the reason written on the line.

## §11 — the window catches up with the terminal

Eleven of §11's rows read "terminal only", which is another way of saying the window had a header it
could sort by and nothing else.

| | Terminal | Window |
|---|---|---|
| Reorder | `{` `}` | drag the header, or `Ctrl+Shift+←`/`→` |
| Resize | `,` `.` | drag the boundary, or `Ctrl+-`/`Ctrl++` |
| Reset | `0` | `Ctrl+0` |
| Auto-size one / all | `a` `A` | `Ctrl+1` / `Ctrl+2` |
| Multi-column sort | `o`, shift-click | shift-click, or Sort by ▸ Break ties with |
| Keyboard sort | `F6` `<` `>` | `F6` `Shift+F6` `F7` |
| Copy cell / row | `y` `Y` | `Ctrl+Shift+C` / `Ctrl+C` |
| Export | `X` | `Ctrl+E`, six formats by extension |
| Case-sensitive | `!` | the Match case box |
| Highlight matches | yes | yes |
| Multi-selection | `Space` | a tick box on the row |
| Select all / invert | `Ctrl+A` `v` | the Edit menu |

The window had no filter box at all — §56's query language was reachable from the terminal and from
`--filter` and from nowhere in the GUI, which is why case-sensitivity and match highlighting were
both stuck. There is one now, above the table, with the case toggle beside it and the parser's
complaint beside that.

The header work deliberately does not go through `ColumnClick`. The toolkit reports a header press as
a bare column index, with no modifier state and no way to see a drag, and §11 wants three gestures on
that header; the control raises that event only when something is subscribed to it, so leaving it
alone hands the whole header to one set of handlers rather than having two of them fight over one
press.

**Freeze / pin columns stays amber**, and needs a toolkit seam rather than more work here:
`TreeListView` paints every column from one `HorizontalOffset` and has no pinned region to paint
into. **Copy selected columns** stays amber too — the rows are done in both front-ends, a column is
not in either, because there is no cell selection to copy one from (§95).

## §83 — grouping

The list can be headed by user, session, service, executable, container, cgroup or package, and the
tree is one of the choices rather than a flag beside them: a list is nested by parentage or headed by
something else, and it can never be two of those at once. `G` in the terminal, View ▸ Group by in the
window, `--group` on the command line, and it survives a restart.

**A heading is not a process.** Its index into the snapshot is deliberately invalid, so a caller that
walks the rows without asking gets an exception rather than the wrong process; it is not counted in
"N of M processes"; the cursor steps past it rather than onto it; and no action can be aimed at it,
because its row carries no process for the request to name. In the window its tag is not a
`ProcessRow`, which is the whole safeguard: every verb there reads the selection as one.

Headings come out in the order the current sort put their first row in, so a table sorted by memory
puts the heaviest group at the top. Ordering them alphabetically would bury the group somebody sorted
the table to find. Folding one hides its members and keeps its count.

Application and publisher are unticked with the reason on the line: naming a group needs something to
read it off, and this program has no notion of an application and no signature verification. A
heading that guessed would not be true.

Package is amber. #66 landed its reader while this was in flight, so it stopped being blocked; the
launch path works (`--group package`, or a saved `grouping=package`, which count as asking for the
field the same way naming the column does), and switching to it inside a running session cannot,
because the probe's expensive readings are chosen when it is built. A session that did not ask heads
its rows "package not looked up" rather than "not packaged" — "nobody looked" and "nothing claims
this file" are different answers and only the second is a finding. That distinction does not come off
the reason code either: a record nobody filled carries the default reason, which reads "the value is
present".

## What the pictures showed

Two new ones, because everything above is layout and layout is what passes its tests and ships
broken. `desktop-grouped.png` and `desktop-filtered.png`, plus a grouped terminal frame and four new
lines in `shoot.log` — the columns and their widths, the sort with its tie-breakers, the grouping and
its heading count, the filter and what the parser made of it.

Three defects came out of reading them rather than out of the suite:

- Every match highlight was drawn out in the tree indent, four columns from the word it had matched.
  The tree column's text starts one indent per level plus the expander cell plus the tick box in from
  the cell's left edge, and the highlight was measured from the edge.
- The grouped picture's first row appeared to belong to no group: selecting the first *process*
  scrolls it into view, which pushes the heading above it off the top.
- The capture rewrote the settings file. It runs against the real one and the window saves once a
  second, so exercising the columns left them reset for whoever regenerated the screenshots.

And three out of reading the code again afterwards: the column chooser would have thrown away a
hand-made column order every time one more column was ticked; a filter box wired to the window's
refresh would have taken a full sample of the machine per character typed; and grouping by package
put every row under "not from a package" on a run that had not collected the field, which is the
confident zero this project keeps finding — that one was caught by looking at a frame, not by a
test.

## Checks

- `dotnet build -c Release` — 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `dotnet test` — 1404 passing (1353 of them on the base this started from, which has since gained
  #66's). The new ones cover the grouping engine, the terminal's headings, the window's column model
  and the settings round trip.
- `--self-test` — OK on all 37 checks.
- Terminal frames read back at 80×24, 120×30 and 160×50; the three goldens are unchanged, because
  nothing here moves the default view.
- Benchmarks: the CPU-per-1000 ceiling fails at 92–115 ms on this machine at load 35, which is the
  band the budget's own comment already documents for a loaded machine. Interleaved A/B against
  `main`, four rounds alternating: main 96.5 / 102.6 / 108.2 / 110.9, this branch 102.1 / 92.3 /
  106.0 / 94.8 — indistinguishable, and this branch touches nothing in the sampling path. The
  allocation budget and the tree-rebuild budget both pass (`view.rebuild.tree.ms` 2.6 against main's
  2.9 over the same rounds).
