author: nikola-jelic
body:
The compatibility matrix in the README said clang failed on every C++ standard
and that C++11, the library's stated baseline, failed too. Both were accurate.
This branch fixes the causes and the process that let them sit there.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| Compiler matrix | 2 of 10 cells | **10 of 10** |
| Tests | 22, g++ / C++14 only | **58**, both compilers × C++14–23 |
| CI | could not fail | fails on regression; runs the suite and a format check |
| Header line coverage | not measured | **99.0%** |

## Why clang failed everywhere

The library defined its own overloads inside `namespace std` — the trigonometry
wrappers, `abs`, `fmod`, `sqrt`, `cbrt`, `to_string`, and the `std::chrono`
converters. That is undefined behaviour. g++ accepted it, clang rejected it
outright, and the difference was never visible because CI only ever ran g++.

Everything now lives in `namespace units` and is found by argument-dependent
lookup. **This is a breaking change** — see *Migration* below.

## Code that had never compiled

Templates are only checked when instantiated, so an uninstantiated function is
closer to a comment than to code. The suite passed 22 tests while several
operators had never been instantiated even once:

- `AbsoluteAngle::operator+` and `operator-` used the member function `value`
  without calling it
- the free `operator+` for `AbsolutePhysicalUnit` named a `DiffUnitType` that
  does not exist
- `abs()` on an `AbsoluteAngle` took a typename pack, but the range is a
  non-type parameter, so the overload could not be deduced against any
  `AbsoluteAngle` at all
- `IntevalAlign`, misspelled, in the inverse trigonometry macros

None of these could be caught by a coverage tool: an uninstantiated template
contributes neither covered nor uncovered lines.

## Correctness fixes

- `num_sqrt<360>` claimed 60, which is the root of 3600, so any `sqrt()` over a
  factor of 360 came out 3.16× too large. 360 has no integer square root, so
  the entry is gone and 3600 is tabulated instead. **Every entry now static
  asserts that it is the root of its own key**, which also caught
  `num_sqrt<100000000>` and an `int` overflow in the assertion itself.
- `dim_to_string` did `"/" + Dim::den` — pointer arithmetic on a string
  literal, not concatenation.
- The dimension separator was only emitted after an exponent, so `m kg`
  rendered as `mkg`.
- `to_string` for `AbsolutePhysicalUnit` had its template parameters in the
  wrong order and could never match the class.
- Half-interval angle normalisation left values below `-circle/2` unnormalised.
- The dimensionless `PhysicalUnit` specialisation had no `value()`, so
  comparing two dimensionless results did not compile.
- `phys_string.hpp` had no include guard and its explicit specialisations were
  not `inline`, so it failed to link when included in two translation units.

## C++11 is real now

`constexpr` constructors had non-empty bodies, which C++11 forbids, and
`phys_chrono.hpp` used a C++17 nested namespace definition that g++ accepted
silently as an extension. The probe now builds with `-pedantic-errors`, which
is what makes the C++11 column mean anything.

`virtual setValue` is gone from `AbsolutePhysicalUnit` and `AbsoluteAngle`: a
vtable pointer in a value type contradicts the zero-overhead goal and blocked
the constructors from being `constexpr`.

## Printing

Rendering glued value, factor and dimensions together with nothing between
them, so a speed in km/h came out as `100.0000005/18m s^-1`.

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `3.500000m s^-1` | `3.5 m/s` |
| `9.810000m s^-2` | `9.81 m/s^2` — or `9.81 m/s²` |
| `50.000000s^-1` | `50 1/s` |
| `23/7m` | `2 (3/7) m` |
| `100.0000005/18m s^-1` | `100 (5/18) m/s` |

Negative exponents become a denominator; a compound one is bracketed so
`m/(s A)` cannot be misread. Precision is selectable and defaults to the
shortest useful form rather than `std::to_string`'s six decimals.
`unit_symbol<T>()` returns the symbol alone, for a column heading or an axis
label. Three styles, with the default settable project-wide at compile time via
`-DUNITS_DEFAULT_STYLE`.

The header now states what it is: a hosted diagnostic aid that allocates, and
is meant to be vendored and edited in place.

## CI

The matrix job wrote its results into the README and pushed them, but always
exited zero, so a completely broken clang column left master green. It now
declares which cells are required and fails when one regresses — verified by
breaking the probe on purpose. Each cell gets its own build directory; reusing
one meant a cached `CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER` could not be changed.

The suite was never run in CI at all, and formatting was only checked by a
local hook. Both are jobs now, the suite across both compilers and C++14–23.
The README commit step is restricted to direct pushes to master, since running
it on a pull request would push a contributor's in-progress state.

`test/compiler_tests/CMakeLists.txt` had `set(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER {CXX_COMPILER})`,
missing the `$`. `test/CMakeLists.txt` shadowed the standard with a plain
`set()`, so `-DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` was silently ignored.

## Migration

```c++
std::sin(angle)                →  using std::sin; sin(angle);   // ADL
std::sqrt(area)                →  using std::sqrt; sqrt(area);
std::abs(length)               →  units::abs(length)
std::asin<A>(x)                →  units::asin<A>(x)             // qualified
std::chrono::duration_cast(t)  →  units::duration_cast(t)
std::to_string(length)         →  units::to_string(length)
```

`AbsoluteAngle`'s `bool HalfInterval` is now `units::AngleRange`, because a
bool could only ever encode two ways of handling the circle boundary:

```c++
units::AbsoluteAngle<double, std::ratio<1>, true>
  →  units::AbsoluteAngle<double, std::ratio<1>, units::AngleRange::Signed>
```

A bool does not convert to a scoped enumeration, so this fails loudly rather
than changing meaning silently. `dim_to_string` is replaced by `DimSymbol`, and
every rendered string changes shape.

## Also

`RadianRatio` goes from 5 to 7 significant digits. A `.clang-format` pins the
LLVM defaults the project already used — it reformats nothing — and CI installs
an exact clang-format version so the job fails on real violations rather than
version drift. Copyright extended to 2024-2026 and the author's surname spelled
Jelić.

## Verification

All eight test cells and all ten matrix cells were run locally before being
wired up. The ODR guard and the CI failure path were both checked by breaking
them: without `inline` the link produces 16 multiple-definition errors, and a
deliberately broken probe makes the matrix script report the failing cells and
exit 1.

author: rowan-claude
body:
Closes #17, and the shape of it changed under a cold read. The branch was force-updated from `71f558a` to `6e09290`.

The first version added a new LESSONS entry stating the ladder in full. A reviewer given the diff and none of my reasoning returned BLOCK, on the finding that the seed already ships most of it. I verified that myself at `origin/main`. `pattern/the-floor-plan.md` lines 48 to 60 already carry vibe and gut, identical from the inside, the ledger as the only separator, log it half-formed, logging is not agreeing, keep the misses because a hit log is a test that cannot fail, and request to look rather than proposition to evaluate. `pattern/knowing.md` line 79 already names the pipeline. Several of my sentences were nearly the shipped words.

What is genuinely absent is one rung. The seed names the two kinds of feeling and the instrument that separates them and then stops, so a reader gets a classifier with no destination. This adds that the two rungs have a third above them, that wisdom is a correct gut over long time rather than a better grade of feeling, that none of the rungs is skippable, and that the ledger is the only material the third can precipitate from. It goes into the bullet where the other two already live rather than opening a second home for the subject in another file.

How the duplicate nearly shipped is worth keeping. My check was a phrase grep over LESSONS.md for the words I had chosen, and the previous commit message reported it as diligence. Concept matching finds the overlap on the first hit. A search shaped by the author's own vocabulary can only confirm that author's own novelty.

Two things are dropped rather than reworded. The four-of-four override count was a hit log with no base rate, offered in support of a rule that a hit log proves nothing. And the claim that wisdom aimed at directly produces the imitation is unfalsifiable, and its hedge relocated it out of a reader's reach instead of qualifying it.

`nova-check links` OK (47 files, 214 links), `nova-check floors` OK (8), `nova-self-talk` OK.

The cold gate on this rewrite is running. Not merging until it returns.

author: nnmarcoo
body:
Closes #50.

The install page told Linux users to `chmod +x bloom-*.AppImage` or `sudo dpkg -i bloom_*.deb`, and pointed Windows users at a `.exe` installer. The release workflow uploads `bloom-*.tar.gz`, `bloom-*.dmg`, `bloom-*.zip` and `bloom-*.msi`. No AppImage, no .deb, no .exe, so anyone on Linux following the page had nothing to download.

Now it describes the tarball. It also documents something that was not written down anywhere: the Linux full build links FFmpeg through an `$ORIGIN/lib` rpath, so `lib/` has to stay next to the binary. Extract the tarball and move `bloom` somewhere on its own and video silently stops working.

The macOS text was already correct and I left it alone.

This makes the docs true today. Shipping an AppImage and a .deb is still the better answer for Linux, and I would rather do that as its own PR than bolt packaging onto a docs fix. Happy to pick it up next if you want it.

Also updated the search index entry, which indexed appimage, dpkg and deb as keywords.

author: myluma
body:
## Why

Scrolling a note with photographs in it was slow, and the cause was in the paint path rather than in layout.

`DocumentLayout.draw` handed `image.draw(in: rect)` whatever `UIImage(data:)` produced from the original file. A 12 MP photo displayed in a ~350pt column meant Core Graphics resampling twelve million source pixels down to a few hundred thousand — on the main thread, on every frame, because `contentOffsetY`'s setter redraws the viewport on each scroll tick and nothing cached the rasterization between frames. `UIImage(data:)` also doesn't decode; it defers that to the first `draw(in:)`, so the JPEG decode landed mid-drag too.

Measured on one 12 MP photo drawn into a 350pt column (simulator, debug — the ratio is the point, not the absolute): **30.5 ms → 2.4 ms per draw**. A single picture was blowing the whole 16.7 ms frame budget.

## What changed

**Decode once, at the size the image is drawn** — new `Sources/EditorUIKit/ImageDecoding.swift`.

- Images go through `CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex`, bounded by the content column. Layout caps every image to that column, so it fixes the most pixels any of them can need. A file-backed photo is read through ImageIO rather than into a `Data` first, so a 20 MB original costs its header plus its thumbnail.
- The decode is forced where the load happens (`kCGImageSourceShouldCacheImmediately`), off the main thread, rather than being left to the first `draw(in:)`.
- The decoded image keeps the **natural point size** of the original and carries the reduction in `UIImage.scale`. Layout measures a picture's box from `UIImage.size`, so the bitmap may shrink but the picture may not. That also makes re-decoding at a wider column (rotation, split view) purely a question of sharpness — it can never move anything — so it happens in the background while the softer bitmap keeps drawing.
- The host's `imageData` hook stays synchronous: it is declared that way and callers rely on bytes it already holds appearing in the very next layout. It downsamples like everything else, so the work is bounded by the box rather than by the file.

**Adopting a loaded image no longer re-flows the document.**

Bytes arriving is the one change that alters the layout without altering the document, so none of the usual triggers fire — it used to be handled by discarding the layout and building it again, once per picture, arriving while the reader scrolls through them, and for an inline image after dropping *every* typeset block in the cache.

- New `DocumentLayout.relayoutImages(matching:)` re-lays only the top-level children that hold the arrived image and shifts the rest.
- New `TextBlockLayoutCache.evict(where:)` drops only the paragraphs holding an inline image, not the whole cache.
- Loads landing in the same turn of the run loop are coalesced into one patch.
- `reloadImages()` keeps the wholesale path — it says nothing about *which* images changed.

**One store, bounded, and disposed of** — new `Sources/EditorUIKit/DocumentImageStore.swift`, replacing a copy each of the same three dictionaries in `EditorTextView` and `DocumentView`.

- A 24 MB LRU budget over decoded bitmaps.
- `prune(keeping:)` on every document change drops bitmaps and cancels loads for images the document no longer holds.
- `purge()` on a memory warning and when the view leaves its window.
- In-flight loads live in a lock-protected box (`ImageLoadTasks`) so `deinit` — which is not main-actor isolated — can cancel a download for a note the reader has already closed.

Eviction never disturbs what is on screen: a laid-out decoration holds its own reference to the image it draws, so the pictures being *presented* stay alive for exactly as long as they are presented, and it is only the rest that is reclaimed.

## For the reviewer

**One behaviour change:** dragging an image out to another app now offers the host's original bytes, or the file behind the node, rather than a re-encode of what is drawn. Without that it would have exported the downsampled thumbnail.

The natural-size invariant is the load-bearing part of the downsampling change — if it were wrong, every image in every document would silently change size. `ImageDownsamplingTests` pins it directly, including for EXIF-rotated photos (orientations 5–8 transpose the image, and the thumbnail is produced with the transform applied), where the assertion is against what `UIImage(data:)` itself reports.

## Testing

- `xcodebuild test -scheme ProseKit-Package -only-testing:EditorUIKitTests` with `PROSEKIT_STRICT=1`: **525 passed, 0 failed** (22 new).
- `PROSEKIT_STRICT=1 swift build` (macOS) clean.
- `swift run` for DocumentModelTests, EditorStateKitTests, SchemaKitTests, EditorSerializationTests: all pass.

New coverage in `Tests/EditorUIKitTests/ImageDownsamplingTests.swift` — the decode (bitmap shrinks to its box, natural size survives, small images are not upsampled, tall images keep their long edge, EXIF-rotated photos), the store (decode-once, prune by document, byte budget, purge, selective cancellation of loads in flight), and the layout patch (blocks above the picture do not move, blocks below do, and the layout is patched rather than replaced).

author: abs313a
body: ## Summary This PR integrates the Omarchy-inspired Quickshell bar presentation into dwm-titus while preserving dwm-titus ownership of the Fedora X11 session, DWM workspace/window state, process lifecycle, helpers, IPC, Control Center, and installation flow. The implementation does not import Omarchy's plugin host, Hyprland integration, Wayland layer-shell behavior, service providers, configuration registry, or command backends. The work in this PR covers the Phase 1 bar integration and the hardening discovered during nested-X11 and real Fedora/DWM testing. The broader Bluetooth, Network, and Volume panel redesign remains follow-up work. ## User-visible bar contract ### Geometry and session behavior - Keeps the existing 30 px top-bar location and exclusive area. - Tiled, floating, and maximized applications respect the reserved bar area. - True fullscreen applications retain DWM's existing fullscreen exception and cover the bar correctly. - Keeps one managed Quickshell process for the session and one panel per screen. - Keeps DWM/X11 as the source of truth for monitors, workspaces, focused windows, and window activation. ### Palette and typography - Background: `#1a1b26` - Foreground/inactive: `#a9b1d6` - Active: `#7aa2f7` - Urgent: `#f7768e` - Bar text and standard glyphs use the approved 11 px size; the dedicated Network and Volume status glyphs retain their intentional 14 px optical size. - No bar module exposes a tooltip. ### Left side 1. CTT logo 2. Workspaces The CTT logo opens the existing dwm-titus Control Center. The primary monitor exposes workspaces 1-9. Secondary panels retain DWM's existing monitor-local workspace partitioning. ### Center - Date/time only: `ddd, d MMM hh:mm` - 24-hour clock - No language indicator - No alternate right-click clock content ### Right side 1. Existing `RunningAppsArea` 2. Bluetooth 3. Network 4. Volume The focused bar does not mount a system tray. The existing tray backend remains available to other shell surfaces, but no tray icons are rendered in this bar. `RunningAppsArea` remains DWM-owned. Terminal windows are excluded only when their class exactly matches a configured `isterminal=1` rule, case-insensitively. Exact matching prevents short rules such as `St` from suppressing GUI applications such as Steam, Postman, or Ristretto. No new Foot or Ghostty policy is added by this PR. - Network changes between disconnected, Wi-Fi strength, and wired/LAN states; wired takes priority when both are connected. - Volume changes between mute, low, medium, and high icons. - Volume uses the local mute icon at 0% even when PipeWire's mute flag is technically off. - Scrolling over the Volume module raises or lowers volume. - Clicking Bluetooth, Network, or Volume continues to route through the existing root-scoped models/helpers and popup coordinator. ## Implementation details - Added small bar-specific QML primitives instead of importing Omarchy's plugin architecture: - `BarIconButton.qml` - `NetworkBarModule.qml` - `VolumeBarModule.qml` - Reworked `DwmPanel.qml` around the focused layout while retaining DWM monitor routing, bar reservation, popup ownership, and fullscreen behavior. - Extended `DwmState.qml` only where needed for primary-monitor workspace visibility and running-app focus. - Added a coalesced trailing refresh path to `NetworkModel.qml` so event bursts settle on the latest NetworkManager state without unbounded refresh work. - Extended `dwm-quickshell-network` with the X11 bar's required wired/Wi-Fi state while excluding QR/barcode, speed-test, and DNS-management features. - Extended the existing control helper/model boundary for the required bar actions; no parallel service layer was introduced. - Fixed Fedora's `_NET_CLIENT_LIST(WINDOW):` `xprop` output parsing in `dwm-quickshell-state`. - Renamed `RunningAppsArea`'s required model property from `state` to `dwmState` to avoid overriding `QQuickItem.state`. - Updated managed startup/tests for one Quickshell process and an intentionally unmounted tray. - Added source-contract, nested-X11, network-refresh, monitor/workspace, helper, and regression coverage. ## Upstream integration history The branch was reconciled with upstream twice during development: 1. Merged the upstream Quickshell design-system work based on `a20ee6f82f54404bc954293268c67fe4ad85030f` in merge commit `9cb46b8398e566d2e929f19ddaea8f8ce45730df`. 2. Merged Phase 3 large surfaces from upstream commit `cdef877abb44a4df48111c4a952d2e9d7d7570cb` in merge commit `7fbbf9425923d3b4ccd669de2da369ca37614e01`. The second merge had one mechanical conflict in the Makefile's `.PHONY` registration. The resolution retains both this PR's bar/Xvfb targets and upstream's large-surface/Xvfb targets. `Theme.qml` merged additively and retains both the `dwmBar*` tokens and upstream's large-surface tokens. ## Dependencies ### Runtime The implementation reuses packages already owned by the dwm-titus Fedora desktop profile: - Quickshell - NetworkManager / `nmcli` - BlueZ / `bluetoothctl` - PipeWire, PipeWire PulseAudio compatibility, and WirePlumber - `pulseaudio-utils` (`pactl`) with the existing `wpctl` fallback - `iproute` and `iputils` - D-Bus and X11 utilities Observed focused results: - Quickshell bar source contract: PASS - Quickshell design system: PASS - Quickshell large-surface source contract: PASS - Quickshell panel menus: PASS - Quickshell command menu: PASS - Quickshell controls helper: PASS - NetworkModel coalesced trailing refresh: PASS - Quickshell network helper: PASS - Quickshell control center helper: PASS - Monitor tag-switch source guard: PASS - System health helper: PASS - Settings provider/input tests: PASS - native DWM build: PASS Real-session acceptance confirmed: - 30 px bar reservation and original top location - CTT logo opens the existing Control Center - primary workspaces 1-9 - center-only 24-hour date/time - no tooltips and no tray - Bluetooth, Network, and Volume click behavior - Wi-Fi/LAN network icon changes - mute/low/medium/high volume icon changes - 0% uses the mute icon independently of the PipeWire mute flag - volume wheel adjustment - popup coordination - one managed Quickshell process - closed-idle CPU sampling - Fedora `xprop` running-app discovery - configured terminals excluded while Browsers and other GUI apps remain visible The final Fedora acceptance was performed through commit `e3b40366929ab75c9cdf3ce4bf41078e5174e515`. ## QML validation notes Fedora `qmllint` originally identified a real `RunningAppsArea.qml` property override (`state` shadowing `QQuickItem.state`); this was corrected by renaming it to `dwmState` and updating the qualified accesses. The Fedora lint run also reported incomplete qmltypes warnings for `PopupAnchor`/`Edges` in `PanelTooltip.qml`. That component is not mounted by the focused no-tooltip bar, and the warnings were attributable to the available Quickshell qmltypes rather than a runtime failure. Nested-X11 and real-session bar tests passed. ## Rollout / test procedure For an existing checkout: ```sh scripts/dev-sync-install.sh ``` If the installer reports that the DWM binary changed, log out and back into the DWM X11 session, then verify: ```sh scripts/dev-sync-install.sh --check pgrep -af quickshell ``` ## Follow-up phases Not claimed complete by this PR: - final Omarchy-inspired Bluetooth panel layout - final Network panel layout without QR, speed-test, DNS - adaptive panel dimensions, 1 px panel borders, and bounded scrolling for dynamic lists - any later additions/new ideas after the basic bar has been accepted

author: alissonaguiar
body:
Reverte a #4.

## Por quê

A #4 partia de "nenhum `enroll` existe em lugar nenhum deste produto". Isso era verdade quando ela foi escrita, e **deixou de ser** com `air-bizapps/twinf-forge#255` (commit `8626bfa`, 2026-08-19), mergeada no `master` às 17:14 UTC de 2026-08-21 — algumas horas antes do merge da #4. A #255 implementa `twinforge enroll` como cliente de device flow (RFC 8628) e o roteia no `case` dos dois launchers, ao lado de `update|rollback|unpin|status`.

A outra metade do texto removido também voltou a valer: o launcher do `master` ganhou um gate `check-lease` que **interrompe o boot** de uma máquina sem lease válida. Então "It will not start until this machine is enrolled with your organization's instance" descreve o comportamento real, não uma promessa vazia.

Com a #4 no ar, o instalador público manda apenas rodar `twinforge` e omite o enrollment — o passo que o produto exige.

## Efeito

`install.sh` e `install.ps1` voltam a imprimir:

```
It will not start until this machine is enrolled with your organization's
instance. Next step:

  twinforge enroll
```

## Consequência do outro lado

`air-bizapps/twinf-forge#251` (que endurece o launcher para recusar palavra desconhecida) tinha esta mesma premissa e vai ser retrabalhada: `enroll` sai da lista de palavras desconhecidas dos testes. O bug que ela conserta continua real — `twinforge stauts` sobe uma instância por fall-through.

author: francoisldaigneault
body:
## Why

The `secrets-scan` CI job runs gitleaks over the full git history. That verdict is correct, but it arrives **after the push** — at which point a leaked secret is burned and must be rotated, not merely removed. Pre-commit is the last moment a secret can still be stopped.

## What

Adds the official gitleaks hook to `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. One repo block, nine lines, nothing else touched.

The `rev` is pinned to **`v8.24.3`** — the exact version the CI job downloads and checksum-verifies — so local and remote cannot disagree about what counts as a secret.

| | CI `secrets-scan` | new pre-commit hook |
|---|---|---|
| Engine | gitleaks v8.24.3 | gitleaks v8.24.3 |
| Scope | full history (`gitleaks git --redact -v .`) | staged diff (`gitleaks git --pre-commit --redact --staged --verbose`) |
| Timing | after push | before commit |

The two are complementary, not redundant: the hook stops new secrets, CI still guards against anything that bypasses it (`--no-verify`, web edits, an unconfigured clone).

## Proof

**RED** — a staged file containing a fake AWS key pair was rejected, citing the file and line, with values redacted:

```
Detect hardcoded secrets.................................................Failed
- hook id: gitleaks
- exit code: 1

Finding:     aws_secret_access_key = "REDACTED"
RuleID:      generic-api-key
File:        tmp_red_secret_test.txt
Line:        2

Finding:     ...ws_access_key_id = "REDACTED
RuleID:      aws-access-token
File:        tmp_red_secret_test.txt
Line:        1

WRN leaks found: 2
```

The test file was deleted and unstaged; the fake secret was never committed.

**GREEN** — `uv run pre-commit run --all-files` passes all 14 hooks, and this PR's own commit passed the hook without `--no-verify`.

## Cost

0.45 s standalone (median of 3), of which gitleaks' own scan is ~27 ms — the rest is pre-commit process startup. Marginal cost inside a full hook run is not measurable above noise: 3.47 s before, 3.48 s after.

## Note

This repo declares no top-level `exclude`, so there is nothing for the hook to inherit. gitleaks runs with `pass_filenames: false` and scans the staged diff directly, so path exclusions would come from a `.gitleaksignore` / gitleaks config rather than from pre-commit's `exclude` — none is needed today.

body: ## Summary - add tenant-scoped REST and MCP two-phase signer activation intake - derive authorization, reservation, operation, and request identifiers server-side and return a redacted status projection - make serializable activation creation converge under concurrency, preserve late exact replay, and classify binding reuse deterministically - require the dedicated `activations:create` agent scope and document the deployment boundary ## Verification - `go test -race ./internal/ascpactivation ./internal/ascpbearer ./internal/controlapi ./internal/mcp ./cmd/control-plane-api ./cmd/ascp-bearer-worker` - `FLOWOPS_TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql:///postgres?host=/tmp\&sslmode=disable go test -race ./internal/controlapi -count=1` - `make check` - `docker build -t flowops:ascp-activation-intake-76af586 .` - container smoke: `/flowops/control-plane-api` and `/flowops/ascp-bearer-worker` executable ## Evidence boundaries - live managed PostgreSQL SQL/provider proof was not run because deployment credentials/evidence were not configured - signer Ring 6 engine, signer RPC server, and WORM provider sidecar remain explicit production integration gates --- ## Summary by cubic Expose tenant-scoped activation intake for two-phase signer requests over REST and MCP. Previously only Go callers could create `SIGN_REQUESTED`; now authenticated agents can request activation after a live authorization, with server-derived scope/ids and redacted responses. - New `internal/ascpactivation` service. Requires `activations:create`. Derives `authorizationId`, `reservationId`, and `requestId`. Enforces `VALIDATED_AND_RESERVED`. Returns a redacted status (no canonical bytes, evidence, prepared handle, or signatures). Supports read-by-operation via the authorization. Concurrent identical requests converge; exact replays return 200; binding changes return 409; serializable/deadlock errors retry up to 3 times; late exact replays remain readable. - Control API: `POST|GET /agent/v1/intents/{operationID}/activation` (agent-only). JSON limit 2 MiB. Unknown fields rejected. 201 on first create, 200 on replay. Typed errors for not found, conflict, and invalid input. - Storage: `internal/ascpbearer` adds `ForAuthorization` and serializable retry handling; authorization ID remains the idempotency key. - MCP: adds tools `ascp.operation.activation.create` and `ascp.operation.activation.get`. `internal/mcp` raises `MaxRequestBytes` to 2 MiB and validates arguments against updated schemas. - Wiring: `cmd/control-plane-api` constructs `ascpbearer.NewActivationStore` and `ascpactivation.New`, passes to the server, and sets MCP `MaxRequestBytes: 2 MiB`. Docs add ADR-0052 and update module/deployment guidance. **Rollout** - Set `FLOWOPS_ASCP_DIRECTORY_CONTRACT` to enable ASCP services; otherwise activation endpoints return 503. - Grant agent credentials the `activations:create` scope where activation is allowed. - Allow up to 2 MiB request bodies for `/agent/v1/intents/*/activation` and MCP at the edge. - No DB migration included; signer worker, signer RPC, and WORM sidecar remain separate gates. Written for commit 76af5860c0bdf0ff48cde9368cd4f8a56b24fa30. Summary will update on new commits.

body:
The four HTTP/1.1 profiles the entry was not subscribed to. Tests go from 10 to 14.

### json-tls / static-tls

The same app behind a `node:https` server on 8081. Every worker binds it exactly
as they all bind 8080, so the cluster shares the port rather than one process
carrying it — the failure mode #1245 fixed on quarkus.

`express.static` already streamed bodies from disk, so the static path needed no
change to take `static-tls`.

### crud

Cache-aside on Redis through `ioredis`, one connection per worker so the cache is
shared across the cluster rather than being a per-worker map, 200ms TTL, explicit
delete on update. `express.json()` is mounted on the two crud routes that carry a
body rather than globally — `/upload` takes a 20MB body it counts as it streams,
and a global parser would buffer and parse it.

### fortunes

Rendered through a view engine, which is what standard mode requires: the
template is its own artifact at `views/fortunes.hbs`, and Handlebars escapes
`{{ }}` by default. The seed's row 11 carries a `<script>` tag and the profile
calls that escape its load-bearing check.

### Validation

**64 passed, 0 failed**, including all four new profiles:

```
json-tls    protocol negotiation, response schema, Content-Type
static-tls  20 files verified, 15 compressed / 5 skipped, 404 path
fortunes    <tr> count=202, runtime row, XSS escape, body size=24754B
crud        list, read, cache-aside MISS->HIT, 404, POST 201, PUT + invalidate
```

body:
## The definitive run

The full benchmark against `src-acfba64`, from zero, under the strengthened oracle:

**P0 98.1% · P1 100% · P2 100%** — 89 questions, 115 requests, both locales, seven multi-turn
journeys, 0 non-200 responses.

One failure, and this PR closes it.

## The finding

Turn 3 of the trust journey answered:

> "A **Trust Root** do **BANZA** é controlada por **três autoridades de assinatura independentes**.
> Uma acção autorizada pela raiz requer assinaturas de **quaisquer duas das três** (**2-de-3**)…"

Turn 4 asked **"Qual é o limiar?"** and was told there is no public source supporting the request.

The alias list required the threshold qualified — "limiar da raiz" — and a reader who has just been
told there are three authorities does not repeat the noun. Measured across the canonical corpus, every
occurrence of "limiar" is the root authority threshold; there is no competing threshold in BANZA, so
the word names its subject unqualified.

Nothing about what is known changes. `def-root-authorization` already carries the 2-of-3 rule, the
distinct-authorities counting, the anti-rollback and the "no production ceremony has been held"
statement. The question could not reach it.

## Evidence

`assurance/banzai-knowledge/baseline/` now holds all four production runs — `src-14df955` (before),
`src-2a01974`, `src-4238558` and `src-acfba64` (definitive) — alongside the corpus, the read-only
probe, the scoring oracle, the root-cause catalogue and the deployment record.

Across them, on the same probe:

| | `14df955` | `2a01974` | `4238558` | `acfba64` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| model answers citing only ADR-001 | 9 of 18 | 4 of 15 | 3 of 14 | — |
| `answer_locale` absent | 18 of 18 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| zero-source refusals | 29% | 19% | 13% | — |
| p50 latency | 1039 ms | 1136 ms | 72 ms | — |

## Status

BANZA remains **PRE-PRODUCTION**; AG-10 remains `NOT_RUN`. Nothing here touches protocol semantics,
trust or governance.

author: iampereziii
body:
Implements `feature-brief-write-path-latency-and-in-flight-feedback.md` (ais repo — [companion PR](https://github.com/iampereziii/ais/pull/new/claude/ui-loading-time-perf-8tmqii) resolves its 17 open items).

You asked me to decide the remaining open questions while you slept. **Every decision I made on your behalf is recorded in the brief's Resolution Log**, marked as delegated so it reads differently from the four you answered yourself. Two things below want your eyes — they're at the bottom under *Needs your call*.

---

## Why clicks felt slow

Not one bug. Four habits, each reasonable where it was introduced:

1. **Correctness-first serial I/O** — every layer re-establishes trust and re-reads state, each `await`ing the last. No step is wrong; the latency is the *sum*, and nobody owned the sum.
2. **One read endpoint doing every read's job** — `GET /api/sessions?limit=100` is the log's endpoint. It became the session screen's and the backlog's too, because it was there and it was correct. The cost is invisible at the call site: the expensive line reads `api.get(...)`.
3. **Feedback treated as polish and parked** — `disabled` was the entire vocabulary, and the one path missing even that was the slowest and most-clicked.
4. **The write path knew more than it said** — every write returns the updated row; `close()` discarded it and re-asked the server for the whole collection.

**None of these is fixed by a cache**, which is the point: every change here is a fix *inside* ADR-0002, not a reason to reopen it.

## Latency

| Change | Effect |
|---|---|
| Proxy forwards its verified identity | **One auth round trip per request, not two.** Every route handler was calling `getUser()` for an answer `proxy.ts` already had. |
| `GET /api/sessions/[id]` | `/session/[id]` stops downloading the last 100 sessions to render one row |
| `/` queries `resume_planned_at` directly | Replaces 50 sessions + all their check-ins + `groupByWeek` + `flattenWeeks` |
| `activeSession()` request-scoped memoised | Layout and page stop issuing the same query twice per navigation |
| Capture resolves a known topic locally | One POST instead of two on the common path |

**Two correctness bugs fell out of this**, both hiding inside performance ones:

- A session older than the most recent 100 was **unreachable** at `/session/[id]` — it was never in the payload to be found.
- A resume cue older than the last 50 sessions **silently stopped pinning** on `/`, because the pin was filtered out of a log page rather than queried.

## Feedback

- `Button` gains `pending`, which implies `disabled`. The **pressed** control spins while its siblings go inert — so the feedback says *which outcome is being recorded*, not merely that something is happening.
- `close()` is guarded in the **handler**, not only by the buttons. A second tap used to hit Rule 5's 409 raised by the *first tap's own successful write*, and report it as **"Nothing was saved"** — the exact opposite of what happened, on the message that most needs to be trustworthy. That branch now tells the truth.
- **No optimism anywhere.** Nothing renders as closed, removed or advanced until the server says so. `dropTask`'s animate-during-request-and-settle-back is the copied pattern.

## Also

- The 1 Hz clock no longer re-renders the whole session screen, or the nav chrome of **every** page. Recorded as craft — **it is not why clicks felt slow**, and I didn't want it mistaken for the fix.
- `lib/perf.ts` measures the two ADR-0001 budgets that until now lived in comments and were judged by feel. Deliberately dependency-free: no analytics SDK, no network call, no third party learning your working habits for the sake of a number you can read in the console.

## Guardrails

Both ADR-0002 rules untouched, no `eslint-disable` anywhere, and a test asserts both. `sw.js` still has no `fetch` handler — this is precisely the "it's just a performance fix" pretext under which one gets added, so it's now asserted in tests as well as lint.

**Verified:** `tsc --noEmit` clean · `npm run lint` clean · **182 tests pass** (25 new) · production build verified, `/` still renders dynamic.

---

## Needs your call

1. **Slice D is half-built, deliberately.** Deleting the duplicate `getUser()` is done. The `getClaims()` swap is *not*, because it only pays off if your Supabase project signs JWTs asymmetrically — check Project Settings → JWT Keys. If it's symmetric, `getClaims()` is a network call just like `getUser()` and there's nothing left to win.

2. **The identity header is trusted, so the proxy makes it unforgeable** — it strips any inbound value *before* setting its own, unconditionally, including for signed-out callers. `currentUserId` keeps `getUser()` as a fallback so a route reached without the proxy fails **closed**. Three tests guard this. It's the one change here with a security surface, so it's worth your reading `src/lib/identity.ts` directly rather than taking my word for it.

Related: `/`'s pinned-rows query is still UTC-based, which is wrong west of UTC — unchanged behaviour, and it belongs to `feature-brief-day-review-local-day-boundary.md` (its AC 7 names that very line). I left it there rather than smuggling a timezone fix into a latency PR.

author: mattkindy
body:
## Summary

The two `boundaryFieldUnused` messages told the reader that the application stores values nothing consumes, on evidence that covers one way of reading a field. The storage pass counts a field as read only when a query asks for it, so a field the code takes off a record a query returned stays invisible. This rewords both messages. It does not change when the check fires, which fields it reports, or its severity, since #510 leaves that open.

On the RealWorld Express and Prisma app, `Comment.body` used to read:

```
[WARNING] boundaryFieldUnused
  Comment declares "body" and code writes it, but no code in the project reads it.
  Likely useless data. The application stores values nothing downstream consumes.
```

and now reads:

```
[WARNING] boundaryFieldUnused
  Comment declares "body" and code here writes it, but no query asks for it back.
  A field the code takes off a record a query returned never counts as a read here,
  so look for one before treating the write as pointless.
```

## What changed

- `storagePairing.ts`: both `boundaryFieldUnused` descriptions say what the pass looked at, that a read off a returned record never reaches the count, and what to look for before acting on the warning. The second sentence is shared by both through `askedForNote`.
- `storagePairing.test.ts`: the unused and write-only tests assert the new sentences.
- `packages/checker/src/storage/README.md`: a bullet saying that the wildcard suppression catches a call that asks for nothing and nothing else, so a Prisma `include`, or a `select` nested under another model's query, still leaves columns looking unread.
- `docs/reference/findings.md`: the quoted examples match the new messages.
- `scripts/dogfood-baseline.json`: regenerated, one more internal unit in `@suss/checker` for the new helper.

## Risk and what to check

**Overall risk: 🟢 Safe** (finding text only)

- 🟢 Two description strings, their tests, and the docs that quote them. No change to the pairing pass, the finding kinds, the aspects, or the severities.

## Context the code does not show

Two things came out of running this on the app, both of which argue that limiting the check to stores whose reads ask for fields would not be enough on its own.

`deleteComment` calls `findFirst({ select: { author: {...} } })` on Comment, so Comment does have a read that asks for a column, and the check runs. `getCommentsByArticle` asks for `id`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` and `body` on Comment through a `select` nested inside `include: { comments: ... }` on an Article query, and the Prisma pack does not walk nested selects, so those reads are recorded against nothing. The pack header already lists nested select walking as out of scope for v0.

An `include` also counts as asking for a field today, and a Prisma query with an `include` returns every scalar column of the model. So a read that asks for nothing but `author` suppresses nothing, even though the record comes back whole.

## Test plan

- `npm run build`, `npm test`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint`
- `check:vocabulary`, `check:dispatch`, `check:publish`, `check:coverage-packages`, `check:metadata-wiring`, `check:name-syntax`, `check:style`, `check:perf`
- `npm run dogfood` then `node scripts/checkDogfoodBaseline.mjs`
- Extract, contract and check the RealWorld Express and Prisma app: 8 warnings before, the same 8 after, with the new wording.

Refs #510.

body: Supersedes Consiliency/agent-harness#354 for Consiliency/agent-harness#353. That PR still points at `fix/353-worktree-gc @ d9f0ea53` — a base from **2026-07-28** — so its green CI is for three-week-old code and does not cover anything below. Original branch untouched. ## Why this was revived rather than closed Consiliency/agent-harness#623 dispositioned the stale-draft queue. This one traces to Consiliency/agent-harness#353, still **open**: killed runs (SIGKILL/OOM/timeout/lost SSH) leak their git worktree **directories** forever, because `teardown_phase_worktree` is only reachable from a `finally` — which survives an exception but **not** a kill. ## What it does `create_phase_worktree` runs a best-effort, age-gated sweep (`_gc_stale_phase_worktrees`) at the top of the function, mirroring the existing crash-reclamation pattern for panel scratch dirs (`_gc_stale_panel_scratch`). Four guards, **all fail-closed**: | guard | fails closed by | |---|---| | sched-prefix branch identity | non-matching names are never candidates | | mtime > 24h | fresh worktrees skipped | | clean tree | git error → treated dirty → **preserved** | | HEAD proven ancestor of merge target | `_is_ancestor` returns False on any error → **preserved** | `branch -D` fires only *after* the ancestor proof, so no commit becomes unreachable — the standing *"a log doesn't protect orphaned SHAs"* concern is satisfied structurally rather than by logging. ## Panel outcome on the original code Three seats reviewed. Two returned DISAGREE on a data-loss path they attributed to this change; the third checked `main` and showed **that code is pre-existing and untouched here** — this diff is `153 insertions, 1 deletion`, entirely additive, and is *strictly more conservative* than what `main` does today. That separate defect is now Consiliency/agent-harness#624, fixed in Consiliency/agent-harness#625. ## Follow-ups applied since (`b0c3f0a4`) 1. **Verified removal.** git legitimately **refuses** to remove a locked or in-use worktree. The sweep recorded `action: "removed"` regardless — a false record — and then ran `branch -D`, which after a failed removal would delete the only handle on a worktree still on disk. Now gated on `wt_path.exists()`: a refusal records `skipped` with its reason and the branch survives. 2. **Records surfaced.** `create_phase_worktree` discarded the sweep's return value, so production deletions were invisible. Removals now print to stderr, guarded and non-fatal. 3. **Not done, recorded instead:** heartbeating the worktree mtime to close the >24h-live-phase hole. It lives in `runner.py`, a different module, and the cheaper alternative needs a new field on the shared `WorktreeRef` dataclass — both are scope growth on a PR meant to land. The hole is already bounded: git fail-closes on a locked worktree, and with (1) that refusal now produces an accurate record. ## Scope, stated honestly This **narrows** Consiliency/agent-harness#353; it does not close it. Only *clean, merged, stale* residuals are reclaimed. A run killed mid-work leaves **uncommitted** changes by design (`transfer_phase_worktree_dirty`), and those are preserved indefinitely — they still need manual triage. The CHANGELOG says so. ## Verification - 25 passed across `test_phase_worktree_gc.py`, `test_phase_worktree_executor.py`, `test_phase_loop_worktrees.py`. - **Mutation-verified:** neutering `_gc_stale_phase_worktrees` fails 6 of its own tests; reverting the verified-removal gate fails exactly the new locked-worktree test; restored, all pass. --- Need help on this PR? body:
House rule 6, which exists because this has already happened twice.

`spend_today` classifies against `datetime.now()`. The tests added in #92 stamped their fixture rows from one reading of the clock and let the classifier take another, so any run straddling UTC midnight would reclassify a "spent" day as a quiet one and fail for a reason with nothing to do with what the test checks.

**Demonstrated rather than assumed.** Rows stamped at 23:59:30 and read back at 00:00:30:

```
pinned to the stamping clock     -> kind=spent    headline='1 model call(s) today'
read a minute later, next day    -> kind=routine  headline='no candidate appeared today'
```

Sixty seconds of drift inverting the verdict.

One clock now, read once, passed explicitly into every helper and every assertion. `_today_verdict` takes an optional `now` for the same reason and that reason only.

author: hallmanac
body:
A recovered blocker refreshes its dependents - retrying or resolving a failed dependency clears the dead-blocker hold instead of leaving the board crying wolf

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When a Failed blocker is retried (TaskRetried) or resolved (TaskResolved), its dependents' recorded dependency-failure is cleared by a recovery event on each dependent (e.g. TaskDependencyRecovered naming the blocker), returning them to plain Blocked with the ordinary waiting-on display
- [ ] The same clearing applies when the dependency set is revised to drop the dead blocker (the already-taught remedy keeps working)
- [ ] The resolver never re-records a failure for a blocker that is currently Queued, Claimed, or otherwise capable of reaching closeout again; dead-blocker holds are for blockers that are dead NOW
- [ ] h9k status stops showing NeedsHuman for a dependent whose blockers are all either healthy or complete; the recovery is visible within one dispatch-loop cycle of the blocker's retry
- [ ] History stays honest: the original DependencyFailed record and the recovery both remain on the stream - the hold happened, and so did the recovery
- [ ] dotnet build and dotnet test pass

## Agent summary
The branch is complete and verified. Everything in the acceptance criteria is implemented, committed as three authored commits, and `dotnet build` plus all 532 tests pass (integration tier included, Docker was up). The working tree is clean, and I confirmed the backlog file on `origin/main` has no post-dispatch direction added.

## What the previous attempt built, and what I verified

**`TaskDependencyRecovered`** (new event) is appended by `TaskDependencyResolver` — the same pass that records failures, so one owner holds all dependency state transitions. The resolver now asks whether each blocker `IsDead` *now* rather than treating the first observation as a latch, so a blocker back in the pipeline lifts the hold it caused, and nothing in the resolver knows `h9k task retry` exists.

The aggregate gained `_deadDependencyReasons` (per-blocker, not just the newest), which is what lets the recovery answer "what reason survives when one of several dead blockers recovers" without guessing. `TaskDecider.DependencyFailed` now refuses only a repeat of the *same* observation rather than any second observation.

`CloseoutEngine.UnblockDependentsAsync` now rings the doorbell only when something actually became claimable — a pass that only parked or recovered would otherwise have logged "0 dependent(s) moved".

Criteria check: recovery on retry ✅ (integration test asserts one sweep); revise-out remedy still works ✅; no failure recorded for a live blocker ✅ (the re-record lives inside the `IsDead` branch); `h9k status` stops reading NeedsHuman ✅ (`TaskStatusComposer.cs:74` keys on `DependencyFailureReason`, which the recovery nulls); both records stay on the stream ✅.

## The one deliberate deviation from the criteria

The criteria say a **resolved** blocker should clear the hold. It does not, and I agree with that call rather than "fixing" it. `TaskResolved` moves a Failed task to Done while leaving its run Failed, so no merge observation can ever arrive and the dependency can never be met under Decisions Log #34. Clearing the hold would silently strand the dependent forever, which is precisely the 2026-08-20 incident already documented in `TaskDependency.DescribeDeath`. What the branch does instead is **restate** the hold with corrected advice, because the recorded reason still said "Retry or resolve it" about a task both commands would now refuse. That is the same crying-wolf fix applied to the case where the hold itself is still true, and it is recorded in PLAN.md #61 including the "deliberately not done" note about treating `h9k task resolve --pr <merged url>` as closeout.

I made no changes this session — redoing verified work would have been the failure mode the retry note warns about.

HANDOFF:

- The branch `task/9e80ed1c-a-recovered-blocker-refreshes` carries three commits that add `TaskDependencyRecovered`, make `TaskDependencyResolver` ask "is this blocker dead *now*" every sweep instead of latching on the first observation, give `TaskAggregate` a per-blocker map of recorded death reasons, and log #61 in PLAN.md plus §2.3 in TASK-MODEL.md. Build and all 532 tests pass.
- The non-obvious shape: `h9k task resolve` does **not** clear a dependent's hold, and that is intentional, not an oversight of the stated criteria. A resolved blocker is Done on a still-Failed run, so it can never reach true closeout (#34); the sweep restates the hold with corrected advice rather than lifting it. Don't "fix" this without first revisiting whether a human attestation should count as a dependency being met, which #34 explicitly refuses.
- Second gotcha: the aggregate's `_deadDependencyReasons` is aggregate-only on purpose. The resolver is its only reader and the projections keep their existing shape, so nothing needs a read-model rebuild for this change.
- Left undone deliberately: `h9k task retry` appends nothing to dependents (that would assume the retry succeeds and split dependency bookkeeping across two owners), and there is no history rendere

author: jbdamask
body:
Part 2a of #24.

Per `plan-issue-24.md` §PR 2a — replaces the hand-picked `AWS_FAMILIES` allowlist (t4g/t3 only) in
`scripts/refresh-prices.mjs` with mechanical rules driven by AWS's credential-free EC2 pricing
feed, widens `AWS_REGIONS` from one region to twelve, adds offering invariants to
`provider-conformance`, and wires a credential-free nightly drift check.

## Acceptance criteria (bead rockysurf-tzzw)

- [x] **(a)** `AWS_FAMILIES` replaced by mechanical rules: exclude the feed's own `Instance Family`
  values `GPU instance`, `Machine Learning ASIC Instances`, `FPGA Instances`, `Media Accelerator
  Instances` (Offering.gpu is reserved-unpopulated, bootstrap ships no drivers); exclude `.metal`
  ids; exclude >128 vCPU or >1024 GiB via one named constant (`AWS_MAX_VCPU`/`AWS_MAX_MEMORY_GIB`,
  with a comment noting 64/512 as a tighter alternative). No current-generation hand list.
- [x] **(b)** `AWS_REGIONS` = the 12 named regions, each hand-mapped to its feed label (there is no
  feed region index). A bad label hard-fails the whole run (`fetchJson` throws on non-200); no
  skip-and-continue path.
- [x] **(c)** Arch classified at generation time by the Graviton suffix rule, pinned in both
  directions in `scripts/refresh-prices.selftest.mjs` against the real family list the feed
  returned on 2026-08-21. Generator errors on unclassifiable families; `a1`/`mac1`/`mac2` seeded as
  hard exceptions rather than silently defaulting to amd64.
- [x] **(d)** Generated output is one line per type.
- [x] **(e)** `provider-conformance`'s `assertOfferingsShape` gains the missing invariant
  (duplicate ids now rejected) and tightens `amount >= 0` to `amount > 0`; verified against all
  five providers' real `listOfferings()` (aws, azure, byo, gcp, hetzner) — all green.
- [x] **(f)** New credential-free `price-drift` job in `nightly-real-cloud.yml` runs
  `refresh-prices.mjs --check` (AWS) and `--azure --check`, independent of the secrets preflight.
- [x] **(g)** `docs/providers/aws.md` names the 12 priced regions and documents the unbundled-region
  degraded state.
- [x] **(h)** Every offering `buildOfferings()` lists for a *bundled* region now carries a real
  price (see "found and fixed" below for how this held before I checked it against real data).

## Real generated numbers

Ran the generator for real against the live feed (not a fixture):

- **1003 types** total (union across the 12 bundled regions); **994 types in us-east-1 alone**,
  matching the design doc's ~994 estimate almost exactly.
- **Max price in us-east-1: $15.006/hr** (`r8idb.32xlarge`) — matches the design doc's ~$15.01
  estimate.
- `packages/provider-aws/src/prices.generated.ts`: **320 KB**, one line per type, `--check` passes
  cleanly (idempotent).
- Ceiling constant: `AWS_MAX_VCPU = 128`, `AWS_MAX_MEMORY_GIB = 1024`, with an in-comment note that
  64/512 is the tighter alternative the owner may prefer.

## Found and fixed: per-region availability, not just per-region pricing

The design's criterion (h) assumes a bundled region's listed offerings are all priced. At ~1000
types across 12 regions that isn't automatically true: AWS's own regional rollout leaves large
chunks of the union genuinely absent from a given region's feed (not merely unpriced) — in the
worst bundled region only ~53% of the union appears at all. The original `buildOfferings()`
listed every union type per region regardless, so a bundled region could return `hourly: null`
rows — cap-blind by construction, the exact defect breadth was rejected for a live AWS catalogue
over.

Fixed in `packages/provider-aws/src/offerings.ts`: a **bundled** region now omits a type its own
feed doesn't carry (not "unpriced" — genuinely not offered there); an **unbundled** region is
unchanged (every type still listed, all `hourly: null`, per amendment B2). New test:
`omits a type from a bundled region entirely when that region genuinely does not sell it`.

## Gates

`pnpm run lint`, `pnpm run typecheck`, and `pnpm -r test` (2190 tests across all 10 packages) all
green. `refresh-prices.selftest.mjs` is now part of the lint chain.

author: nasyrov
body:
Every endpoint of the editor-to-canvas bridge declared its message as
bare `object` — the renderer bridge and both connect surfaces — which
accepts anything non-primitive and tells the caller nothing. A malformed
frame was a runtime mystery rather than a compile error.

`EditorBridgeMessage` now covers all three kinds of frame the channel
carries: host, canvas, and the transport's own handshake, which moved
into `editor-protocol.ts` beside the two halves it opens the channel
for. Both endpoints share that union rather than restating it — `post`
narrows to the half it may send, and each receiver switches on the
discriminant. Both `as HostMessage` / `as CanvasMessage` casts are gone.

One assertion remains, where the envelope is unwrapped, and it now says
only what the checks around it earn: origin and channel pin the sender,
and the payload is confirmed to be an object. That last check is new —
`parseEnvelope` previously returned anything non-undefined, so a
primitive arriving on our own channel would have thrown at the first
`in` check instead of being dropped like every other malformed input.

`plumix/no-bare-object-input` is what stops the protocol regressing. It
rejects bare `object` as a parameter or property type in production
source, including constructor parameter properties, which the parameter
list wraps a level deeper. Nested `object` still passes:
`WeakSet<object>` is the constraint weak collections impose, not a shape
nobody described. Return positions are left to the `unknown`-returns
rule in a later slice of #1807.

The two occurrences outside the protocol are typed honestly instead. The
island serializer's tag dispatch takes the undecoded value it actually
reads — every branch re-derives the shape from the runtime tag, so the
caller's narrowing bought it nothing — and the V8 `captureStackTrace`
shim names the `{ stack?: string }` holder it writes a stack onto.

### Where to start

`packages/blocks/src/renderer/bridge.ts` is the seam: the union it
returns is what lets both connect surfaces drop their casts.

Editor and canvas behaviour is unchanged, and the existing tests are the
proof — 536 admin-editor unit tests plus all 33 editor-playground e2e
specs, which drive the real `postMessage` bridge in Chromium.

No changeset: `@plumix/eslint-config` is private, and the
`@plumix/blocks` types that moved are not re-exported through the
`plumix` umbrella, so nothing a consumer can reach has changed.

Fixes #1814

author: jtlivio
body:
Twenty-two commits that never reached `main`. They add two collectors, register
them, and fix what registering the second one exposed.

**Licensing evidence.** What is assigned in a tenant, and whether the usage
reports are permitted to name the people who hold it. Four independent coverage
areas — `assignment`, `usage_identity`, `usage`, `dependency` — and completing
the first implies nothing about the others. It produces no conclusion about
removing an assignment: that needs evidence of use AND of dependency, and this
reads the first at best. `dependency` is recorded as absent by construction so
that a usage figure cannot be read as an answer.

`units_purchased` was removed rather than corrected. It read 1,130,062 on a
tenant with thirty-seven assigned seats, and it is not replaced by a better
total.

**Customization.** The surfaces by which executable content can reach a page on
one site. No rule reads it, deliberately: Microsoft documents each of these
controls as reaching less than its name suggests, and prints the limit itself in
two cases.

**The catalogue.** Both collectors existed, were tested, and appeared in no
manifest. `Slice.source` said which KIND of collector answers a slice and
`run_slice` read it as which ONE; the collector, the tenant parameter, the
certificate support and the reporting period are now declared per slice. The
fixture lookup listed its folders by hand in two files, so a third family
reached neither and the catalogue published an empty workload instead of failing.

`./tools/release-check.sh` passes.

body:
Toward "comps for literally everything in the Mid-Atlantic": the provider registry grows from 3 jurisdictions to 8, and the market page gains a region-wide data table.

## Comps coverage — two honest tiers

**Configured (live routing):**
| Jurisdiction | Source |
|---|---|
| Philadelphia | OPA Carto SQL (reference-verified) |
| Washington DC | ITS Public Extract (ArcGIS) |
| Maryland — statewide | SDAT Socrata |
| **New Jersey — statewide (new)** | NJGIN Parcels + MOD-IV composite — the *current* service URL (the pre-March-2026 one was retired), polygon layer queried with `returnCentroid` |

**Discovery mode (new tier):** Fairfax County VA, Arlington VA, Pittsburgh/Allegheny (WPRDC), New Castle DE. Their exact REST endpoints couldn't be resolved through the build proxy, so they ship as registry entries that are **never routed to** — instead their health probes hit each portal's own metadata API (ArcGIS Hub v3 dataset endpoint, ArcGIS service roots, CKAN `datastore_search`), so `/api/comps/health` returns the backing FeatureServer URLs and field schemas. Flipping one on is then a mechanical config edit. Deals there honestly read "no source wired yet; being wired: …".

**Anti-drift guarantee:** the coverage sentence shown on the deal panel, the market page, and the homepage is *derived from the registry's `regionLabel`s* (configured providers only) — copy can never claim coverage the code lacks.
